Your company follows Site Reliability Engineering principles. You are preparing a postmortem for an incident caused by a software change that severely impacted users. You want to prevent a severe incident from occurring again in the future. What should you do?

options.text: Identify engineers responsible for the incident and escalate to the senior management.
Ensure that test cases that catch errors of this type are run successfully before new software releases.
Follow up with the employees who reviewed the changes and prescribe practices they should follow in the future.
Design a policy that will require on-call teams to immediately call engineers and management to discuss a plan of action if an incident occurs.

questions.explanation:
SRE postmortems should result in blameless, concrete preventative action items that improve systems and processes. Requiring successful pre-release execution of test cases that detect the relevant error type directly reduces the likelihood that the same software-change failure reaches users. Google SRE guidance recommends preventative fixes and emphasizes that changing automated systems and processes is more reliable than trying to change human behavior.

**Learn more:** [Google SRE Workbook: Postmortem Culture: Learning from Failure](https://sre.google/workbook/postmortem-culture/)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are designing a hosting architecture in Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) for business-critical applications. The applications expose custom metrics for monitoring with Prometheus. You need to collect the application metrics for alerting and troubleshooting. You want to minimize manual effort and ongoing maintenance while following Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Install Prometheus servers in the GKE clusters. Configure Prometheus to scrape and forward the custom metrics to the Cloud Monitoring API.
Install the OpenTelemetry collector in the GKE clusters. Configure it to collect and export the custom metrics to Cloud Monitoring.
Modify each application to use the Cloud Monitoring API to push the custom metrics.
Configure Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus collection in the GKE clusters to collect the custom metrics.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus managed collection is Google’s recommended approach for Kubernetes environments. It collects Prometheus metrics from GKE workloads while the managed Kubernetes operator handles collector deployment, scrape configuration, scaling, and related operational maintenance; the collected data supports Cloud Monitoring querying and alerting.

**Learn more:** [Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus](https://docs.cloud.google.com/stackdriver/docs/managed-prometheus) · [Get started with managed collection](https://docs.cloud.google.com/stackdriver/docs/managed-prometheus/setup-managed?hl=en)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company runs services using Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). The GKE clusters in the development environment run applications with verbose logging enabled. Developers inspect logs by using the `kubectl logs` command and do not use Cloud Logging. Applications do not have a defined uniform logging structure.  
  
You need to minimize the costs associated with application logging while continuing to collect GKE operational logs. What should you do?

options.text: Run the gcloud container clusters update --logging=SYSTEM command for the development cluster.
Run the gcloud container clusters update --logging=WORKLOAD command for the development cluster.
Run the gcloud logging sinks update _Default --disabled command in the project associated with the development environment.
Add the severity >= DEBUG resource.type =

questions.explanation:
GKE `SYSTEM` logging collects system logs required for cluster operations, while `WORKLOAD` logging collects logs generated by non-system application containers. Configuring the development cluster with `--logging=SYSTEM` prevents verbose application workload logs from being ingested into Cloud Logging while preserving GKE operational/system logs. [About GKE logs](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/about-logs)

**Learn more:** [About GKE logs](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/about-logs)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are configuring a CI/CD pipeline natively in Google Cloud. You want builds in a pre-production Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) environment to be automatically load-tested before promotion to the production GKE environment. You must ensure that only builds that pass this test are deployed to production. You want to follow Google-recommended practices. How should you configure this pipeline with Binary Authorization?

options.text: Create an attestation for the builds that pass the load test by requiring the lead quality assurance engineer to sign the attestation by using their personal private key.
Create an attestation for the builds that pass the load test by using a private key stored in Cloud Key Management Service (Cloud KMS) with a service account JSON key stored as a Kubernetes Secret.
Create an attestation for the builds that pass the load test by using a private key stored in Cloud Key Management Service (Cloud KMS) authenticated through Workload Identity.

Create an attestation for the builds that pass the load test by requiring the lead quality assurance engineer to sign the attestation by using a key stored in Cloud Key Management Service (Cloud KMS).

questions.explanation:
Binary Authorization can require a trusted attestation before an image is deployed to production. An automated load-test workload should create the attestation only after the test succeeds, using an asymmetric signing key held in Cloud KMS. Workload Identity Federation for GKE is the recommended way for a GKE workload to obtain the IAM authorization needed to use Google Cloud APIs, avoiding less-secure, long-lived service account JSON keys stored as Kubernetes Secrets.

**Learn more:** [Create a Binary Authorization attestation in a Cloud Build pipeline](https://cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/cloud-build) · [About Workload Identity Federation for GKE](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/workload-identity)

",["$","$L54",null,{"choices":{"A":"A scalable in-memory caching system.","B":"The organization's public-facing website.","C":"A distributed, eventually consistent NoSQL database cluster with sufficient quorum.","D":"A GPU-accelerated video rendering platform that retrieves and stores videos in a storage bucket."},"correctAnswer":"D","explanation":"Preemptible VMs may be stopped without notice, so they are appropriate for fault-tolerant batch workloads that can be retried. 50:[["$","p",null,{"children":"Your company follows Site Reliability Engineering principles. You are preparing a postmortem for an incident caused by a software change that severely impacted users. You want to prevent a severe incident from occurring again in the future. What should you do?"}],"
",["$","$L54",null,{"choices":{"A":"Identify engineers responsible for the incident and escalate to the senior management.","B":"Ensure that test cases that catch errors of this type are run successfully before new software releases.","C":"Follow up with the employees who reviewed the changes and prescribe practices they should follow in the future.","D":"Design a policy that will require on-call teams to immediately call engineers and management to discuss a plan of action if an incident occurs."},"correctAnswer":"B","explanation":"SRE postmortems should result in blameless, concrete preventative action items that improve systems and processes. Requiring successful pre-release execution of test cases that detect the relevant error type directly reduces the likelihood that the same software-change failure reaches users. Google SRE guidance recommends preventative fixes and emphasizes that changing automated systems and processes is more reliable than trying to change human behavior.

**Learn more:** [Google SRE Workbook: Postmortem Culture: Learning from Failure](https://sre.google/workbook/postmortem-culture/)","trackingInfo":{"questionId":"9e99b129-9569-4de3-ab66-707bffb85967","examProvider":"google","examName":"professional-cloud-devops-engineer","mode":"default"}}]]

",["$","$L54",null,{"choices":{"A":"Create an attestation for the builds that pass the load test by requiring the lead quality assurance engineer to sign the attestation by using their personal private key.","B":"Create an attestation for the builds that pass the load test by using a private key stored in Cloud Key Management Service (Cloud KMS) with a service account JSON key stored as a Kubernetes Secret.","C":"Create an attestation for the builds that pass the load test by using a private key stored in Cloud Key Management Service (Cloud KMS) authenticated through Workload Identity.","D":"Create an attestation for the builds that pass the load test by requiring the lead quality assurance engineer to sign the attestation by using a key stored in Cloud Key Management Service (Cloud KMS)."},"correctAnswer":"C","explanation":"Binary Authorization can require a trusted attestation before an image is deployed to production. You support the backend for a mobile phone game running on a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster. The application serves HTTP requests from users.  
  
You need to implement a solution to reduce network costs. What should you do?

options.text: Configure the VPC as a Shared VPC Host project.
Configure your network services on the Standard Tier.
Configure your Kubernetes cluster as a Private Cluster.
Configure a Google Cloud HTTP Load Balancer as Ingress.

questions.explanation:
For HTTP traffic, GKE Ingress provisions an external Application Load Balancer. With container-native load balancing, the load balancer targets Pod endpoints directly through network endpoint groups, avoiding the extra load-balancing hop through a node and its NodePort. External GKE Ingress/Application Load Balancers do not support Standard Tier routing.

**Learn more:** [Best practices for running cost-optimized Kubernetes applications on GKE](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/best-practices-for-running-cost-effective-kubernetes-applications-on-gke) · [Configure external traffic with Network Service Tiers](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/network-tiers)

You need to enforce multiple constraint templates across your Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) clusters. The constraints include policy parameters, such as restrictions on the Kubernetes API. You must ensure that the policy parameters are kept in a GitHub repository and are automatically applied when changes occur. What should you do?

options.text: Set up a GitHub action to trigger Cloud Build when there is a parameter change. In Cloud Build, run a gcloud CLI command to apply the change.
When there is a change in GitHub. use a web hook to send a request to Anthos Service Mesh, and apply the change.
Configure Anthos Config Management with the GitHub repository. When there is a change in the repository, use Anthos Config Management to apply the change.
Configure Config Connector with the GitHub repository. When there is a change in the repository, use Config Connector to apply the change.

questions.explanation:
Anthos Config Management provides GitOps-based configuration management for Kubernetes clusters: it uses the Git repository as the source of truth and reconciles repository changes into the enrolled clusters. Constraint templates and parameterized Policy Controller constraints can therefore be versioned in GitHub and automatically applied consistently across GKE clusters.

**Learn more:** [Safe rollouts with Config Sync](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/config-sync/docs/tutorials/safe-rollouts-with-config-sync) · [Constraint template library | Policy Controller](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/policy-controller/docs/latest/reference/constraint-template-library)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization is beginning to containerize with Google Cloud. You require a fully managed storage solution for container images and Helm charts. Identify a storage solution with native integration with existing Google Cloud services, including Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), Cloud Run, VPC Service Controls, and Identity and Access Management (IAM). What should you do?

options.text: Use Docker to configure a Cloud Storage driver pointed at the bucket owned by your organization.
Configure an open source container registry server to run in GKE with a restrictive role-based access control (RBAC) configuration.
Configure Artifact Registry as an OCI-based container registry for both Helm charts and container images.
Configure Container Registry as an OCI-based container registry for container images.

questions.explanation:
Artifact Registry is a fully managed Google Cloud artifact repository service that supports container images and Helm 3 charts stored as OCI artifacts in Docker repositories. It integrates with GKE and Cloud Run deployments, uses IAM for access control, and can be protected by VPC Service Controls.

**Learn more:** [Artifact Registry overview](https://cloud.google.com/artifact-registry/docs/overview) · [Work with Helm charts](https://cloud.google.com/artifact-registry/docs/helm)

questions.domain: Optimizing performance and cost
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You work for a global organization and run a monolithic application on Compute Engine. You need to choose a machine type for the application that optimizes CPU utilization with the fewest steps. You want to use historical system metrics to determine the machine type for the application and follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Use the Recommender API and apply the suggested recommendations.
Create an Agent Policy to automatically install Ops Agent in all VMs.
Install the Ops Agent in a fleet of VMs by using the gcloud CLI.
Review the Cloud Monitoring dashboard for the VM and choose the machine type with the lowest CPU utilization.

questions.explanation:
Compute Engine machine type rightsizing recommendations use historical CPU and memory utilization metrics to identify a suitable VM machine type. The Recommender API exposes these recommendations programmatically, providing the direct Google-recommended method for selecting and applying a rightsizing recommendation.

**Learn more:** [Apply machine type recommendations to VM instances](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/apply-machine-type-recommendations-for-instances) · [Use the Recommender API](https://docs.cloud.google.com/recommender/docs/use-api)

questions.domain: Implementing observability practices and troubleshooting issues
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are diagnosing an issue with an application running in a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster that has Binary Authorization enabled. You need to run a temporary Pod for troubleshooting by using an unsigned utility container image from Artifact Registry. When you try to apply the Pod configuration from a YAML file, the Binary Authorization policy blocks the deployment. You must use the most secure and auditable solution to run the Pod. What should you do?

options.text: Change enforcementMode in the Binary Authorization policy to ALWAYS_ALLOW.
Add the imaqe-policy.k8s.io/break-glass label to the Pod configuration.
Temporarily disable Binary Authorization on the GKE cluster.
Add the container image to the admissionWhitelistPatterns node in the Binary Authorization policy.

questions.explanation:
Binary Authorization breakglass is an emergency, Pod-specific policy override enabled with the `image-policy.k8s.io/break-glass: "true"` label. It permits the otherwise denied image for that deployment while automatically recording a breakglass event in Cloud Audit Logs, preserving an auditable exception without weakening cluster-wide policy.

**Learn more:** [Use breakglass (GKE, Distributed Cloud)](https://cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/using-breakglass) · [View audit logs for GKE](https://cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/viewing-audit-logs)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You use Terraform to manage an application deployed in a Google Cloud environment. The application runs on instances deployed by a managed instance group. The Terraform code is deployed through a CI/CD pipeline. When you change the machine type on the instance template used by the managed instance group, the pipeline fails during the `terraform apply` stage with the following error message:  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783848187263-brikxzqc.png)  
  
You need to update the instance template while minimizing disruption to the application and the number of pipeline runs.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Delete the managed instance group, and recreate it after updating the instance template.
Add a new instance template, update the managed instance group to use the new instance template, and delete the old instance template.
Remove the managed instance group from the Terraform state file, update the instance template, and reimport the managed instance group.
Set the create_before_destroy meta-argument to true in the lifecycle block on the instance template.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud does not allow deletion of an instance template while a managed instance group references it. Setting `create_before_destroy = true` in the instance template resource’s `lifecycle` block makes Terraform create the replacement template before destroying the existing one, allowing the managed instance group to switch references first and avoiding the failed deletion order.

**Learn more:** [Get, list, and delete instance templates — Compute Engine](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instance-templates/get-list-delete-instance-templates) · [Lifecycle meta-argument reference — Terraform](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/meta-arguments/lifecycle)

options.text: 1. Install a Git hook to require developers to run unit tests before pushing the code to a central repository.2. Trigger Cloud Build to build the application container. Deploy the application container to a testing environment, and run integration tests.3. If the integration tests are successful, deploy the application container to your production environment, and run acceptance tests.

Trigger Cloud Build to build and deploy the application container to the production environment.

If the integration tests are successful, the pipeline deploys the application container to the production environment. After that, run acceptance tests.

1. Trigger Cloud Build to run unit tests when the code is pushed. If all unit tests are successful, build and push the application container to a central registry.2. Trigger Cloud Build to deploy the container to a testing environment, and run integration tests and acceptance tests.3. If all tests are successful, the pipeline deploys the application to the production environment and runs smoke tests

questions.explanation:
Cloud Build triggers can start CI/CD workflows in response to source-code changes. A sound pipeline runs unit tests on each push, builds and stores the container image only after those tests pass, deploys that tested image to a test environment for integration and acceptance tests, and promotes it to production only when those tests succeed. Smoke tests after production deployment verify that the deployed application is operational.

**Learn more:** [Overview of Cloud Build](https://cloud.google.com/build/docs/overview) · [CI/CD pipeline for developing and delivering containerized apps](https://cloud.google.com/architecture/app-development-and-delivery-with-cloud-code-gcb-cd-and-gke)

Your team is getting ready to launch a new API on Cloud Run. The API uses an OpenTelemetry agent to send distributed tracing data to Cloud Trace to monitor how long each request takes. The team has observed inconsistent trace collection. You need to fix the issue. What should you do?

options.text: Use an HTTP health check.
Configure CPU to be always-allocated.
Increase the CPU limit in Cloud Run from 2 to 4.
Configure CPU to be allocated only during request processing.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Run instance-based billing, formerly called CPU always allocated, provides CPU even outside request processing. This supports background and asynchronous work performed by monitoring agents such as OpenTelemetry, preventing trace-export work from being paused after a response is returned.

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company’s security team requires read-only access to Data Access audit logs in the `_Required` bucket. You want to grant the required permissions to the security team according to the principle of least privilege and Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Assign the roles/logging.viewer role to each member of the security team.
Assign the roles/logging.viewer role to a group with all the security team members.
Assign the roles/logging.privateLogViewer role to each member of the security team.
Assign the roles/logging.privateLogViewer role to a group with all the security team members.

questions.explanation:
The Private Logs Viewer role (`roles/logging.privateLogViewer`) grants read-only access to Data Access audit logs, whereas Logs Viewer does not. Granting that role to a group containing the security team follows Google Cloud IAM guidance to manage shared access through groups instead of individual user grants.

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are conducting an experiment to determine whether users like a new feature in a web application. Soon after deploying the feature as a canary release, you see a spike in 500 errors returned to users, and monitoring indicates higher latency. You want to minimize the negative effect on users as quickly as possible. What should you do first?

options.text: Roll back the experimental canary release.
Start monitoring latency, traffic, errors, and saturation.
Record data for the postmortem document of the incident.
Trace the origin of 500 errors and the root cause of increased latency.

questions.explanation:
A canary deployment that correlates with a sharp rise in user-facing errors and latency should be rolled back immediately to stop exposing users to the suspected faulty release. Rollback is the fastest mitigation; monitoring, root-cause investigation, and postmortem documentation follow once user impact is contained.

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You manage a Google Cloud environment for 20 different business units, with 50 production projects and 50 development projects located directly under the organization node. This flat hierarchy makes it hard to apply security policies consistently to all production projects and to track the combined costs of the production and development environments separately. You need to reorganize the resource hierarchy to address these issues. What should you do?

options.text: Create folders for the production and development environments, and move the projects into these folders.
Create a folder for each business unit, and move the corresponding projects into these folders.
Apply labels for each environment to each project to identify the environment.
Create a common services project for each business unit.

questions.explanation:
Folders organize projects into logical groups such as environments and serve as policy-inheritance points. A production folder and a development folder let environment-specific IAM and organization policies apply consistently to every child project, while separating the projects into environment groups for cost organization and reporting.

**Learn more:** [About resource hierarchy | Resource Manager | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/resource-manager/docs/cloud-platform-resource-hierarchy) · [Manage projects within folders | Resource Manager | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/resource-manager/docs/manage-projects-within-folder)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are deploying an application that requires access to sensitive information. You need to make sure this information is encrypted and that the risk of exposure is minimized in the event of a breach. What should you do?

options.text: Store the encryption keys in Cloud Key Management Service (KMS) and rotate the keys frequently
Inject the secret at the time of instance creation via an encrypted configuration management system.
Integrate the application with a Single sign-on (SSO) system and do not expose secrets to the application.
Leverage a continuous build pipeline that produces multiple versions of the secret for each instance of the application.

questions.explanation:
The recommended approach is to keep secrets out of source code, container images, and build pipelines, and instead deliver them securely to each instance only when it is created. Using an encrypted configuration management system to inject the secret at instance creation time ensures the secret remains encrypted at rest and in transit until it is needed, limits its exposure to only the specific running instance, and avoids storing plaintext credentials in images, logs, or version control — thereby minimizing the blast radius if a breach occurs. This aligns with Google Cloud's guidance on secret management, which emphasizes retrieving secrets at runtime/deploy time through secure, access-controlled channels rather than embedding them in artifacts or exposing them broadly.

**Learn more:** [Secret Manager documentation - Google Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/secret-manager/docs) · [Best practices for using Secret Manager](https://cloud.google.com/secret-manager/docs/best-practices)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are developing an application that runs on Cloud Run. The application must access a third-party API using an API key. You need to identify a secure method to store and use the API key in the application while following Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Save the API key in Secret Manager as a secret. Reference the secret as an environment variable in the Cloud Run application.
Save the API key in Secret Manager as a secret key. Mount the secret key under the /sys/api_key directory, and decrypt the key in the Cloud Run application.
Save the API key in Cloud Key Management Service (Cloud KMS) as a key. Reference the key as an environment variable in the Cloud Run application.
Encrypt the API key by using Cloud Key Management Service (Cloud KMS), and pass the key to Cloud Run as an environment variable. Decrypt and use the key in Cloud Run.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud recommends storing sensitive dependency values, including API keys, in Secret Manager. Cloud Run can expose a Secret Manager secret to the container as a secret-backed environment variable, with access controlled through the service identity's Secret Manager permissions.

**Learn more:** [Configure secrets for services | Cloud Run](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/configuring/services/secrets)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A team is developing a service that performs compute-intensive processing on batches of data. Data is processed more quickly according to the machine's CPU speed and CPU count. These data batches vary in size and can arrive at any time from multiple third-party sources. You must ensure that third parties can upload their data securely. You want to minimize costs while ensuring the data is processed as quickly as possible. What should you do?

options.text: Provide a secure file transfer protocol (SFTP) server on a Compute Engine instance so that third parties can upload batches of data, and provide appropriate credentials to the server.Create a Cloud Function with a google.storage.object.finalize Cloud Storage trigger. Write code so that the function can scale up a Compute Engine autoscaling managed instance groupUse an image pre-loaded with the data processing software that terminates the instances when processing completes.

Provide a Cloud Storage bucket so that third parties can upload batches of data, and provide appropriate Identity and Access Management (IAM) access to the bucket.Use a standard Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster and maintain two services: one that processes the batches of data, and one that monitors Cloud Storage for new batches of data.Stop the processing service when there are no batches of data to process.

Provide a Cloud Storage bucket so that third parties can upload batches of data, and provide appropriate Identity and Access Management (IAM) access to the bucket.Create a Cloud Function with a google.storage.object.finalize Cloud Storage trigger. Write code so that the function can scale up a Compute Engine autoscaling managed instance group.Use an image pre-loaded with the data processing software that terminates the instances when processing completes.

Provide a Cloud Storage bucket so that third parties can upload batches of data, and provide appropriate Identity and Access Management (IAM) access to the bucket.Use Cloud Monitoring to detect new batches of data in the bucket and trigger a Cloud Function that processes the data.Set a Cloud Function to use the largest CPU possible to minimize the runtime of the processing.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Storage provides a secure upload destination controlled with IAM permissions. A Cloud Storage object-finalize event can initiate processing when a new batch is uploaded. Compute Engine managed instance groups can autoscale by adding VMs as demand increases and removing them as demand falls; an instance template can supply the preinstalled processing software. This matches an irregular, CPU-bound batch workload while avoiding continuously running processing capacity.

**Learn more:** [Upload objects from a file system | Cloud Storage](https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/uploading-objects) · [Autoscaling groups of instances | Compute Engine](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/autoscaler)

You are configuring a CI pipeline in Cloud Build. When you test the pipeline, the following `cloudbuild.yaml` definition results in 5 minutes for each of the `foo` and `bar` steps.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783888158862-frd9ku51.png)  
  
The `foo` and `bar` steps are independent of one another. The `baz` step requires both the `foo` and `bar` steps to complete before it starts. You want to use parallelism to reduce build times. What should you do?

options.text: Modify the build script to add -options:machineType: 'E2_HIGHCPU_8'
Modify the build script to add -options:machineType: 'E2_HIGHCPU_32'
![](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783888162854-mrs9dd3v.png)
![](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783888166396-qvn839x6.png)

questions.explanation:
Cloud Build steps execute sequentially by default. Setting the later independent step to `waitFor: ['-']` makes it start at build start alongside the first step. A subsequent step without `waitFor` waits for all preceding steps, or it can explicitly list both step IDs, so `baz` starts only after `foo` and `bar` succeed. [Configuring the order of build steps](https://docs.cloud.google.com/build/docs/configuring-builds/configure-build-step-order)

**Learn more:** [Configuring the order of build steps | Cloud Build](https://docs.cloud.google.com/build/docs/configuring-builds/configure-build-step-order)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You manage an application that exposes an HTTP endpoint without a load balancer. HTTP response latency is important to the user experience. You need to understand the HTTP latencies experienced by all of your users. You use Stackdriver Monitoring. What should you do?

options.text: ג€¢ In your application, create a metric with a metricKind set to DELTA and a valueType set to DOUBLE. ג€¢ In Stackdriver's Metrics Explorer, use a Stacked Bar graph to visualize the metric.
ג€¢ In your application, create a metric with a metricKind set to CUMULATIVE and a valueType set to DOUBLE. ג€¢ In Stackdriver's Metrics Explorer, use a Line graph to visualize the metric.
ג€¢ In your application, create a metric with a metricKind set to GAUGE and a valueType set to DISTRIBUTION. ג€¢ In Stackdriver's Metrics Explorer, use a Heatmap graph to visualize the metric.

ג€¢ In your application, create a metric with a metricKind set to METRIC_KIND_UNSPECIFIED and a valueType set to INT64. ג€¢ In Stackdriver's Metrics Explorer, use a Stacked Area graph to visualize the metric.

questions.explanation:
HTTP response latency is typically recorded as a distribution because it preserves the population of request durations in histogram buckets, allowing the latency experience across users to be analyzed. A `GAUGE` metric with a `DISTRIBUTION` value type is valid for this purpose, and a Heatmap displays a distribution-valued time series over time and latency buckets.

**Learn more:** [Value types and metric kinds | Cloud Monitoring](https://docs.cloud.google.com/monitoring/api/v3/kinds-and-types) · [About distribution-valued metrics | Cloud Monitoring](https://docs.cloud.google.com/monitoring/charts/charting-distribution-metrics)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are running an application on Compute Engine and collecting its logs through Stackdriver. You discover that some personally identifiable information (PII) is leaking into certain log entry fields. You want to prevent these fields from being written into new log entries as quickly as possible.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Use the filter-record-transformer Fluentd filter plugin to remove the fields from the log entries in flight.
Use the fluent-plugin-record-reformer Fluentd output plugin to remove the fields from the log entries in flight.
Wait for the application developers to patch the application, and then verify that the log entries are no longer exposing PII.
Stage log entries to Cloud Storage, and then trigger a Cloud Function to remove the fields and write the entries to Stackdriver via the Stackdriver Logging API.

questions.explanation:
The Stackdriver/Cloud Logging agent on Compute Engine is a Fluentd-based agent. You can edit its local configuration to insert the built-in `filter_record_transformer` filter plugin, which can remove or transform specific fields (using its `remove_keys` parameter) from log records as they flow through the agent, before they are ever sent to Cloud Logging. This is the fastest remediation because it only requires updating the Fluentd agent configuration on the instance and restarting the agent — it does not require an application code change, and it avoids the extra latency and engineering effort of an intermediate storage-and-processing pipeline.

**Learn more:** [record_transformer | Fluentd](https://docs.fluentd.org/filter/record_transformer) · [fluentd-docs-gitbook filter/record_transformer.md](https://github.com/fluent/fluentd-docs-gitbook/blob/1.0/filter/record_transformer.md)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to establish SLOs for a high-traffic web application. Customers are currently satisfied with the application's performance and availability. Current measurements over a 28-day window show a 90th-percentile latency of 160 ms and a 95th-percentile latency of 300 ms. What latency SLO should you publish?

options.text: 90th percentile - 150 ms95th percentile - 290 ms
90th percentile - 160 ms95th percentile - 300 ms
90th percentile - 190 ms95th percentile - 330 ms
90th percentile - 300 ms95th percentile - 450 ms

questions.explanation:
Latency SLO thresholds should reflect the level of performance at which users are satisfied, with modest headroom above current observed percentile latency to accommodate ordinary variation. A 190 ms p90 target and a 330 ms p95 target retain a meaningful performance commitment without setting the objective exactly at the current baseline. Google Cloud guidance defines SLOs around user happiness and recommends 28 days as a starting measurement period.

**Learn more:** [Overview — Google Cloud Observability](https://docs.cloud.google.com/stackdriver/docs/solutions/slo-monitoring/sli-metrics/overview) · [Concepts in service monitoring — Google Cloud Observability](https://docs.cloud.google.com/stackdriver/docs/solutions/slo-monitoring)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are the on-call Site Reliability Engineer for a microservice deployed in a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Autopilot cluster. Your company operates an online store that publishes order messages to Pub/Sub, and a microservice consumes those messages and updates stock information in the warehousing system. A sales event has increased orders, and stock information is not being updated fast enough. Consequently, many orders are being accepted for products that are out of stock. You review the microservice metrics and compare them with typical levels:  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783848807687-a4rcj26d.png)  
  
You must ensure the warehouse system accurately reflects product inventory when orders are placed while minimizing customer impact. What should you do?

options.text: Decrease the acknowledgment deadline on the subscription.
Add a virtual queue to the online store that allows typical traffic levels.
Increase the number of Pod replicas.
Increase the Pod CPU and memory limits.

questions.explanation:
Rising oldest-unacknowledged-message age together with a large increase in undelivered messages indicates that Pub/Sub subscribers are not keeping up with the message volume. Adding Pod replicas creates more concurrent subscriber instances and raises processing throughput, reducing the backlog and inventory-update delay. The Pods are not near their CPU or memory limits, so increasing those limits is not the relevant response.

**Learn more:** [Monitor Pub/Sub in Cloud Monitoring](https://docs.cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/monitoring) · [Troubleshooting a pull subscription](https://docs.cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/pull-troubleshooting)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your CTO has asked that you implement an internal postmortem policy for every incident. You want to define the characteristics of a good postmortem so that the policy succeeds at your company. What should you do? (Choose two.)

options.text: Ensure that all postmortems include what caused the incident, identify the person or team responsible for causing the incident, and how to prevent a future occurrence of the incident.
Ensure that all postmortems include what caused the incident, how the incident could have been worse, and how to prevent a future occurrence of the incident.
Ensure that all postmortems include the severity of the incident, how to prevent a future occurrence of the incident, and what caused the incident without naming internal system components.
Ensure that all postmortems include how the incident was resolved and what caused the incident without naming customer information.
Ensure that all postmortems include all incident participants in postmortem authoring and share postmortems as widely as possible.

questions.explanation:
Effective postmortems are blameless learning records: they analyze the causes of an incident, identify how its impact or outcome could be improved, and produce actions that prevent recurrence. Collaborative authorship by incident participants improves completeness, while broad internal sharing spreads the lessons learned and helps prevent similar incidents elsewhere. Google SRE guidance recommends blameless analysis, corrective actions, collaboration, and sharing postmortems as widely as possible.

**Learn more:** [Google SRE: Postmortem Culture—Learning from Failure](https://sre.google/sre-book/postmortem-culture/) · [Google SRE Workbook: Postmortem Culture](https://sre.google/workbook/postmortem-culture/)

You are troubleshooting problems in your production application running on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). You determined that a recently updated container image is the source of the issue, but the exact code change was not identified. The deployment currently points to the `latest` tag. You need to update the cluster so it runs a container version that functions as intended. What should you do?

options.text: Create a new tag called stable that points to the previously working container, and change the deployment to point to the new tag.
Alter the deployment to point to the sha256 digest of the previously working container.
Build a new container from a previous Git tag, and do a rolling update on the deployment to the new container.
Apply the latest tag to the previous container image, and do a rolling update on the deployment.

questions.explanation:
A `sha256` image digest is an immutable identifier for one specific container-image version, whereas tags such as `latest` can be moved to different images. Referencing the previously working image by digest pins the deployment to the known-good artifact and provides a reliable rollback target.

**Learn more:** [Kubernetes Documentation: Images](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/containers/images/)

questions.domain: Building and implementing CI/CD pipelines, including continuous testing, for application, infrastructure, and machine learning workloads
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your application runs on Google Cloud Platform (GCP), and you need to set up Jenkins to deploy application releases to GCP. Your goal is to streamline the release process, reduce operational toil, and keep user data secure. What should you do?

options.text: Implement Jenkins on local workstations.
Implement Jenkins on Kubernetes on-premises.
Implement Jenkins on Google Cloud Functions.
Implement Jenkins on Compute Engine virtual machines.

questions.explanation:
Compute Engine is the platform Google Cloud officially supports and documents for hosting Jenkins. The Google Compute Engine plugin for Jenkins allows the Jenkins controller to automatically provision build-agent VMs from instance templates when jobs need to run, and automatically delete those instances when idle—directly reducing operational toil compared to manually managing on-premises infrastructure or local workstations. Compute Engine also integrates with GCP's native security controls (IAM, service accounts, VPC firewalls, encryption at rest and in transit), which keeps user data secure. In contrast, local workstations lack centralized security and scalability, on-premises Kubernetes keeps the deployment pipeline outside GCP's managed environment (increasing operational burden), and Cloud Functions cannot host a persistent, stateful process like the Jenkins controller due to its short-lived, stateless execution model.

**Learn more:** [Using Jenkins on Google Compute Engine for distributed builds | Google Cloud Blog](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/gcp/using-jenkins-on-google-compute-engine-for-distributed-builds) · [Google Compute Engine | Jenkins plugin](https://plugins.jenkins.io/google-compute-engine/)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You manage applications deployed on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) clusters in multiple Google Cloud projects. You need a centralized, scalable solution for collecting and querying Prometheus metrics from these clusters with a flexible query language. You want to follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Install Prometheus server on an admin cluster with cluster autoscaler enabled, and expose the Prometheus endpoint for queries.
Configure the Ops Agent to collect metrics, and run queries in Metrics Explorer.
Configure Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus with managed collection, and run queries in Metrics Explorer.
Deploy a Prometheus server as a sidecar to your applications on each cluster, and run queries in Cloud Monitoring.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus provides managed, cross-project Prometheus monitoring at scale. Google recommends managed collection for Kubernetes environments such as GKE because it avoids the work of deploying, scaling, sharding, configuring, and maintaining Prometheus servers. Its metrics can be queried with PromQL in Cloud Monitoring Metrics Explorer.

**Learn more:** [Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus](https://docs.cloud.google.com/stackdriver/docs/managed-prometheus) · [Query using Cloud Monitoring](https://docs.cloud.google.com/stackdriver/docs/managed-prometheus/query-cm?hl=en)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company uses a CI/CD pipeline that uses Cloud Build and Artifact Registry to deploy container images to Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). Images are tagged with the most recent commit hash and promoted to production after successful tests in the development and pre-production environments. A recent production deployment caused the application to fail because of untested integration functionality, requiring a disruptive manual rollback. During that rollback, you observed many old, unused container images accumulating in Artifact Registry. You need to improve rollout and rollback management and remove the old container images. What should you do?

options.text: Set up a rollback pipeline in Cloud Build, and implement an Artifact Registry cleanup policy.
Adopt Cloud Deploy for managing deployments, and implement an Artifact Registry cleanup policy.
Deploy Cloud Service Mesh across the GKE clusters, and manually clean up Artifact Registry images.
Adopt Cloud Deploy for managing deployments, and schedule a Cloud Build job for container image cleanup.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Deploy provides managed deployment pipelines for GKE and can roll a target back by creating a rollout from a previously successful release. Artifact Registry cleanup policies automatically delete artifact versions that meet defined criteria while preserving versions covered by keep policies, making them the appropriate native mechanism for removing unused container images.

**Learn more:** [Overview of Cloud Deploy](https://docs.cloud.google.com/deploy/docs/overview) · [Roll back a target](https://docs.cloud.google.com/deploy/docs/roll-back)

You are creating the CI/CD pipeline for an application deployed to Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). The application uses a Kubernetes Deployment, Service, and Ingress. The application team has asked that it be deployed by using the blue/green deployment methodology. You need to implement the rollback actions. What should you do?

options.text: Run the kubectl rollout undo command.
Delete the new container image, and delete the running Pods.
Update the Kubernetes Service to point to the previous Kubernetes Deployment.
Scale the new Kubernetes Deployment to zero.

questions.explanation:
A blue/green deployment runs an upgraded parallel set of application instances and switches traffic to it when ready. In Kubernetes, the Service selects the Pods that receive traffic, so rollback requires changing the Service selector to target the previous Deployment's Pods. [Google Cloud: Best practices for CI/CD to GKE](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/best-practices-continuous-integration-delivery-kubernetes)

**Learn more:** [Best practices for continuous integration and delivery to Google Kubernetes Engine](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/best-practices-continuous-integration-delivery-kubernetes)

questions.question: Your application's performance on Google Cloud has worsened since the most recent release. You suspect downstream dependencies may be making some requests take longer to finish. You need to investigate the application and identify the cause. What should you do?

options.text: Configure Error Reporting in your application.
Configure Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus in your application.
Configure Cloud Profiler in your application.
Configure Cloud Trace in your application.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Trace provides distributed tracing and latency data for end-to-end requests, including operations such as RPC calls to downstream dependencies. Its traces and spans expose where time is spent, allowing a slow dependency to be identified. [Cloud Trace overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/trace/docs/overview)\
\
**Learn more:** [Cloud Trace overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/trace/docs/overview)

questions.domain: Optimizing performance and cost
questions.question: Your application's performance on Google Cloud has worsened since the most recent release. You suspect downstream dependencies may be making some requests take longer to finish. You need to investigate the application and identify the cause. What should you do?

options.text: Add additional network interface controllers (NICs) to your VMs.
Deploy a Cloud NAT gateway and attach the gateway to the subnet of the VMs.
Change the machine type for your VMs to n2-standard-8.
Deploy the Ops Agent to export additional monitoring metrics.

questions.explanation:
Compute Engine network bandwidth is tied to the N2 machine type. An `n2-standard-2` VM has up to 10 Gbps default egress bandwidth, while an `n2-standard-8` VM has up to 16 Gbps. Resizing to `n2-standard-8` increases the VM’s available network-throughput limit.

**Learn more:** [General-purpose machine family for Compute Engine](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/general-purpose-machines)

questions.domain: Applying site reliability engineering practices
questions.question: Your team operates a critical service with a 99.9% availability SLO. Several incidents have nearly exhausted the quarter’s error budget. The team plans to release new features next week. What should you do to avoid exceeding the error budget while following Google-recommended practices?

options.text: Release the features but implement an automatic rollback if new errors occur.
Release the features sequentially for each subset of users to minimize potential impact on the SLO.
Postpone the feature release and focus on reliability improvements until the error budget refreshes.
Postpone the feature release and focus on building a backlog of features to deploy until the error budget refreshes.

questions.explanation: When an error budget is nearly depleted, feature releases should be paused and effort redirected to reliability work. This preserves the remaining allowable unreliability and aligns development velocity with the service’s SLO performance.

questions.domain: Implementing observability practices and troubleshooting issues
questions.question: Your team operates a critical service with a 99.9% availability SLO. Several incidents have nearly exhausted the quarter’s error budget. The team plans to release new features next week. What should you do to avoid exceeding the error budget while following Google-recommended practices?

options.text: Increase the number of replicas for the application’s GKE deployment and enable Horizontal Pod Autoscaling.
In Cloud Logging, create a logs-based metric that counts slow requests. Set up a Cloud Monitoring alert to be notified when the count exceeds a certain threshold.
Review the deployment history in Cloud Deploy, and roll back to a previous version of the application to see if the issue is resolved.
Use Cloud Trace to analyze the distributed traces of the checkout process. Examine the trace waterfalls to identify which service or operation is introducing the most latency.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Trace captures end-to-end distributed traces with timing for individual operations (spans). Examining trace waterfalls reveals where time is spent across the checkout workflow, allowing the service or operation causing the latency to be identified.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Trace overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/trace/docs/overview?hl=en) · [View latency of app requests](https://docs.cloud.google.com/trace/docs/trace-app-latency)

questions.domain: Applying site reliability engineering practices
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to define Service Level Objectives (SLOs) for a high-traffic, multi-region web application. Customers expect the application to always be available and to have fast response times, and they are currently satisfied with its performance and availability.  
  
Based on current measurements over a 28-day window:  
  
- 90th percentile latency: 120ms  
- 95th percentile latency: 275ms  
  
What latency SLO would you recommend the team publish?

options.text: 90 percentile ג€
90 percentile ג€
90 percentile ג€
90 percentile ג€

questions.explanation: SLO targets should not simply mirror current measured performance, because doing so leaves no error budget — any minor regression would instantly breach the SLO. The recommended practice is to set the SLO slightly looser than the currently observed performance (while still meeting user expectations for a fast, reliable experience), giving the team room to absorb normal variability and future changes without violating the objective. Given current values of 120ms (p90) and 275ms (p275... p95), a target of 150ms (p90) and 300ms (p95) provides that reasonable buffer while remaining consistent with what customers already find satisfactory.

questions.domain: Applying site reliability engineering practices
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your product is presently deployed across three Google Cloud Platform (GCP) zones, with users split among the zones. You can fail over between zones, but doing so results in a 10-minute service disruption for the affected users. You generally have a database failure once per quarter and can detect it within five minutes.  
  
You are cataloging reliability risks for a new real-time chat feature in your product. For each risk, you record:  
  
- Mean Time to Detect (MTTD) in minutes  
- Mean Time to Repair (MTTR) in minutes  
- Mean Time Between Failure (MTBF) in days  
- User Impact Percentage  
  
The chat feature requires a new database system that takes twice as long to successfully fail over between zones. You want to account for the risk of the new database failing in one zone. What values would apply to the database-failover risk with the new system?

options.text: MTTD: 5 MTTR: 10 MTBF: 90 Impact: 33%
MTTD: 5 MTTR: 20 MTBF: 90 Impact: 33%
MTTD: 5 MTTR: 10 MTBF: 90 Impact: 50%
MTTD: 5 MTTR: 20 MTBF: 90 Impact: 50%

questions.explanation: Detection remains five minutes. A failure occurring once per quarter gives an MTBF of approximately 90 days. Doubling the original 10-minute zonal failover disruption produces a 20-minute MTTR. Because users are divided among three zones, a failure in one zone affects approximately 33% of users.

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Application artifacts are built and deployed through a CI/CD pipeline. You need the CI/CD pipeline to securely access application secrets, and you also want to rotate those secrets more easily if a security breach occurs. What should you do?

options.text: Prompt developers for secrets at build time. Instruct developers to not store secrets at rest.
Store secrets in a separate configuration file on Git. Provide select developers with access to the configuration file.
Store secrets in Cloud Storage encrypted with a key from Cloud KMS. Provide the CI/CD pipeline with access to Cloud KMS via IAM.
Encrypt the secrets and store them in the source code repository. Store a decryption key in a separate repository and grant your pipeline access to it.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Storage can hold secrets outside the source repository, Cloud KMS protects the stored data through encryption, and IAM can grant the CI/CD pipeline only the access it requires. This centralizes secret access and supports revoking access or replacing protected secret material after a compromise. Google Cloud recommends Secret Manager for purpose-built secret storage and rotation; among the listed choices, Cloud Storage protected with Cloud KMS and IAM is the appropriate secure design.

**Learn more:** [Secret Manager overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/secret-manager/docs/overview) · [About rotation schedules](https://docs.cloud.google.com/secret-manager/docs/rotation-recommendations)

You are setting up Cloud Logging for a new application running on a Compute Engine instance that has a public IP address. A user-managed service account is attached to the instance. You have confirmed that the required agents are running on the instance, but no log entries from the instance appear in Cloud Logging. You want to fix the issue by using Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Export the service account key and configure the agents to use the key.
Update the instance to use the default Compute Engine service account.
Add the Logs Writer role to the service account.
Enable Private Google Access on the subnet that the instance is in.

questions.explanation:
The attached service account must have the Logs Writer role (`roles/logging.logWriter`), which grants `logging.logEntries.create` to write log entries. Attached service-account credentials are the recommended authentication mechanism for Compute Engine workloads; exporting a service-account key is unnecessary. Private Google Access is not required when the instance has a public IP address.

**Learn more:** [Access control with IAM | Cloud Logging](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/access-control) · [Authorize the Logging agent | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/agent/logging/authorization)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an application running in Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). It consists of several microservices deployed to GKE by using Deployments and Services. One microservice has an issue in which a Pod begins returning 403 errors after it has run for more than five hours. Your development team is working on a solution, but the issue will not be fixed for a month.  
  
You need to maintain continued operations until the microservice is fixed. You want to follow Google-recommended practices and use the fewest steps. What should you do?

options.text: Create a cron job to terminate any Pods that have been running for more than five hours.
Add a HTTP liveness probe to the microservice's deployment.
Monitor the Pods, and terminate any Pods that have been running for more than five hours.
Configure an alert to notify you whenever a Pod returns 403 errors.

questions.explanation:
An HTTP liveness probe continually checks whether the container is healthy. HTTP responses from 200 through 399 are successful probe results, so a 403 response fails the probe. After the configured failure threshold, the kubelet restarts the unhealthy container; the Deployment then preserves the intended running workload without manual Pod termination or alert-driven remediation.

**Learn more:** [Kubernetes: Configure Liveness, Readiness and Startup Probes](https://v1-33.docs.kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-liveness-readiness-startup-probes/) · [Kubernetes: Liveness, Readiness, and Startup Probes](https://v1-35.docs.kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/liveness-readiness-startup-probes/)

questions.domain: Implementing observability practices and troubleshooting issues
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are responsible for supporting a web application running on Compute Engine that provides a booking service to thousands of users. Shortly after a new feature is released, your monitoring dashboard shows that all users are experiencing latency at login. You want to mitigate the impact of this incident on your users. What should you do first?

options.text: Roll back the recent release.
Review the Stackdriver monitoring.
Upsize the virtual machines running the login services.
Deploy a new release to see whether it fixes the problem.

questions.explanation:
When a service disruption occurs immediately after a new release, the fastest and safest mitigation is to roll back that release, since it is the most probable cause of the regression and reverting it restores the previously known-good, stable state for all affected users. This follows standard incident management and SRE practice of prioritizing rapid mitigation of user impact over root-cause investigation or further changes during an active incident. Reviewing monitoring data or deploying additional changes (including a new release intended as a fix) does not immediately stop the user-facing impact and can prolong or worsen the outage, while resizing VMs addresses a capacity assumption that isn't confirmed as the actual cause.

**Learn more:** [Site Reliability Engineering - Managing Incidents](https://sre.google/sre-book/managing-incidents/) · [Google Cloud Architecture Framework: Reliability - Incident response](https://cloud.google.com/architecture/framework/reliability)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company has an application deployed on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) that consists of 12 microservices. Multiple teams are concurrently developing features across three environments: Dev, Staging, and Prod. Developers report dependency-test failures and delayed releases because deployments from multiple feature branches share the Dev GKE cluster.  
  
A cost-effective solution is needed so developers can test microservice features in a stable development environment that is isolated from other development work. What should you do?

options.text: Automate CI pipelines by using Cloud Build for container image creation and Kubernetes manifest updates from main branch merge requests. Integrate with Config Sync to test new im-ages in dynamically created namespaces on the Dev GKE cluster with autoscaling enabled. Im-plement a post-test namespace cleanup routine.

Automate CI pipelines by using Cloud Build to create container images and update Kuber-netes manifests for each commit. Use Cloud Deploy for progressive delivery to Dev, Staging, and Prod GKE clusters. Enable Config Sync for consistent Kubernetes configurations across en-vironments.

Use Cloud Build to automate CI pipelines and update Kubernetes manifest files from feature branch commits. Integrate with Config Sync to test new images in dynamically created namespaces on the Dev GKE cluster with autoscaling enabled. Implement a post-test namespace cleanup routine.

Use Cloud Build to automate CI pipelines and update Kubernetes manifest files from feature branch commits. Integrate with Config Sync to test new images in dynamically created GKE Dev clusters for each feature branch, which are deleted upon merge request.

questions.explanation:
Feature-branch CI builds can deploy each change into its own temporary namespace in the existing Dev GKE cluster. Namespace isolation prevents one feature’s services and dependencies from interfering with another’s while avoiding the cost of creating a separate cluster for every branch. Config Sync supports GitOps reconciliation and can provision and manage namespaces and namespace-scoped configuration; removing the temporary namespace after testing releases the associated resources.

**Learn more:** [Config Sync overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/config-sync/docs/overview) · [Sync objects to multiple namespaces](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/config-sync/docs/how-to/namespace-scoped-objects)

You are creating reusable infrastructure-as-code modules. Each module includes integration tests that deploy the module in a test project. You use GitHub for source control.  
  
You need to test your feature branch continuously and ensure that all code is tested before changes are accepted. You must implement a solution that automates the integration tests. What should you do?

options.text: Use a Jenkins server for CI/CD pipelines. Periodically run all tests in the feature branch.
Ask the pull request reviewers to run the integration tests before approving the code.
Use Cloud Build to run the tests. Trigger all tests to run after a pull request is merged.
Use Cloud Build to run tests in a specific folder. Trigger Cloud Build for every GitHub pull request.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Build can use GitHub pull-request triggers to automatically run a build for pull-request commits, providing test feedback before changes are accepted. The build configuration can run the integration tests located in the relevant module folder, so each pull request is continuously validated before merge.

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are building and deploying a microservice on Cloud Run for your organization. Many internal applications use the service. You are deploying a new release and must test the new version extensively in the staging and production environments while minimizing impact on users and developers. What should you do?

options.text: Deploy the new version of the service to the staging environment. Split the traffic, and allow 1% of traffic through to the latest version. Test the latest version. If the test passes, gradually roll out the latest version to the staging and production environments.

Deploy the new version of the service to the staging environment. Split the traffic, and allow 50% of traffic through to the latest version. Test the latest version. If the test passes, send all traffic to the latest version. Repeat for the production environment.

Deploy the new version of the service to the staging environment with a new-release tag without serving traffic. Test the new-release version. If the test passes, gradually roll out this tagged version. Repeat for the production environment.

Deploy a new environment with the green tag to use as the staging environment. Deploy the new version of the service to the green environment and test the new version. If the tests pass, send all traffic to the green environment and delete the existing staging environment. Repeat for the production environment.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Run can deploy a new revision with zero traffic and a revision tag, allowing the revision to be tested directly through its tagged URL without affecting existing users. After validation, traffic can be gradually migrated to that tagged revision, reducing rollout risk in both staging and production.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Run rollbacks, gradual rollouts, and traffic migration](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/rollouts-rollbacks-traffic-migration)

questions.domain: Applying site reliability engineering practices
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your team is preparing a postmortem following an incident involving your external-facing application. The team wants to enhance its postmortem policy with triggers that determine whether an incident needs a postmortem. Based on Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) practices, which triggers should be defined in the postmortem policy? (Choose two.)

options.text: An external stakeholder asks for a postmortem
Data is lost due to an incident.
An internal stakeholder requests a postmortem.
The monitoring system detects that one of the instances for your application has failed.
The CD pipeline detects an issue and rolls back a problematic release.

questions.explanation:
SRE guidance identifies data loss of any kind as a common postmortem trigger. It also states that any stakeholder may request a postmortem, without limiting that request to external stakeholders; consequently, both internal and external stakeholder requests meet that criterion.

**Learn more:** [Google SRE Book: Postmortem Culture: Learning from Failure](https://sre.google/sre-book/postmortem-culture/)

questions.domain: Applying site reliability engineering practices
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are responsible for a stateless, web-based API that runs on a single Compute Engine instance in the europe-west2-a zone. The Service Level Indicator (SLI) for service availability is currently below the defined Service Level Objective (SLO). A postmortem investigation shows that requests to the API frequently time out, and these timeouts occur because the API receives a high volume of requests and runs out of memory.  
  
You need to improve the service's availability. What should you do?

options.text: Change the specified SLO to match the measured SLI
Move the service to higher-specification compute instances with more memory
Set up additional service instances in other zones and load balance the traffic between all instances
Set up additional service instances in other zones and use them as a failover in case the primary instance is unavailable

questions.explanation:
Because the API is stateless, it can be scaled out horizontally rather than scaled up on a single instance. The root cause of the timeouts is that a single instance cannot handle the request volume and exhausts its memory; provisioning additional instances in other zones and placing them behind a load balancer distributes incoming traffic across all instances, reducing per-instance load (and thus memory pressure) while also removing the single-zone point of failure. This directly increases the measured availability toward the SLO. Adjusting the SLO (A) doesn't fix the service, upsizing a single instance (B) doesn't address the single point of failure or true scalability needs, and a failover-only configuration (D) leaves idle capacity that doesn't help distribute the live traffic causing the resource exhaustion — only active load balancing across zones solves both the load and availability problems.

**Learn more:** [Distributing load across instances - Load Balancing overview](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/load-balancing-overview) · [Designing reliable systems - Google SRE / architecture framework](https://cloud.google.com/architecture/framework/reliability)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are the Site Reliability Engineer responsible for operating your company’s data services and products. You regularly address operational challenges with your company’s data-ingestion processes, including unpredictable data volumes and high costs. You have recently learned that a new data-ingestion product will be developed in Google Cloud. You need to work with the product development team to provide operational input for the new product. What should you do?

options.text: Deploy the prototype product in a test environment, run a load test, and share the results with the product development team.

When the initial product version passes the quality assurance phase and compliance assessments, deploy the product to a staging environment. Share error logs and performance metrics with the product development team.
When the new product is used by at least one internal customer in production, share error logs and monitoring metrics with the product development team.
Review the design of the product with the product development team to provide feedback early in the design phase.

questions.explanation:
SREs should engage during the design phase so operational requirements—such as scalable capacity for variable ingestion volumes, cost efficiency, monitoring, and reliability—are built into the product before implementation. Google Cloud’s operational-excellence guidance identifies operational requirements and best practices for the design and implementation phases, helping solutions achieve operational efficiency and scalability.

**Learn more:** [Well-Architected Framework: Operational excellence pillar](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/framework/operational-excellence) · [Evaluating where your team lies on the SRE spectrum](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/devops-sre/evaluating-where-your-team-lies-on-the-sre-spectrum)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have a group of applications running on a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster and are using Stackdriver Kubernetes Engine Monitoring. You are moving a new containerized application required by your company into production. The application was written by a third party and cannot be modified or reconfigured. It writes log information to `/var/log/app_messages.log`, and you want to send these log entries to Stackdriver Logging. What should you do?

options.text: Use the default Stackdriver Kubernetes Engine Monitoring agent configuration.
Deploy a Fluentd daemonset to GKE. Then create a customized input and output configuration to tail the log file in the application's pods and write to Stackdriver Logging.

Install Kubernetes on Google Compute Engine (GCE) and redeploy your applications. Then customize the built-in Stackdriver Logging configuration to tail the log file in the application's pods and write to Stackdriver Logging.

Write a script to tail the log file within the pod and write entries to standard output. Run the script as a sidecar container with the application's pod. Configure a shared volume between the containers to allow the script to have read access to /var/log in the application container.

questions.explanation:
GKE’s logging agent collects logs written to container standard output and standard error, rather than arbitrary files within a container. A sidecar container can tail the application log file from a shared volume and write each entry to standard output, allowing Stackdriver Logging to collect it. [About GKE logs](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/about-logs)

**Learn more:** [About GKE logs](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/about-logs)
