questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have configured a CI/CD pipeline in Cloud Build that builds container images. The containers are stored in Artifact Registry. You must ensure that only images built by the Cloud Build pipeline in your production project are deployed to your Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster. You want to minimize the manual effort needed for implementation and ongoing maintenance. What should you do?

options.text: Enable Binary Authorization on the GKE cluster. Create a Cloud Run function triggered by Artifact Registry INSERT events to verify that pushed containers have the projects/PROJECT_ID/attestors/built-by-cloud-build attestor.
Configure Artifact Registry to only allow the Cloud Build service account to push containers.

Enable Binary Authorization on the GKE cluster. Create a Cloud Key Management Service (Cloud KMS) keyring and the built-by-cloud-build attestor. After Cloud Build pushes the container, use the key to create an attestation. Update the Binary Authorization policy to require the projects/PROJECT_ID/attestors/built-by-cloud-build attestor.
Enable Binary Authorization on the GKE cluster. Configure the Binary Authorization policy to require the projects/PROJECT_ID/attestors/built-by-cloud-build attestor.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Build automatically creates the `built-by-cloud-build` attestor and signs successful image builds with attestations. Enabling Binary Authorization for GKE and requiring `projects/PROJECT_ID/attestors/built-by-cloud-build` in its policy enforces that only images built by Cloud Build in that project can be deployed, without maintaining a custom signing key or event-driven verification function.

**Learn more:** [Deploy only images built by Cloud Build](https://cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/deploy-cloud-build)

questions.domain: Implementing observability practices and troubleshooting issues
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have deployed a fleet of Compute Engine instances in Google Cloud. You must ensure that the instances' monitoring metrics and logs are visible in Cloud Logging and Cloud Monitoring to your company's operations and cybersecurity teams. You need to grant the necessary roles to the Compute Engine service account by using Identity and Access Management (IAM), while adhering to the principle of least privilege. What should you do?

options.text: Grant the logging.logWriter and monitoring.metricWriter roles to the Compute Engine service accounts.
Grant the logging.admin and monitoring.editor roles to the Compute Engine service accounts.
Grant the logging.editor and monitoring.metricWriter roles to the Compute Engine service accounts.
Grant the logging.logWriter and monitoring.editor roles to the Compute Engine service accounts.

questions.explanation:
The Logs Writer role (`roles/logging.logWriter`) grants permission to write log entries, while the Monitoring Metric Writer role (`roles/monitoring.metricWriter`) provides the write-only permissions needed to send metrics. Together, these roles allow the instances to publish the required telemetry without granting unnecessary administrative or configuration-editing permissions.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Logging roles and permissions](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iam/docs/roles-permissions/logging) · [Cloud Monitoring roles and permissions](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iam/docs/roles-permissions/monitoring)

questions.domain: Applying site reliability engineering practices

options.text: An explanation of the root cause of the incident.
A list of employees responsible for causing the incident
A list of action items to prevent a recurrence of the incident
Your opinion of the incident's severity compared to past incidents
Copies of the design documents for all the services impacted by the incident

questions.explanation:
Google's SRE practice defines a postmortem as a written record of an incident that documents its impact, the root cause(s), and the follow-up action items needed to prevent recurrence. A blameless postmortem culture explicitly avoids assigning blame to individuals (ruling out naming responsible employees) and focuses on systemic, factual analysis rather than subjective opinions (ruling out comparing severity to past incidents) or unrelated reference material like design documents. The two components essential to preventing recurrence are identifying the root cause and defining concrete, owned action items that address the underlying causes.

**Learn more:** [Google SRE - Blameless Postmortem for System Resilience](https://sre.google/sre-book/postmortem-culture/) · [Google SRE - Postmortem Practices for Incident Management](https://sre.google/workbook/postmortem-culture/)

Your team uses Cloud Build for every CI/CD pipeline. You want to use Cloud Build’s `kubectl` builder to deploy new images to Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). You need to authenticate to GKE while minimizing development effort. What should you do?

options.text: Assign the Container Developer role to the Cloud Build service account.
Specify the Container Developer role for Cloud Build in the cloudbuild.yaml file.
Create a new service account with the Container Developer role and use it to run Cloud Build.
Create a separate step in Cloud Build to retrieve service account credentials and pass these to kubectl.

questions.explanation:
The Cloud Build service account is the identity used by Cloud Build steps. Granting it the Google Kubernetes Engine Developer (Container Developer) role provides the required GKE permissions for a `kubectl` deployment, avoiding a separate service account or manually retrieving and passing credentials.

**Learn more:** [Deploying to GKE | Cloud Build](https://docs.cloud.google.com/build/docs/deploying-builds/deploy-gke)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your Cloud Run application sends unstructured text-string logs to Cloud Logging. You want to transform the unstructured logs into JSON-based structured logs. What should you do?

options.text: Modify the application to use Cloud Logging software development kit (SDK), and send log entries with a jsonPayload field.
Install a Fluent Bit sidecar container, and use a JSON parser.
Install the log agent in the Cloud Run container image, and use the log agent to forward logs to Cloud Logging.
Configure the log agent to convert log text payload to JSON payload.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Logging represents structured log data in the `jsonPayload` field. Writing structured entries through the Cloud Logging client library with a `jsonPayload` changes the application’s output from unstructured text logging to structured logging. Cloud Run is a managed environment that captures application logs without installing or configuring a log agent.

**Learn more:** [Logging and viewing logs in Cloud Run](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/logging) · [Structured logging](https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/structured-logging)

questions.domain: Implementing observability practices and troubleshooting issues
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You manage an application that writes logs to Stackdriver Logging. You need to grant certain team members the ability to export logs. What should you do?

options.text: Grant the team members the IAM role of logging.configWriter on Cloud IAM.
Configure Access Context Manager to allow only these members to export logs.
Create and grant a custom IAM role with the permissions logging.sinks.list and logging.sink.get.
Create an Organizational Policy in Cloud IAM to allow only these members to create log exports.

questions.explanation:
Log exports use Cloud Logging sinks. The Logs Configuration Writer role (`roles/logging.configWriter`) provides permission to create and manage sinks, including the required `logging.sinks.create` permission for creating an export.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Logging access control with IAM](https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/access-control) · [Cloud Logging sinks.create method](https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/reference/v2/rest/v2/sinks/create)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You use a multi-step Cloud Build pipeline to build and deploy your application to Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). You want to integrate with a third-party monitoring platform by sending an HTTP POST containing build information to a webhook. You want to minimize development effort. What should you do?

options.text: Add logic to each Cloud Build step to HTTP POST the build information to a webhook.
Add a new step at the end of the pipeline in Cloud Build to HTTP POST the build information to a webhook.
Use Stackdriver Logging to create a logs-based metric from the Cloud Build logs. Create an Alert with a Webhook notification type.

You are preparing to deploy a new feature of a web-based application to production, and you want to use Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) to carry out a phased rollout to half of the web server pods.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Use a partitioned rolling update.
Use Node taints with NoExecute.
Use a replica set in the deployment specification.
Use a stateful set with parallel pod management policy.

questions.explanation:
A partitioned rolling update, configured via the `updateStrategy.rollingUpdate.partition` field on a StatefulSet, lets you control exactly how many pods (by ordinal index) receive an update while the remaining pods stay on the prior version. This provides the fine-grained, phased rollout capability needed to update only half of the web server pods before continuing further, which is not something a plain ReplicaSet, node taints, or a parallel pod management policy provides.

**Learn more:** [StatefulSets - Partitions | Kubernetes Documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/statefulset/#partitions)

Your team has an application built using a Dockerfile. Cloud Build performs the build, and the resulting artifacts are stored in Artifact Registry. Your team reports that builds are slow. You need to improve build speed while following Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Use the --cache-from parameter, and point to Artifact Registry. Add the most frequently modified files to the later stages of the build process.
Use the --cache-from parameter, and point to Artifact Registry. Add the most frequently modified files to the earlier stages of the build process.
Cache the container layers of the build process to Cloud Storage. Add the most frequently modified files to the earlier stages of the build process.
Cache the container layers of the build process to Cloud Storage. Add the most frequently modified files to the later stages of the build process.

questions.explanation:
Google recommends using --cache-from pointing to a previously built image in your registry (Artifact Registry) so Cloud Build reuses cached layers. Because --cache-from rebuilds every layer from the first changed layer to the end of the build, you must place the most frequently modified files in the LATER stages of the Dockerfile, keeping stable dependencies in earlier, cacheable layers. Option B (earlier stages) invalidates the cache on every code change and defeats the optimization. Caching layers to Cloud Storage (C/D) is not the Google-recommended Docker layer-cache mechanism for this scenario.

**Learn more:** [Speeding up builds](https://docs.cloud.google.com/build/docs/optimize-builds/speeding-up-builds)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are setting up a Cloud Deploy pipeline to deploy an application to Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). The application is deployed as a Deployment. You must configure the Deployment to use two replicas in the development environment and five replicas in the production environment. All other configuration parameters must remain consistent across environments. You must also minimize development overhead when updating manifests in the future. How should you configure the `skaffold.yaml` file?

options.text: Create multiple profiles, and configure the manifests.kustomize section.
Create a single profile, and configure the manifests.kustomize section.
Create multiple profiles, and configure the manifests.rawYaml section.
Create a single profile, and configure the manifests.rawYaml section.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Deploy uses separate Skaffold profiles to render target-specific manifests. Kustomize enables a shared base Deployment and environment-specific overlays that patch only the replica count, preserving every other configuration setting and avoiding duplicated manifests.

**Learn more:** [Manage manifests in Cloud Deploy](https://docs.cloud.google.com/deploy/docs/using-skaffold/managing-manifests)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company operates in a highly regulated domain that requires retaining all organization logs for seven years. You want to minimize logging-infrastructure complexity by using managed services. You must prevent any future loss of log capture or stored logs caused by misconfiguration or human error. What should you do?

options.text: Use Cloud Logging to configure an aggregated sink at the organization level to export all logs into a BigQuery dataset.
Use Cloud Logging to configure an aggregated sink at the organization level to export all logs into Cloud Storage with a seven-year retention policy and Bucket Lock.
Use Cloud Logging to configure an export sink at each project level to export all logs into a BigQuery dataset
Use Cloud Logging to configure an export sink at each project level to export all logs into Cloud Storage with a seven-year retention policy and Bucket Lock.

questions.explanation:
An organization-level aggregated Cloud Logging sink centrally routes log entries from the organization and its child resources, reducing the risk and administrative overhead of per-project configurations. A Cloud Storage bucket with a seven-year retention policy and Bucket Lock preserves exported log objects for that required period; locking the retention policy is irreversible and protects the retention configuration from subsequent changes.

**Learn more:** [Aggregated sinks overview | Cloud Logging](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/export/aggregated_sinks_overview?hl=en) · [Bucket Lock | Cloud Storage](https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/bucket-lock)

questions.domain: Optimizing performance and cost
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization plans to raise an application's availability target from 99.9% to 99.99% at an investment of $2,000. The application currently generates $1,000,000 in revenue. You must decide whether the availability increase is worth the investment for a single year of use. What should you do?

options.text: Calculate the value of improved availability to be $900, and determine that the increase in availability is not worth the investment.
Calculate the value of improved availability to be $1,000, and determine that the increase in availability is not worth the investment.
Calculate the value of improved availability to be $1,000, and determine that the increase in availability is worth the investment.
Calculate the value of improved availability to be $9,000, and determine that the increase in availability is worth the investment.

questions.explanation:
Increasing availability from 99.9% to 99.99% reduces the potential unavailable portion from 0.1% to 0.01%, an improvement of 0.09%. For $1,000,000 in annual revenue, that improvement is worth $900 per year. Because $900 is less than the $2,000 cost, the investment does not pay for itself within one year. AWS describes availability as a percentage of uptime over a period such as a year and notes that higher availability targets typically increase cost.

**Learn more:** [Availability – AWS Well-Architected Reliability Pillar](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/reliability-pillar/availability.html)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are investigating an ongoing anomaly that involves a high volume of requests. You created a custom dashboard in Cloud Monitoring and determined that the requests originate from one type of client. You want to let your company’s development team investigate the issue further by using your custom dashboard. You want to follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Export the custom dashboard as a JSON file and share the file with the development team.
Export the dashboard time series data in CSV format. Instruct the development team to use BigQuery to analyze the data.
Grant the development team the roles/monitoringViewer IAM role at the project level and share the custom dashboard URL with the development team.
Grant the development team the roles/viewer IAM role at the project level and share the custom dashboard URL with the development team.

questions.explanation:
The project-level Monitoring Viewer role (`roles/monitoring.viewer`) provides read-only access to Cloud Monitoring, including custom dashboards and their data. Google Cloud recommends granting this least-privilege role to people who need to view a dashboard and sharing the dashboard URL with them.

**Learn more:** [Share a custom dashboard](https://docs.cloud.google.com/monitoring/charts/share-dashboards?hl=en) · [Control access with IAM](https://docs.cloud.google.com/monitoring/access-control?hl=en)

questions.domain: Implementing observability practices and troubleshooting issues
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You use Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus with managed collection to collect metrics from your service running on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). After you deploy the service, no metric data appears in Cloud Monitoring, and you have not seen any error messages. You need to troubleshoot the issue. What should you do?

options.text: Determine if your service has exceeded its quota for writes to the Cloud Monitoring API.
Verify that your PodMonitoring configuration references a valid port.
Check if the Grafana service is installed on your GKE cluster.
Confirm that your service has the monitoring.servicesViewer IAM role.

questions.explanation:
With managed collection, an absence of errors combined with no Cloud Monitoring data most commonly indicates a metric-exporter or scrape-configuration problem. A valid `PodMonitoring` scrape configuration must reference the correct metrics port so the managed collector can discover and scrape the endpoint.

**Learn more:** [Troubleshooting Managed Service for Prometheus](https://docs.cloud.google.com/stackdriver/docs/managed-prometheus/troubleshooting?hl=en)

questions.domain: Applying site reliability engineering practices
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are part of an organization that follows SRE practices and principles. You are assuming management of a new service from the Development Team and conduct a Production Readiness Review (PRR). Following the PRR analysis phase, you determine that the service currently cannot meet its Service Level Objectives (SLOs). You want to ensure the service can meet its SLOs in production. What should you do next?

options.text: Adjust the SLO targets to be achievable by the service so you can bring it into production.
Notify the development team that they will have to provide production support for the service.
Identify recommended reliability improvements to the service to be completed before handover.
Bring the service into production with no SLOs and build them when you have collected operational data.

questions.explanation:
A PRR analysis that reveals SLO gaps should produce recommended reliability improvements that are prioritized, agreed with the development team, and completed before the service handover. The PRR process requires sufficient improvements for a service to be ready for SRE production support.

**Learn more:** [Google SRE Book: The Evolving SRE Engagement Model](https://sre.google/sre-book/evolving-sre-engagement-model/)

You are setting up a Cl pipeline. The build step for Cl pipeline integration testing needs access to APIs within your private VPC network. Your security team requires that API traffic not be exposed publicly. You need to implement a solution that minimizes management overhead. What should you do?

options.text: Use Cloud Build private pools to connect to the private VPC.
Use Cloud Build to create a Compute Engine instance in the private VPC. Run the integration tests on the VM by using a startup script.
Use Cloud Build as a pipeline runner. Configure a cross-region internal Application Load Balancer for API access.
Use Cloud Build as a pipeline runner. Configure a global external Application Load Balancer with a Google Cloud Armor policy for API access.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Build private pools are fully managed worker pools that can establish a private connection to a managed VPC, enabling build workers to access VPC resources exclusively through internal IP addresses. Public egress can also be disabled, so integration tests can call the private APIs without publicly exposing that traffic.

**Learn more:** [Using Cloud Build in a private network](https://docs.cloud.google.com/build/docs/private-pools/use-in-private-network) · [Private pools overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/build/docs/private-pools/private-pools-overview)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You deployed an application to a large Standard Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster. The application is stateless, with multiple pods running concurrently. It receives variable traffic. You need to ensure a consistent user experience despite traffic changes while optimizing cluster resource usage.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Configure a cron job to scale the deployment on a schedule
Configure a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler.
Configure a Vertical Pod Autoscaler
Configure cluster autoscaling on the node pool.

questions.explanation:
A Horizontal Pod Autoscaler automatically increases or decreases the number of replicas for a workload in response to metrics such as CPU, memory, custom metrics, or external traffic metrics. This lets a stateless application add Pods during demand increases and remove unneeded Pods when demand falls, preserving responsiveness while using capacity efficiently.

**Learn more:** [Horizontal Pod autoscaling | Google Kubernetes Engine](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/horizontalpodautoscaler?hl=en)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You recently deployed an application in Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) and now need to release a new version. You require the ability to immediately roll back to the application's previous version if the new version has issues. Which deployment model should you use?

options.text: Perform a rolling deployment, and test your new application after the deployment is complete.
Perform A/B testing, and test your application periodically after the deployment is complete.
Perform a canary deployment, and test your new application periodically after the new version is deployed.
Perform a blue/green deployment, and test your new application after the deployment is complete.

questions.explanation:
A blue/green deployment runs an upgraded application version in a parallel environment alongside the existing production version and switches traffic to the new environment when ready. Because the prior environment remains available, traffic can be switched back quickly if the new version has problems. Google Cloud describes blue-green deployment as deploying parallel upgraded instances and switching traffic when ready.

**Learn more:** [Best practices for continuous integration and delivery to Google Kubernetes Engine](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/best-practices-continuous-integration-delivery-kubernetes)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are building a CI/CD pipeline to perform Terraform deployments of Google Cloud resources. The CI/CD tooling runs in Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) and uses an ephemeral Pod for every pipeline run. You must ensure that the pipelines running in the Pods have the required Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions to carry out the Terraform deployments. You want to follow Google-recommended identity-management practices. What should you do? (Choose two.)

options.text: Create a new Kubernetes service account, and assign the service account to the Pods. Use Workload Identity to authenticate as the Google service account.

Create a new JSON service account key for the Google service account, store the key as a Kubernetes secret, inject the key into the Pods, and set the GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS environment variable.
Create a new Google service account, and assign the appropriate IAM permissions.
Create a new JSON service account key for the Google service account, store the key in the secret management store for the CI/CD tool, and configure Terraform to use this key for authentication.
Assign the appropriate IAM permissions to the Google service account associated with the Compute Engine VM instances that run the Pods.

questions.explanation:
Workload Identity Federation for GKE lets a Kubernetes service account used by a Pod authenticate to Google Cloud without exporting or storing service-account keys. A dedicated Google IAM service account must be granted the least-privilege IAM roles needed for the Terraform deployment, and the Pod's Kubernetes service account can be configured to use that identity. Using JSON keys or the node Compute Engine service account is less secure and can over-provision permissions.

**Learn more:** [About Workload Identity Federation for GKE](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/workload-identity) · [Authenticate to Google Cloud APIs from GKE workloads](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/workload-identity)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization operates in a highly regulated domain. The security team requires that only trusted container images be deployed to Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). You need to implement a solution that satisfies the security team’s requirements while minimizing management overhead. What should you do?

options.text: Configure Binary Authorization in your GKE clusters to enforce deploy-time security policies.
Grant the roles/artifactregistry.writer role to the Cloud Build service account. Confirm that no employee has Artifact Registry write permission.
Use Cloud Run to write and deploy a custom validator. Enable an Eventarc trigger to perform validations when new images are uploaded.
Configure Kritis to run in your GKE clusters to enforce deploy-time security policies.

questions.explanation:
Binary Authorization provides managed deploy-time policy enforcement for GKE. Policies can require trusted attestations for container images, and the enforcer blocks images that do not satisfy the policy before they are deployed.

**Learn more:** [Binary Authorization overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/overview) · [Get started using the Google Cloud CLI (GKE)](https://cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/getting-started-cli)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization keeps all application logs from multiple Google Cloud projects in a central Cloud Logging project. Your security team wants to enforce a rule that each project team can view only its own logs, while only the operations team can view all logs. You need to design a solution that satisfies the security team’s requirements while minimizing costs. What should you do?

options.text: Grant each project team access to the project _Default view in the central logging project. Grant togging viewer access to the operations team in the central logging project.

Create Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles for each project team and restrict access to the _Default log view in their individual Google Cloud project. Grant viewer access to the operations team in the central logging project.
Create log views for each project team and only show each project team their application logs. Grant the operations team access to the _AllLogs view in the central logging project.
Export logs to BigQuery tables for each project team. Grant project teams access to their tables. Grant logs writer access to the operations team in the central logging project.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Logging log views can restrict a principal to a subset of entries in a centralized log bucket. Create a filtered view for each project team that includes only that team’s application logs, and grant the team access only to its view. The automatically created `_AllLogs` view includes every log entry in the bucket, so granting the operations team access to it provides the required full visibility without exporting or duplicating logs to BigQuery.

**Learn more:** [Configure log views on a log bucket](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/logs-views?hl=en) · [Access control with IAM](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/access-control)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are evaluating Java applications in production. Cloud Profiler and Cloud Trace are installed and configured by default for every application. You need to identify which applications require performance tuning. What should you do? (Choose two.)

options.text: Examine the wall-clock time and the CPU time of the application. If the difference is substantial increase the CPU resource allocation.
Examine the wall-clock time and the CPU time of the application. If the difference is substantial, increase the memory resource allocation.
Examine the wall-clock time and the CPU time of the application. If the difference is substantial, increase the local disk storage allocation.

Examine the latency time the wall-clock time and the CPU time of the application. If the latency time is slowly burning down the error budget, and the difference between wall-clock time and CPU time is minimal mark the application for optimization.
Examine the heap usage of the application. If the usage is low, mark the application for optimization.

questions.explanation:
Wall-clock time includes time spent waiting, whereas CPU time measures time actively executing instructions. A substantial wall-clock versus CPU-time difference can indicate a resource bottleneck, making additional memory allocation an appropriate action. Nearly equal wall-clock and CPU times indicate CPU-intensive code; if its latency is consuming the error budget, the application should be marked for optimization.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Profiler: Profiling concepts](https://docs.cloud.google.com/profiler/docs/concepts-profiling) · [Cloud Profiler overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/profiler/docs/about-profiler)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company operates an ecommerce website built with JVM-based applications and a microservice architecture in Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). Application load rises during the day and falls at night. Your operations team has configured the application with enough Pods to support the evening peak load. You want to automate scaling so that only the required number of Pods and nodes run for the current load. What should you do?

options.text: Configure the Vertical Pod Autoscaler, but keep the node pool size static.
Configure the Vertical Pod Autoscaler, and enable the cluster autoscaler.
Configure the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, but keep the node pool size static.
Configure the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, and enable the cluster autoscaler.

questions.explanation:
The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler automatically increases or decreases the number of Pods according to configured workload metrics. The GKE cluster autoscaler automatically resizes node pools to provide capacity for Pods and remove unneeded capacity. Together, they scale both application replicas and nodes with changing demand.

**Learn more:** [Horizontal Pod autoscaling | Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE)](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/horizontalpodautoscaler) · [About GKE cluster autoscaling | Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE)](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/cluster-autoscaler)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your team runs microservices in Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). You want to detect error-budget consumption to protect customers and establish release policies. What should you do?

options.text: Create SLIs from metrics. Enable Alert Policies if the services do not pass.
Use the metrics from Anthos Service Mesh to measure the health of the microservices.
Create a SLO. Create an Alert Policy on select_slo_burn_rate.
Create a SLO and configure uptime checks for your services. Enable Alert Policies if the services do not pass.

questions.explanation:
An SLO establishes the allowed error budget, and a Cloud Monitoring alerting policy using `select_slo_burn_rate` detects when that budget is being consumed too rapidly. Burn-rate alerts provide the signal needed to protect customers and gate releases according to reliability objectives.

**Learn more:** [Alerting on your burn rate | Google Cloud Observability](https://docs.cloud.google.com/stackdriver/docs/solutions/slo-monitoring/alerting-on-budget-burn-rate) · [Creating an alerting policy | Google Cloud Observability](https://docs.cloud.google.com/stackdriver/docs/solutions/slo-monitoring/api/create-policy-api)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your development team has released a new version of your service's API. You need to roll out this new API version while causing the least possible disruption to third-party developers and end users of third-party applications that use the API. What should you do?

options.text: Introduce the new version of the API. Announce deprecation of the old version of the API. Deprecate the old version of the API. Contact remaining users of the old API. Provide best effort support to users of the old API. Turn down the old version of the API.

Announce deprecation of the old version of the API. Introduce the new version of the API. Contact remaining users on the old API. Deprecate the old version of the API. Turn down the old version of the API. Provide best effort support to users of the old API.

Announce deprecation of the old version of the API. Contact remaining users on the old API. Introduce the new version of the API. Deprecate the old version of the API. Provide best effort support to users of the old API. Turn down the old version of the API.

Introduce the new version of the API. Contact remaining users of the old API. Announce deprecation of the old version of the API. Deprecate the old version of the API. Turn down the old version of the API. Provide best effort support to users of the old API.

questions.explanation: Minimizing disruption requires following an orderly API lifecycle: first make the new version available, then formally announce that the old version will be deprecated (giving users advance notice), then mark it as deprecated, then proactively contact any developers still using the old version, then continue offering best-effort support to those stragglers, and only after all that turn down (retire) the old version. This sequence avoids cutting off developers before they have a replacement, before they've been warned, or before they've had a chance to migrate with support.

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are responsible for the reliability of a high-volume enterprise application. Numerous users report that an important subset of the application's functionality — a data-intensive reporting feature — is consistently failing with an HTTP 500 error. When you investigate your application's dashboards, you notice a strong correlation between the failures and a metric that represents the size of an internal queue used for generating reports. You trace the failures to a reporting backend that is experiencing high I/O wait times. You quickly resolve the issue by resizing the backend's persistent disk (PD).  
  
You now need to create an availability Service Level Indicator (SLI) for the report generation feature. How should you define it?

options.text: As the I/O wait times aggregated across all report generation backends
As the proportion of report generation requests that result in a successful response
As the application's report generation queue size compared to a known-good threshold
As the reporting backend PD throughout capacity compared to a known-good threshold

questions.explanation:
An availability SLI should reflect the user-facing outcome rather than an internal implementation detail. Google's Site Reliability Engineering guidance defines availability SLIs as the proportion (ratio) of valid requests that are served successfully — for example, the ratio of report generation requests that return a successful response versus those that fail. Metrics like internal queue size, I/O wait time, or disk throughput are useful for root-cause diagnosis of a specific incident, but they are proxy/cause-level signals tied to one particular failure mode and current system architecture. If defined as the SLI, they would fail to detect future outages caused by different underlying issues and would not directly represent whether users are actually experiencing successful report generation. Defining the SLI as the proportion of successful report generation requests ensures it accurately and durably measures the reliability experienced by users.

**Learn more:** [Google SRE Workbook - Implementing SLOs](https://sre.google/workbook/implementing-slos/) · [Google SRE Book - Service Level Objectives](https://sre.google/sre-book/service-level-objectives/)

An external application sends encrypted files to a Cloud Storage bucket. The files use an HMAC-SHA256 key and contain sensitive data that must be loaded into BigQuery for analysis each day after midnight.  
  
You need to create a secure, automated solution to decrypt the files and load them into BigQuery. You want to follow Google-recommended practices while minimizing the required development effort. What should you do?

options.text: 1. Import the encryption key into the same Cloud Storage bucket.2. Create a Cloud Build pipeline that decrypts the file before loading the file into BigQuery.3. Create a Cloud Scheduler trigger that runs every day at the required time.

1. Create a Cloud Key Management Service (Cloud KMS) key ring and import the encryption key.2. Create an Artifact Registry repository, and push the image containing the script to the Artifact Registry repository.3. Create a Cloud Run job that executes the image on a schedule.4. Grant the Cloud Run service agent the Cloud KMS CryptoKey Encrypter/Decrypter role.

1. Create a Cloud Key Management Service (Cloud KMS) key ring and import the encryption key.2. Create a Cloud Build trigger that uses Cloud KMS to decrypt the file before loading the file into BigQuery.3. Create a Cloud Scheduler trigger that runs every day at the required time.

1. Import the encryption key into the same Cloud Storage bucket.2. Create a script that pulls the key from Cloud Storage and decrypts the file.3. Create an Artifact Registry repository containerize the script and push the container to the Artifact Registry repository.4. Create a Cloud Run job that executes on a schedule.

questions.explanation:
Cloud KMS securely manages imported key material instead of exposing it in Cloud Storage. A containerized Cloud Run job provides an appropriate managed execution environment for a finite decrypt-and-load workload, and it can be invoked on a schedule through Cloud Scheduler. Granting the job identity the Cloud KMS CryptoKey Encrypter/Decrypter role permits the required cryptographic operation while avoiding storage of the key alongside the encrypted data.

**Learn more:** [Key import | Cloud Key Management Service](https://cloud.google.com/kms/docs/key-import) · [Permissions and roles | Cloud Key Management Service](https://cloud.google.com/kms/docs/reference/permissions-and-roles)

questions.domain: Implementing observability practices and troubleshooting issues

options.text: Enable VPC Flow Logs on the production VPC network frontend and backend subnets only with a sample volume scale of 0.5.
Enable VPC Flow Logs on the production VPC network frontend and backend subnets only with a sample volume scale of 1.0.
Enable VPC Flow Logs on the testing and production VPC network frontend and backend subnets with a volume scale of 0.5. Apply changes in testing before production.
Enable VPC Flow Logs on the testing and production VPC network frontend and backend subnets with a volume scale of 1.0. Apply changes in testing before production.

questions.explanation:
VPC Flow Logs should be enabled only on the production VPC's frontend and backend subnets, since that is where the suspected malicious activity is occurring; enabling flow logs on the testing environment is unnecessary and wasteful. The sampling rate must be set to 1.0 so that all flows are captured (a rate of 0.5 would only log a random half of the flows, risking missing the intermittent malicious communication). This aligns with Google Cloud's guidance that VPC Flow Logs sampling rate controls what fraction of flows are logged, and a value of 1.0 captures 100% of flows for full analysis fidelity.

**Learn more:** [VPC Flow Logs overview](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/flow-logs)

You are configuring Cloud Logging sinks to export log entries from Cloud Logging to BigQuery for later analysis. Your organization has a Google Cloud folder named Dev that contains development projects and a folder named Prod that contains production projects. Log entries from development projects must be exported to dev_dataset, and log entries from production projects must be exported to prod_dataset. You need to minimize the number of log sinks you create and ensure that the log sinks also apply to future projects. What should you do?

options.text: Create a single aggregated log sink at the organization level.
Create a log sink in each project.
Create two aggregated log sinks at the organization level, and filter by project ID.
Create an aggregated log sink in the Dev and Prod folders.

questions.explanation:
A folder-level aggregated sink configured to include child resources routes logs from all projects beneath that folder, including projects added later. Creating one aggregated sink in Dev with dev_dataset as its BigQuery destination and one in Prod with prod_dataset as its destination meets the separate-routing requirement with the fewest sinks.

**Learn more:** [Collate and route organization- and folder-level logs to supported destinations](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/export/aggregated_sinks) · [Aggregated sinks overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/export/aggregated_sinks_overview?hl=en)

questions.domain: Implementing observability practices and troubleshooting issues
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company runs applications in a private VPC with no internet access. Internal APIs are accessible only from within the VPC network. You need to monitor the availability of these internal APIs using a solution that follows Google-recommended practices and minimizes manual effort and maintenance. What should you do?

options.text: Deploy the application on a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) instance configured with a liveness and readiness probe.
Configure private uptime checks.
Create a Cloud Run function with a VPC connector to ping the internal endpoints. Configure public uptime checks against the Cloud Run function.
Create a synthetic monitor, and use Cloud VPN to access the private endpoints.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Monitoring private uptime checks are a managed mechanism for sending HTTP or TCP requests to resources in a customer VPC through private network access. They are purpose-built for availability monitoring of internal endpoints, avoiding the custom implementation and ongoing maintenance required by an intermediary Cloud Run function, VPN setup, or synthetic monitor.

**Learn more:** [Create private uptime checks | Cloud Monitoring](https://docs.cloud.google.com/monitoring/uptime-checks/private-checks?hl=en)

questions.domain: Bootstrapping and maintaining a Google Cloud organization
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You work for a company that handles highly sensitive user data. You are designing the Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) infrastructure for your company, including several applications that will be deployed in development and production environments. Your design must safeguard data from unauthorized access by other applications while minimizing the required management overhead. What should you do?

options.text: Create one cluster for the organization with separate namespaces for each application and environment combination.
Create one cluster for each application with separate namespaces for production and development environments.
Create one cluster for each environment (development and production) with each application in its own namespace within each cluster.
Create one cluster for the organization with separate namespaces for each application.

questions.explanation:
Separate GKE clusters for development and production isolate environments whose access scope and workloads differ. Within each environment cluster, placing every application in its own namespace enables namespace-scoped RBAC and network policies to isolate applications, while retaining the lower operational overhead of shared multi-tenant clusters.

**Learn more:** [Cluster multi-tenancy | Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE)](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/multitenancy-overview) · [Best practices for enterprise multi-tenancy | Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE)](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/best-practices/enterprise-multitenancy)

questions.domain: Implementing observability practices and troubleshooting issues
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to share a Cloud Monitoring custom dashboard with a partner team. What should you do?

options.text: Provide the partner team with the dashboard URL to enable the partner team to create a copy of the dashboard.
Export the metrics to BigQuery. Use Looker Studio to create a dashboard, and share the dashboard with the partner team.
Copy the Monitoring Query Language (MQL) query from the dashboard, and send the ML query to the partner team.
Download the JSON definition of the dashboard, and send the JSON file to the partner team.

questions.explanation:
A Cloud Monitoring custom dashboard’s JSON definition is the portable template used to create or copy the dashboard in another project. A dashboard URL only lets authorized recipients view the existing dashboard, whereas the JSON file lets the partner team recreate the dashboard definition in its own project.

**Learn more:** [Create and manage custom dashboards](https://docs.cloud.google.com/monitoring/charts/dashboards) · [Share a custom dashboard](https://docs.cloud.google.com/monitoring/charts/share-dashboards?hl=en)

After migrating an e-commerce application to Google Cloud Platform (GCP), you want to get the application ready for the upcoming busy season. What should you do first to prepare for the busy season?

options.text: Load teat the application to profile its performance for scaling.
Enable AutoScaling on the production clusters, in case there is growth.
Pre-provision double the compute power used last season, expecting growth.
Create a runbook on inflating the disaster recovery (DR) environment if there is growth.

questions.explanation:
Before making any scaling decisions—such as enabling autoscaling, adding compute capacity, or updating disaster recovery plans—you need concrete data on how the application performs under increasing load. Load testing identifies bottlenecks, resource limits, and scaling thresholds, which provides the foundation for informed capacity planning. Without this performance profile, decisions like doubling compute resources or configuring autoscaling policies would be based on guesswork rather than data, risking both under-provisioning (outages during peak load) and over-provisioning (wasted cost). This aligns with Google Cloud's recommended practice of performance testing and capacity planning prior to major traffic events, as outlined in Google Cloud's architecture framework guidance on reliability and scalability.

**Learn more:** [Google Cloud Architecture Framework: Reliability - Design for scale](https://cloud.google.com/architecture/framework/reliability)

You manage an application running in Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) that uses the blue/green deployment methodology. Extracts from the Kubernetes manifests are shown below:  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783848649633-w8ka02bh.png)  
  
The `app-green` Deployment was updated to use the new version of the application. During post-deployment monitoring, you notice that most user requests are failing. This behavior was not observed in the testing environment. You need to reduce the incident’s impact on users and allow the developers to troubleshoot the issue. What should you do?

options.text: Update the Deployment app-blue to use the new version of the application.
Update the Deployment app-green to use the previous version of the application.
Change the selector on the Service app-svc to app: my-app.
Change the selector on the Service app-svc to app: my-app, version: blue.

questions.explanation:
A Kubernetes Service directs traffic to Pods that match all of its selector labels. Pointing `app-svc` to `app: my-app, version: blue` removes the failing green Pods from its endpoints and routes user traffic to the unchanged blue deployment. The green deployment remains running for troubleshooting.

**Learn more:** [Kubernetes Labels and Selectors](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/labels/) · [Kubernetes Service](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/service/)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You currently keep the virtual machine (VM) utilization logs in Stackdriver. You need to deliver an easy-to-share, interactive VM utilization dashboard that updates in real time and includes information aggregated quarterly. You want to use Google Cloud Platform solutions. What should you do?

options.text: 1. Export VM utilization logs from Stackdriver to BigQuery. 2. Create a dashboard in Data Studio. 3. Share the dashboard with your stakeholders.

1. Export VM utilization logs from Stackdriver to Cloud Pub/Sub. 2. From Cloud Pub/Sub, send the logs to a Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) system. 3. Build the dashboards in the SIEM system and share with your stakeholders.

1. Export VM utilization logs from Stackdriver to BigQuery. 2. From BigQuery, export the logs to a CSV file. 3. Import the CSV file into Google Sheets. 4. Build a dashboard in Google Sheets and share it with your stakeholders.

1. Export VM utilization logs from Stackdriver to a Cloud Storage bucket. 2. Enable the Cloud Storage API to pull the logs programmatically. 3. Build a custom data visualization application. 4. Display the pulled logs in a custom dashboard.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Logging can route log entries to BigQuery, enabling SQL aggregation of VM utilization data by quarter. A BigQuery data source can be used in Looker Studio (formerly Data Studio) to create and share interactive reports, with configurable data freshness for BigQuery-backed reporting.

**Learn more:** [View logs routed to BigQuery](https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/export/bigquery) · [A typical Looker Studio workflow](https://docs.cloud.google.com/looker/docs/studio/a-typical-looker-studio-workflow)

questions.domain: Bootstrapping and maintaining a Google Cloud organization
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company has recently migrated to Google Cloud. You must design a fast, reliable, and repeatable way for the company to provision new projects and basic resources in Google Cloud. What should you do?

options.text: Use the Google Cloud console to create projects.
Write a script by using the gcloud CLI that passes the appropriate parameters from the request. Save the script in a Git repository.
Write a Terraform module and save it in your source control repository. Copy and run the terraform apply command to create the new project.
Use the Terraform repositories from the Cloud Foundation Toolkit. Apply the code with appropriate parameters to create the Google Cloud project and related resources.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Foundation Toolkit Terraform modules and blueprints provide reusable, deployable infrastructure-as-code patterns for provisioning and managing Google Cloud resources at scale. Using the foundation code with request-specific parameters consistently creates the project and its related baseline resources, supporting standardized and repeatable deployments.

**Learn more:** [Terraform blueprints and modules for Google Cloud](https://docs.cloud.google.com/docs/terraform/blueprints/terraform-blueprints) · [Managing infrastructure as code with Terraform, Cloud Build, and GitOps](https://docs.cloud.google.com/docs/terraform/resource-management/managing-infrastructure-as-code)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You administer a retail website for your company. The website comprises several microservices running in a GKE Standard node pool with node autoscaling enabled. Each microservice has resource limits and a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler configured. During a busy period, you receive alerts for one microservice. When you inspect the Pods, half have an `OOMKilled` status, and the Pod count is at the minimum autoscaling limit. You need to resolve this issue. What should you do?

options.text: Update the node pool to use a machine type with more memory.
Increase the maximum number of nodes in the node pool.
Increase the maximum replica limit of the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler.
Increase the memory resource limit of the microservice.

questions.explanation:
A container is marked `OOMKilled` when it exceeds its configured memory limit. Increasing the microservice’s memory resource limit raises that hard per-container boundary to accommodate peak memory usage; adding node capacity or changing autoscaler replica limits does not itself increase the memory available to an individual container.

**Learn more:** [Troubleshoot OOM events | Google Kubernetes Engine](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/troubleshooting/oom-events?hl=en)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company uses Cloud Deploy with multiple delivery pipelines to deploy applications to different environments. The development team currently has no access to any of these pipelines. You need to grant the team access only to the development delivery pipeline while following Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: In the Google Cloud console, grant the development team the roles/clouddeploy.operator role. Add deny conditions to all pipelines other than the development delivery pipeline.

In the Google Cloud console, create a custom IAM role with all clouddeploy.automations.* permissions and an allow policy for only the development delivery pipeline. Grant this IAM role to the development team.
Grant the development team the roles/clouddeploy.operator role in a policy file. Apply the policy file to the development target.
Grant the development team the roles/clouddeploy.developer role in a policy file. Apply this policy file to the development delivery pipeline.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Deploy supports fine-grained IAM access on an individual delivery-pipeline resource. Binding the predefined Cloud Deploy Developer role in an IAM policy and applying that policy to the development delivery pipeline grants the team only the required pipeline-level access, consistent with least privilege.

**Learn more:** [Use IAM to restrict Cloud Deploy access](https://cloud.google.com/deploy/docs/securing/iam) · [IAM roles and permissions for Cloud Deploy](https://cloud.google.com/deploy/docs/iam-roles-permissions)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are reviewing a deployment pipeline in Google Cloud Deploy. You need to reduce pipeline toil and minimize the time required to complete an end-to-end deployment. What should you do? (Choose two.)

options.text: Create a trigger to notify the required team to complete the next step when manual intervention is required.
Divide the automation steps into smaller tasks.
Use a script to automate the creation of the deployment pipeline in Google Cloud Deploy.
Add more engineers to finish the manual steps.
Automate promotion approvals from the development environment to the test environment.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Deploy automation can automatically promote a release to the next target after a successful rollout, removing manual promotion and approval-related delay between development and test. Splitting automation into smaller tasks makes the deployment workflow easier to automate and optimize independently, reducing bottlenecks in the end-to-end process.

**Learn more:** [Automate your deployment | Cloud Deploy](https://docs.cloud.google.com/deploy/docs/automation) · [Using automation rules | Cloud Deploy](https://docs.cloud.google.com/deploy/docs/automation-rules)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your team is designing a new application to deploy in Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). You must configure monitoring to collect and aggregate various application-level metrics in a central location. You want to use Google Cloud Platform services while minimizing the effort needed to set up monitoring. What should you do?

options.text: Publish various metrics from the application directly to the Stackdriver Monitoring API, and then observe these custom metrics in Stackdriver.
Install the Cloud Pub/Sub client libraries, push various metrics from the application to various topics, and then observe the aggregated metrics in Stackdriver.
Install the OpenTelemetry client libraries in the application, configure Stackdriver as the export destination for the metrics, and then observe the application's metrics in Stackdriver.
Emit all metrics in the form of application-specific log messages, pass these messages from the containers to the Stackdriver logging collector, and then observe metrics in Stackdriver.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Monitoring supports user-defined (custom) metrics written through the Cloud Monitoring API. These metrics can be charted, aggregated, alerted on, and viewed centrally in Cloud Monitoring, without introducing an additional messaging pipeline or deriving metrics from logs.

**Learn more:** [Create user-defined metrics with the API](https://docs.cloud.google.com/monitoring/custom-metrics/creating-metrics) · [User-defined metrics overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/monitoring/custom-metrics)

You support a high-traffic web application and want to ensure the home page loads within a timely period. As an initial step, you decide to implement a Service Level Indicator (SLI) representing home page request latency, with an acceptable page-load time of 100 ms. What is Google’s recommended method for calculating this SLI?

options.text: Bucketize the request latencies into ranges, and then compute the percentile at 100 ms.
Bucketize the request latencies into ranges, and then compute the median and 90th percentiles.
Count the number of home page requests that load in under 100 ms, and then divide by the total number of home page requests.
Count the number of home page request that load in under 100 ms, and then divide by the total number of all web application requests.

questions.explanation:
A request-based latency SLI is the ratio of good requests to all relevant requests. With a 100 ms threshold, each home page request that completes in under 100 ms is a good request; dividing that count by all home page requests yields the latency SLI.

**Learn more:** [Concepts in service monitoring](https://docs.cloud.google.com/stackdriver/docs/solutions/slo-monitoring) · [Request-response services](https://docs.cloud.google.com/stackdriver/docs/solutions/slo-monitoring/sli-metrics/req-resp-metrics)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your team of Infrastructure DevOps Engineers is growing, and you are starting to use Terraform to manage infrastructure. You need a way to implement code versioning and to share code with other team members. What should you do?

options.text: Store the Terraform code in a version-control system. Establish procedures for pushing new versions and merging with the master.
Store the Terraform code in a network shared folder with child folders for each version release. Ensure that everyone works on different files.
Store the Terraform code in a Cloud Storage bucket using object versioning. Give access to the bucket to every team member so they can download the files.
Store the Terraform code in a shared Google Drive folder so it syncs automatically to every team member's computer. Organize files with a naming convention that identifies each new version.

questions.explanation:
Terraform configuration files are source code and should be managed using a version-control system (VCS) such as Git. Using a VCS with established branching, push, and merge procedures provides proper history tracking, collaborative code review (via pull/merge requests), conflict resolution, and rollback capability — all essential for a growing team working on shared infrastructure code. Shared network folders, object storage bucket versioning, or synced Google Drive folders do not provide the branching, merging, and review workflows necessary for safe collaborative code changes, making them unsuitable substitutes for a proper VCS. This aligns with HashiCorp's and Google Cloud's recommended practices for managing Terraform configurations as code in a repository like Git.

**Learn more:** [Terraform - Recommended Practices - Using Version Control](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cloud-docs/recommended-practices/part1#version-control) · [Managing infrastructure as code with Terraform, Cloud Build, and GitOps](https://cloud.google.com/architecture/managing-infrastructure-as-code)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company runs Jenkins on Google Cloud VM instances for CI/CD. You need to extend its functionality to use Terraform for infrastructure-as-code automation. Ensure that the Jenkins instance running Terraform is authorized to create Google Cloud resources while following Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Confirm that the Jenkins VM instance has an attached service account with the appropriate Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions.
Use the Terraform module so that Secret Manager can retrieve credentials.
Create a dedicated service account for the Terraform instance. Download and copy the secret key value to the GOOGLE_CREDENTIALS environment variable on the Jenkins server.
Add the gcloud auth application-default login command as a step in Jenkins before running the Terraform commands.

questions.explanation: A workload running on a Google Cloud VM can authenticate through the service account attached to that VM, which Terraform can use through Application Default Credentials. Assigning that service account the required IAM permissions follows least-privilege practice and avoids storing downloaded service-account keys or using interactive login commands in CI/CD automation.

questions.domain: Applying site reliability engineering practices
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You manage a microservice that exposes a public-facing API (Service A). Service A is time-critical and has a response SLO of 500 ms. Service A makes synchronous calls to an internal API (Service B), which is known to become unreliable under heavy load, causing connection timeout errors or 500 errors. Service B collects request information for the transactions handled by Service A.  
  
You need to reduce the impact of Service B problems on Service A users. What should you do?

options.text: Increase the size of the queue in front of the thread pool used by Service A instances.
Implement retry logic with exponential back-offs when calling Service B.
Implement a circuit breaker to store the request data in a database.
Implement rate limiting in Service A to limit the number of requests to Service B.

questions.explanation:
A circuit breaker prevents an unreliable downstream service from causing cascading failures or consuming Service A’s response-time budget. When Service B is unhealthy, a fallback that stores the request data in a database preserves the information for later processing without making Service A users wait on failing synchronous calls. Google Cloud recommends circuit breakers and graceful degradation to reduce traffic to failing or overloaded services and prevent cascading failures.

**Learn more:** [Patterns for scalable and resilient apps](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/scalable-and-resilient-apps)

questions.domain: Optimizing performance and cost
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are conducting a semi-annual capacity-planning exercise for your flagship service. You anticipate service-user growth of 10% month over month during the next six months. Your fully containerized service runs on Google Cloud Platform (GCP) in a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Standard regional cluster spanning three zones, with cluster autoscaler enabled. You currently use approximately 30% of your total deployed CPU capacity and require resilience to the loss of a zone. You want users to experience minimal negative impact from this growth or from a zone failure, while avoiding unnecessary costs. How should you prepare for the predicted growth?

options.text: Verify the maximum node pool size, enable a horizontal pod autoscaler, and then perform a load test to verify your expected resource needs.
Because you are deployed on GKE and are using a cluster autoscaler, your GKE cluster will scale automatically, regardless of growth rate.
Because you are at only 30% utilization, you have significant headroom and you won't need to add any additional capacity for this rate of growth.
Proactively add 60% more node capacity to account for six months of 10% growth rate, and then perform a load test to make sure you have enough capacity.

questions.explanation:
GKE Cluster Autoscaler scales node pools only within their configured minimum and maximum limits, and it adds capacity when Pods cannot be scheduled. Horizontal Pod Autoscaler adjusts workload replica counts in response to CPU, memory, or other supported metrics, allowing application capacity to grow with demand. Confirming the node-pool maximum and validating the expected load ensures that enough capacity remains available when demand rises and when one of the three zones fails, without pre-provisioning unnecessary nodes.

**Learn more:** [About GKE cluster autoscaling](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/cluster-autoscaler) · [Horizontal Pod autoscaling](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/horizontalpodautoscaler)

questions.domain: Applying site reliability engineering practices
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You support a popular mobile game application that runs on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) across multiple Google Cloud regions, with several Kubernetes clusters in each region. You receive a report that no users in one particular region are able to connect to the application. Following Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) practices, what should you do first to resolve this incident?

options.text: Reroute the user traffic from the affected region to other regions that don't report issues.
Use Stackdriver Monitoring to check for a spike in CPU or memory usage for the affected region.
Add an extra node pool that consists of high memory and high CPU machine type instances to the cluster.
Use Stackdriver Logging to filter on the clusters in the affected region, and inspect error messages in the logs.

questions.explanation:
SRE incident response practice emphasizes mitigating customer impact as the immediate priority, deferring root-cause analysis until after service is restored. Since users in only one region are affected while other regions remain healthy, the fastest mitigation is to redirect that region's traffic to unaffected regions, restoring access for impacted users. Investigating logs or metrics (Stackdriver Logging/Monitoring) is appropriate for root-cause analysis but should happen after mitigation, and provisioning new node pools addresses a capacity concern rather than the reported connectivity failure.

**Learn more:** [Troubleshoot GKE | Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/troubleshooting)

questions.domain: Applying site reliability engineering practices
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an application deployed on Cloud Run. A new application version was recently deployed with the canary deployment strategy. Your Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) teammate tells you that an SLO has been exceeded for this application. You need to restore application health as quickly as possible. What should you do first?

options.text: Configure traffic splitting to send 100% of the traffic to the latest revision.
Configure traffic splitting to send 100% of the traffic to the previous revision.
Create a new revision using the last known good version of the application.
Identify the cause of the latency by using Cloud Trace.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Run supports rollback by changing the traffic split so that the previous revision receives 100% of traffic and the currently serving revision receives 0%. This immediately limits further exposure to the failing canary while preserving the known-good revision; diagnosis can follow after service health is restored.

**Learn more:** [Rollbacks, gradual rollouts, and traffic migration | Cloud Run](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/rollouts-rollbacks-traffic-migration)

questions.question: You support an e-commerce application running on a large Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster deployed on-premises and on Google Cloud Platform. The application consists of containerized microservices. You want to identify the containers using the most CPU and memory. What should you do?

options.text: Use Stackdriver Kubernetes Engine Monitoring.
Use Prometheus to collect and aggregate logs per container, and then analyze the results in Grafana.
Use the Stackdriver Monitoring API to create custom metrics, and then organize your containers using groups.
Use Stackdriver Logging to export application logs to BigQuery, aggregate logs per container, and then analyze CPU and memory consumption.

questions.explanation: Stackdriver Kubernetes Engine Monitoring provides Kubernetes workload resource metrics, including per-container CPU and memory utilization, enabling identification of the containers with the highest consumption.

questions.domain: Applying site reliability engineering practices
questions.question: You support an e-commerce application running on a large Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster deployed on-premises and on Google Cloud Platform. The application consists of containerized microservices. You want to identify the containers using the most CPU and memory. What should you do?

options.text: Focus on developing new features rather than avoiding the outages from recurring.
Focus on identifying the contributing causes of the incident rather than the individual responsible for the cause.
Plan individual meetings with all the engineers involved. Determine who approved and pushed the new release to production.
Use the Git history to find the related code commit. Prevent the engineer who made that commit from working on production services.

questions.explanation:
Google's SRE practices call for blameless postmortems, where the goal is to identify the technical and process factors — the contributing causes — that led to an incident, rather than assigning blame to the individual(s) involved. This approach encourages engineers to be forthcoming with details about what happened without fear of punishment, which leads to more accurate root-cause analysis and more effective preventive action items. Singling out or restricting a specific engineer (as in the other options) undermines this culture and discourages honest reporting in the future.

**Learn more:** [Postmortem Culture: Learning from Failure — Google SRE Book](https://sre.google/sre-book/postmortem-culture/)

questions.domain: Implementing observability practices and troubleshooting issues
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company operates applications in Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). Several applications depend on ephemeral volumes. You observed that some applications were unstable because of the DiskPressure node condition on worker nodes. You must identify which Pods are causing the problem, but you do not have execute access to workloads or nodes. What should you do?

options.text: Check the node/ephemeral_storage/used_bytes metric by using Metrics Explorer.
Check the container/ephemeral_storage/used_bytes metric by using Metrics Explorer.
Locate all the Pods with emptyDir volumes. Use the df -h command to measure volume disk usage.
Locate all the Pods with emptyDir volumes. Use the df -sh * command to measure volume disk usage.

questions.explanation:
The `container/ephemeral_storage/used_bytes` Cloud Monitoring metric reports local ephemeral-storage usage for each Kubernetes container. In Metrics Explorer, it can be filtered or grouped by resource labels to identify the Pods consuming the storage. The node-level metric provides only aggregate node usage and cannot identify the responsible Pods.

**Learn more:** [GKE system metrics](https://docs.cloud.google.com/monitoring/api/metrics_kubernetes)

questions.domain: Applying site reliability engineering practices
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You experience a large number of outages in the production systems you support. You receive alerts for every outage; the alerts result from unhealthy systems that automatically restart within a minute. You want to establish a process that prevents staff burnout while following Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) practices. What should you do?

options.text: Eliminate alerts that are not actionable
Redefine the related SLO so that the error budget is not exhausted
Distribute the alerts to engineers in different time zones
Create an incident report for each of the alerts

questions.explanation:
Alerts for failures that recover automatically within a minute are not actionable by staff. SRE practice is to alert humans on significant, actionable events, so eliminating non-actionable alerts reduces alert fatigue and repetitive operational toil without masking conditions that require intervention.

**Learn more:** [Google SRE Workbook: Alerting on SLOs](https://sre.google/workbook/alerting-on-slos/) · [Google SRE Workbook: Eliminating Toil](https://sre.google/workbook/eliminating-toil/)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You support an application running on Compute Engine. The application connects to a Cloud SQL instance to store and retrieve data. After an application update, users report errors that show database timeout messages. The number of concurrently active users has stayed stable. You need to identify the most likely cause of the database timeout. What should you do?

options.text: Check the serial port logs of the Compute Engine instance.
Use Stackdriver Profiler to visualize the resources utilization throughout the application.
Determine whether there is an increased number of connections to the Cloud SQL instance.
Use Cloud Security Scanner to see whether your Cloud SQL is under a Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attack.

questions.explanation:
Database connections consume resources on both the database server and the application, and Cloud SQL imposes connection limits. An application update can increase or leak connections even when the active-user count is unchanged, exhausting available connections or causing requests to wait until they time out. Checking whether the Cloud SQL instance has an increased connection count directly validates that likely cause. [Debug connection issues — Cloud SQL](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/debugging-connectivity)

**Learn more:** [Debug connection issues — Cloud SQL](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/debugging-connectivity) · [Manage database connections — Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/manage-connections)
