options.text: Create a trigger on the Cloud Build job. Set the repository event setting to ‘Pull request’.
Add the OWNERS file to the Included files filter on the trigger.
Create a trigger on the Cloud Build job. Set the repository event setting to ‘Push to a branch’
Configure a branch protection rule for the main branch on the repository.
Enable the Approval option on the trigger.

questions.explanation:
A Cloud Build trigger configured for a push to the `main` branch automatically initiates builds only when commits are pushed to that branch. A GitHub branch protection rule can require pull requests and approving reviews before changes are merged into `main`, allowing the change control team to enforce approval while retaining automated builds. Cloud Build trigger approvals instead pause builds after invocation and do not govern approval of GitHub pushes.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Build: Create and manage build triggers](https://docs.cloud.google.com/build/docs/automating-builds/create-manage-triggers) · [GitHub Docs: Managing a branch protection rule](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-protected-branches/managing-a-branch-protection-rule)

You work for a healthcare company, and regulations require that all resources be created in a United States-based region. You tried to create a secret in Secret Manager but received this error message:  
  
`Constraint constraints/gcp.resourceLocations violated for [orgpolicy:projects/000000] attempting to create a secret in [global]`  
  
You need to resolve the error while staying compliant with the regulations. What should you do?

options.text: Remove the organization policy referenced in the error message.
Create the secret with an automatic replication policy.
Create the secret with a user-managed replication policy.
Add the global region to the organization policy referenced in the error message.

questions.explanation:
Secret Manager automatic replication requires the `global` location to be permitted and can replicate secret payload data without geographic restriction. A user-managed replication policy lets the secret be replicated only to selected, organization-policy-allowed U.S. locations, satisfying the location constraint and the data-residency requirement.

**Learn more:** [Choose a secret replication policy](https://cloud.google.com/secret-manager/docs/choosing-replication) · [Services that support restricting resource locations](https://cloud.google.com/organization-policy/reference/restrict-locations-supported-services)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are running an application on a virtual machine (VM) that uses a custom Debian image. The image has the Stackdriver Logging agent installed, and the VM has the `cloud-platform` scope. The application logs information through syslog.  
  
You want to use Stackdriver Logging in the Google Cloud Platform Console to visualize the logs. However, syslog does not appear in the **"All logs"** drop-down list of the Logs Viewer. What should you do first?

options.text: Look for the agent's test log entry in the Logs Viewer.
Install the most recent version of the Stackdriver agent.
Verify the VM service account access scope includes the monitoring.write scope.
SSH to the VM and execute the following commands on your VM: ps ax | grep fluentd.

questions.explanation:
On Linux, the Stackdriver Logging agent runs as `fluentd`; it must be running before syslog entries can be collected and appear in Cloud Logging. The `cloud-platform` scope already covers the necessary API access, while `monitoring.write` applies to Monitoring metrics rather than log ingestion. Google’s Logging agent troubleshooting guidance directs users to verify the agent process with `ps ax | grep fluentd`.

**Learn more:** [Troubleshoot the Logging agent](https://docs.cloud.google.com/stackdriver/docs/solutions/agents/logging/troubleshooting)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are operating an application on Compute Engine and collecting logs with Stackdriver. You find that personally identifiable information (PII) is leaking into certain log-entry fields. Every PII entry starts with the text `userinfo`.  
  
You need to capture these log entries in a secure location for later review while preventing them from leaking into Stackdriver Logging. What should you do?

options.text: Create a basic log filter matching userinfo, and then configure a log export in the Stackdriver console with Cloud Storage as a sink.
Use a Fluentd filter plugin with the Stackdriver Agent to remove log entries containing userinfo, and then copy the entries to a Cloud Storage bucket.
Create an advanced log filter matching userinfo, configure a log export in the Stackdriver console with Cloud Storage as a sink, and then configure a log exclusion with userinfo as a filter.

Use a Fluentd filter plugin with the Stackdriver Agent to remove log entries containing userinfo, create an advanced log filter matching userinfo, and then configure a log export in the Stackdriver console with Cloud Storage as a sink.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Logging sinks can use an advanced inclusion filter to route matching log entries to a Cloud Storage destination. An exclusion filter on the default sink prevents entries matching `userinfo` from being stored in the default Cloud Logging bucket, while the separately configured export sink retains the matched entries in Cloud Storage for review.

**Learn more:** [Route logs to supported destinations](https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/export/configure_export_v2) · [Configure default resource settings for Cloud Logging](https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/default-settings)

questions.domain: Optimizing performance and cost
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are responsible for supporting a web application that runs on App Engine and relies on Cloud SQL and Cloud Storage for data storage. Following a brief spike in website traffic, you observe a significant increase in latency for all user requests, along with higher CPU usage and a greater number of processes running the application.  
  
Initial troubleshooting reveals the following:  
  
- After the traffic spike subsided and load levels returned to normal, users continue to experience high latency.  
- Requests for content from the Cloud SQL database and images from Cloud Storage exhibit the same elevated latency.  
- No changes were made to the website around the time the latency increase began.  
- There has been no increase in the number of errors experienced by users.  
  
You anticipate another spike in website traffic in the near future and want to ensure that users do not experience latency during that time. What should you do?

options.text: Upgrade the GCS buckets to Multi-Regional.
Enable high availability on the CloudSQL instances.
Move the application from App Engine to Compute Engine.
Modify the App Engine configuration to have additional idle instances.

questions.explanation:
App Engine's automatic scaling spins up new instances in response to traffic spikes, and each new instance incurs a startup (cold-start) delay while it initializes the runtime and establishes connections to backend services such as Cloud SQL and Cloud Storage. This explains why latency rose uniformly for both database and storage requests without any increase in errors or code changes — the bottleneck is instance startup overhead, not the backend services themselves or application logic. Configuring the App Engine service to maintain additional idle (warm) instances ensures that during future traffic spikes there are already-initialized instances ready to serve requests immediately, avoiding the cold-start latency penalty. Upgrading Cloud Storage to multi-regional or enabling Cloud SQL high availability would not address instance startup latency, and migrating to Compute Engine would forgo App Engine's managed scaling without solving the underlying cold-start issue.

**Learn more:** [How Instances are Managed - App Engine standard environment](https://cloud.google.com/appengine/docs/standard/how-instances-are-managed) · [Configuring your app with app.yaml - App Engine](https://cloud.google.com/appengine/docs/standard/python3/config/appref)

You must run a business-critical workload on a fixed group of Compute Engine instances for several months. The workload is stable and uses the exact resources allocated to it. You want to reduce this workload’s cost with no performance impact. What should you do?

options.text: Purchase Committed Use Discounts.
Migrate the instances to a Managed Instance Group.
Convert the instances to preemptible virtual machines.
Create an Unmanaged Instance Group for the instances used to run the workload.

questions.explanation:
Committed Use Discounts are designed for predictable, steady-state Compute Engine usage. They provide discounted pricing in exchange for committing to a specified amount of resource usage for a term, without requiring a change to the workload’s instance performance or availability characteristics.

**Learn more:** [Committed use discounts (CUDs) for Compute Engine](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/committed-use-discounts-overview?hl=en)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to create a Cloud Monitoring SLO for a service that will be published soon. You want to confirm that requests to the service are handled in fewer than 300 ms at least 90% of the time per calendar month. You need to identify the metric and evaluation method to use. What should you do?

options.text: Select a latency metric for a request-based method of evaluation.
Select a latency metric for a window-based method of evaluation.
Select an availability metric for a request-based method of evaluation.
Select an availability metric for a window-based method of evaluation.

questions.explanation:
A latency metric measures whether requests meet a response-time threshold. Request-based evaluation calculates the proportion of individual requests that satisfy that threshold out of all requests during the calendar-month compliance period, matching a target of at least 90% of requests completing in fewer than 300 ms.

**Learn more:** [Concepts in service monitoring](https://docs.cloud.google.com/stackdriver/docs/solutions/slo-monitoring) · [Creating an SLO](https://docs.cloud.google.com/stackdriver/docs/solutions/slo-monitoring/ui/create-slo?hl=en)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],While creating and assigning action items in a postmortem following an outage, the outage itself has been resolved, but you still need to address the underlying root causes. You want to make sure your team handles these action items quickly and efficiently. How should you assign owners and collaborators to the action items?

options.text: Assign one owner for each action item and any necessary collaborators.
Assign multiple owners for each item to guarantee that the team addresses items quickly.
Assign collaborators but no individual owners to the items to keep the postmortem blameless.
Assign the team lead as the owner for all action items because they are in charge of the SRE team.

questions.explanation:
Google's SRE postmortem practices recommend giving each action item a single, clearly designated owner (with additional collaborators as needed) so there is unambiguous accountability for driving the item to resolution. Multiple owners create diffusion of responsibility, no owner conflicts with the goal of actually completing remediation work (blameless refers to not assigning blame for the incident, not avoiding ownership of follow-up tasks), and funneling all ownership through the team lead does not scale and ignores subject-matter fit for each task.

**Learn more:** [Postmortem Culture: Learning from Failure - Google SRE Book](https://sre.google/sre-book/postmortem-culture/) · [Google SRE Workbook - Postmortems](https://sre.google/workbook/postmortem-culture/)

questions.domain: Applying site reliability engineering practices
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are responsible for supporting a large service that has a clearly defined Service Level Objective (SLO). The development team ships new releases of this service several times per week.  
  
If a major incident occurs that causes the service to fall short of its SLO, you want the development team to redirect its efforts away from new feature work and toward improving the service's reliability.  
  
What should you do in advance, before any major incident happens?

options.text: Develop an appropriate error budget policy in cooperation with all service stakeholders.
Negotiate with the product team to always prioritize service reliability over releasing new features.
Negotiate with the development team to reduce the release frequency to no more than once a week.
Add a plugin to your Jenkins pipeline that prevents new releases whenever your service is out of SLO.

questions.explanation:
An error budget policy, developed collaboratively with all stakeholders (development, product management, and SRE/operations), defines in advance what happens when the error budget is exhausted — including that engineering effort shifts from feature development to reliability work. Establishing this policy ahead of time ensures there is organizational agreement and a clear, pre-negotiated process to follow when an incident causes an SLO miss, rather than having to negotiate priorities reactively during or after a crisis. This is the standard Google SRE practice for aligning reliability and feature-velocity trade-offs.

**Learn more:** [Error Budget Policy - Google SRE Workbook](https://sre.google/workbook/error-budget-policy/) · [Motivation for Error Budgets - Google SRE Book](https://sre.google/sre-book/embracing-risk/)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You receive a Cloud Monitoring alert that indicates possible malicious activity on a node in your Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster. The alert suggests that a container running on that node might be compromised. You must isolate the node to prevent further compromise while you investigate the issue, while also minimizing disruption to applications running in the cluster. What should you do?

options.text: Taint the suspicious node to prevent Pods that have interacted with it from being scheduled on other nodes in the cluster
Scale down the deployment associated with the compromised container to zero other nodes
Restart the node to disrupt the malicious activity, and force all Pods to be restructured on other nodes.
Cordon the node to prevent new Pods from being scheduled, the drain the node to safely remove existing Pods and reschedule them to other nodes.

questions.explanation:
Cordoning prevents new Pods from being scheduled onto the suspect node. Draining then evicts its existing workloads so managed workloads can be rescheduled to other nodes, reducing exposure while preserving application availability. In GKE security incident mitigation, draining respects PodDisruptionBudgets, which helps limit disruption.

**Learn more:** [Mitigate security incidents | GKE security](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/security-mitigations)

questions.domain: Applying site reliability engineering practices
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company is actively building a new web service using site reliability engineering (SRE) practices. You lead the company’s SRE team and are getting the service ready for production. You must ensure the team follows Google-recommended SRE practices during this productionalization process. Which two actions should you take next? (Choose two.)

options.text: Establish monitoring and alerting systems.
Start to document infrastructure system guidelines.
Collaborate with the product team to design the service.
Implement redundancy measures.
Provide early engagement consulting to discuss architecture and design choices in detail.

questions.explanation:
Google SRE describes productionalization as including extra resources for redundancy and sustainable operational practices such as monitoring and alerting. These measures provide resilience against failures and enable prompt detection and response to production-impacting conditions.

**Learn more:** [Google SRE Workbook: Continuous Improvement for Reliable Service](https://sre.google/workbook/engagement-model/)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization operates a containerized web application on-premises. As part of its migration plan to Google Cloud, you must choose a deployment strategy and platform that satisfy these acceptance criteria:  
  
1. The platform must be capable of routing traffic from Android devices to an Android-specific microservice.  
2. The platform must support arbitrary percentage-based traffic splitting.  
3. The deployment strategy must support continuous testing of multiple versions of any microservice.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Deploy the canary release of the application to Cloud Run. Use traffic splitting to direct 10% of user traffic to the canary release based on the revision tag.
Deploy the canary release of the application to App Engine. Use traffic splitting to direct a subset of user traffic to the new version based on the IP address.
Deploy the canary release of the application to Compute Engine. Use Anthos Service Mesh with Compute Engine to direct 10% of user traffic to the canary release by configuring the virtual service.

Deploy the canary release to Google Kubernetes Engine with Anthos Service Mesh. Use traffic splitting to direct 10% of user traffic to the new version based on the user-agent header configured in the virtual service.

questions.explanation:
Anthos Service Mesh on Google Kubernetes Engine supports fine-grained routing based on HTTP request headers, including routing requests with a `user-agent: Android` header to an Android-specific service. Its routing configuration also supports weight-based traffic splitting across multiple service versions, enabling canary deployments and continuous testing while versions run concurrently.

**Learn more:** [Advanced traffic management overview | Cloud Service Mesh](https://cloud.google.com/service-mesh/docs/service-routing/advanced-traffic-management) · [Cloud Service Mesh service routing APIs overview](https://cloud.google.com/service-mesh/v1.24/docs/service-routing/service-routing-overview)

You are working on a Google Cloud project that has been in production for several months and need to update an IAM policy to give a team member additional permissions. You must proactively identify any potential risks related to these IAM policy changes before applying them to the production environment. What should you do?

options.text: Implement the IAM policy changes. Use the recent change recommendations to monitor for any unintended consequences.
Use the change risk recommendations to assess the potential impact of the IAM policy changes, and identify any associated risks before applying them.
Grant the new team member the Project Owner role. Reevaluate permissions after their task is complete.
Use the Cloud deprecation and breaking changes general recommender to assess the impact of the IAM policy changes on any potentially deprecated or soon-to-be-changed services.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud Change Risk Recommendations proactively flag risky changes to important resources, including IAM policy changes, so their potential impact and associated risks can be assessed before deployment. Recent change recommendations evaluate changes already made, while the deprecation and breaking-changes recommender addresses upcoming service deprecations rather than IAM policy modifications.

**Learn more:** [Change risk recommendations | Recommender | Google Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/recommender/docs/change-risk-recommendations)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You recently created a Cloud Build pipeline to deploy Terraform code kept in a GitHub repository. You make Terraform code changes in short-lived branches and occasionally use tags during development. When releases are ready for deployment, you tag them with a semantic version. You need the pipeline to apply the Terraform code whenever there is a new release, while minimizing operational overhead. What should you do?

options.text: Create a build trigger with the \d+\.\d+\.\d+ tag pattern.
Create a build trigger with the \d+\.\d+\.\d+ branch pattern.
Create a build trigger with the .* tag pattern.
Create a build trigger with the .* branch pattern.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Build supports triggers for a new tag and evaluates the tag value against a regular expression. Restricting a tag trigger to `\d+\.\d+\.\d+` runs the Terraform deployment only for semantic-version release tags, excluding development tags and all branch changes.

**Learn more:** [Create and manage build triggers | Cloud Build](https://docs.cloud.google.com/build/docs/automating-builds/create-manage-triggers)

questions.domain: Bootstrapping and maintaining a Google Cloud organization
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization uses Helm to package containerized applications. Its applications reference both public and private charts. The security team has identified use of a public Helm repository as a risk. You want to manage every chart consistently, with native access control and VPC Service Controls. What should you do?

options.text: Store public and private charts in OCI format by using Artifact Registry.
Store public and private charts by using GitHub Enterprise with Google Workspace as the identity provider.

Store public and private charts by using Git repository. Configure Cloud Build to synchronize contents of the repository into a Cloud Storage bucket. Connect Helm to the bucket by using https://[bucket].storage-googleapis.com/[helmchart] as the Helm repository.
Configure a Helm chart repository server to run in Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) with Cloud Storage bucket as the storage backend.

questions.explanation:
Artifact Registry can centrally store Helm 3 charts as OCI container images in Docker repositories. It uses IAM for repository access control and supports VPC Service Controls security perimeters, allowing public dependencies to be imported and managed alongside private charts under the same controls.

**Learn more:** [Work with Helm charts | Artifact Registry](https://cloud.google.com/artifact-registry/docs/helm) · [Protect repositories in a service perimeter | Artifact Registry](https://cloud.google.com/artifact-registry/docs/securing-with-vpc-sc)

questions.domain: Optimizing performance and cost
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are building applications that run on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), with each team responsible for a different application. You need to set up Development and Production environments for every team while keeping costs as low as possible. Teams must not be able to access the environments belonging to other teams.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Create one GCP Project per team. In each project, create a cluster for Development and one for Production. Grant the teams IAM access to their respective clusters.
Create one GCP Project per team. In each project, create a cluster with a Kubernetes namespace for Development and one for Production. Grant the teams IAM access to their respective clusters.

Create a Development and a Production GKE cluster in separate projects. In each cluster, create a Kubernetes namespace per team, and then configure Identity Aware Proxy so that each team can only access its own namespace.

Create a Development and a Production GKE cluster in separate projects. In each cluster, create a Kubernetes namespace per team, and then configure Kubernetes Role-based access control (RBAC) so that each team can only access its own namespace.

questions.explanation:
Using a single Development cluster and a single Production cluster (rather than a separate project and cluster pair per team) minimizes the number of clusters and their associated overhead, keeping costs low. Within each cluster, creating one Kubernetes namespace per team provides logical separation of each team's resources. Kubernetes RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) is the native mechanism for restricting access to specific namespaces — by binding Roles/RoleBindings scoped to a namespace to each team's users or groups, you ensure a team can only view or modify resources in its own namespace, satisfying the isolation requirement without the cost of provisioning additional clusters or projects. Identity-Aware Proxy, by contrast, is intended for controlling access to HTTP(S) applications behind a load balancer and is not the appropriate control for restricting access to Kubernetes namespaces/API objects.

**Learn more:** [Best practices for GKE RBAC](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/best-practices/rbac) · [Cluster multi-tenancy | Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE)](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/multitenancy-overview)

You are designing a CI/CD pipeline that deploys a containerized application from your GitHub repository to Artifact Registry. The build process must trigger whenever a new tag is created. The build requires approval from the [email protected] Google group. To satisfy your company’s security requirements, you must avoid static credentials and federation with any other system.  
  
How should you configure the CI/CD pipeline?

options.text: 1. Create a GitHub trigger in Cloud Build to execute a build whenever a new tag is created.2. Create a Cloud Build approval.3. Grant the roles/cloudbuild.builds.approver role to the [email protected] Google group, and grant the roles/artifactregistry.writer role to the service account used by the trigger.

1. Use GitHub Actions to create a workflow to containerize the application and push the container to Artifact Registry when a new tag is created.2. Create a GitHub team with the same members as the [email protected] Google group, and add the team as a mandatory approval.3. On the Google Cloud project, create a service account and a service account key.4. Use the key on the workflow to authenticate with Google Cloud.5. Grant the roles/artifactregistry.writer role to the service account.

1. Create an SSH key and add it as a deploy key on GitHub.2. Create a Cloud Build trigger that uses the SSH key to pull the repository.3. Create a Cloud Build approval.4. Grant the roles/cloudbuild.builds.editor role to the [email protected] Google group, and grant the roles/artifactregistry.writer role to the service account used by the trigger.

1. Use GitHub Actions to create a workflow to containerize the application and push the container to Artifact Registry when a new tag is created.2. Create a GitHub team with the same members as the [email protected] Google group, and add the team as a mandatory approval.3. Create a workload identity pool on Google Cloud to authorize the identity of the GitHub workflow.4. Grant the roles/artifactregistry.writer role to the workload identity pool authorized entity.

questions.explanation:
A Cloud Build GitHub trigger can be configured for a **Push new tag** event and to require approval before its build executes. The `roles/cloudbuild.builds.approver` role grants the permission to approve or reject pending builds, so it should be assigned to the required Google group. The service account used by the trigger needs `roles/artifactregistry.writer` to upload the container image to Artifact Registry. This native Cloud Build integration avoids both a static service-account key and external workload identity federation.

**Learn more:** [Create and manage build triggers](https://docs.cloud.google.com/build/docs/automating-builds/create-manage-triggers) · [Gate builds on approval](https://docs.cloud.google.com/build/docs/securing-builds/gate-builds-on-approval)

You have an application running in production on Cloud Run. Your team has recently completed development of a new application version (revision B). You want to test the new revision with 10% of your clients while using the least effort. What should you do?

options.text: Deploy the new revision to the existing service without traffic allocated. Tag the revision and share the URL with 10% of your clients.
Create a new service, and deploy the new revisions on the new service. Deploy a new revision of the old application where the application routes a percentage of the traffic to the new service.
Create a new service, and deploy the new revision on that new service. Create a load balancer to split the traffic between the old service and the new service.
Deploy the new revision to the existing service without traffic allocated. Split the traffic between the old revision and the new revision.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Run can deploy a new revision with zero traffic and then split a service's traffic between the existing and new revisions. Assigning 10% of traffic to revision B performs a gradual rollout with the existing revision receiving the remaining traffic, requiring no additional service or load balancer.

**Learn more:** [Rollbacks, gradual rollouts, and traffic migration | Cloud Run](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/rollouts-rollbacks-traffic-migration?hl=en)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are rolling out a new version of your application to a multi-zone Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster. The deployment is progressing smoothly, but some Pods in one specific zone are showing higher error rates. You need to selectively revert the update for the Pods with errors while minimizing user impact. What should you do?

options.text: Scale down the Pods in the affected zone. Redeploy the new version of the application.
Drain the affected nodes. Redeploy the new version of the application to the remaining nodes.
Modify the Deployment to use the Pod template from the previous version of your application. Perform a rolling update to replace the Pods in the affected zone.
Use the kubectl rollout undo command to roll back the entire deployment. Redeploy the new version of the application, excluding the affected zone.

questions.explanation:
Changing a Deployment’s Pod template triggers a rolling update, which gradually replaces Pods while maintaining application availability. Restoring the previous application template is the rollback mechanism that returns replacement Pods to the prior version; scaling down Pods or draining nodes does not itself restore that version. `kubectl rollout undo` instead rolls back the entire Deployment.

**Learn more:** [Kubernetes: Update a Deployment Without Downtime](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/run-application/update-deployment-rolling/) · [Kubernetes: Deployments](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],An application deployed on Google Kubernetes Engine calls several backend services for each incoming request, but the overall response time is too slow. You need to determine which downstream service or services are responsible for the delay. What should you do?

options.text: Analyze VPC flow logs along the path of the request.
Investigate the Liveness and Readiness probes for each service.
Create a Dataflow pipeline to analyze service metrics in real time.
Use a distributed tracing framework such as OpenTelemetry or Stackdriver Trace.

questions.explanation:
Distributed tracing tools such as OpenTelemetry combined with Cloud Trace (Stackdriver Trace) capture timing spans for each service call within a single request, allowing you to visualize the full request path and pinpoint exactly which downstream service is adding latency. VPC flow logs only capture network flow metadata and are not designed to show per-request application latency. Liveness and Readiness probes check container health/availability, not request processing time. Dataflow is a data processing service for batch/streaming pipelines and is not suited for real-time request-level latency diagnosis. Google Cloud's Cloud Trace documentation specifically recommends distributed tracing to identify performance bottlenecks across microservices.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Trace overview](https://cloud.google.com/trace/docs/overview) · [OpenTelemetry and Cloud Trace](https://cloud.google.com/trace/docs/setup)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have a CI/CD pipeline that uses Cloud Build to build new Docker images and push them to Docker Hub. You use Git for code versioning. After changing the Cloud Build YAML configuration, you find that the pipeline is no longer building new artifacts. You need to fix the issue in accordance with Site Reliability Engineering practices. What should you do?

options.text: Disable the CI pipeline and revert to manually building and pushing the artifacts.
Change the CI pipeline to push the artifacts is Container Registry instead of Docker Hub.
Upload the configuration YAML file to Cloud Storage and use Error Reporting to identify and fix the issue.
Run a Git compare between the previous and current Cloud Build Configuration files to find and fix the bug.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Build uses the build configuration file to define the instructions and steps that create and publish artifacts. Comparing the current YAML configuration with the previous known-good version in Git identifies the change that caused the build regression, so it can be fixed without replacing the automated and reproducible CI/CD process.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Build build configuration file schema](https://docs.cloud.google.com/build/docs/build-config-file-schema) · [Cloud Build troubleshooting](https://docs.cloud.google.com/build/docs/troubleshooting)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are designing a deployment approach for your applications on Google Cloud. As part of deployment planning, you want to use live traffic to collect performance metrics for new versions of your applications. You need to test under the full production load before the applications are launched. What should you do?

options.text: Use A/B testing with blue/green deployment.
Use canary testing with continuous deployment.
Use canary testing with rolling updates deployment.
Use shadow testing with continuous deployment.

questions.explanation:
Shadow testing mirrors live production traffic to a new application version, allowing its performance to be measured under full production load without making that version responsible for user-facing responses. Canary testing exposes the new version to only a subset of traffic, so it does not satisfy the full-load requirement.

**Learn more:** [Use a deployment strategy | Cloud Deploy | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/deploy/docs/deployment-strategies)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You use Artifact Registry to store container images built with Cloud Build. You must ensure that every existing and newly added image is continuously scanned for vulnerabilities. You also need to track who pushed each image to the registry. What should you do?

options.text: Configure Artifact Registry to automatically scan new images and periodically re-scan all images. Use Cloud Audit Logs to track image uploads and identify the user who pushed each image.
Configure Artifact Registry to send vulnerability scan results to a Cloud Storage bucket. Use a separate script to parse results and notify a security team.
Configure Artifact Registry to automatically re-scan images daily. Enable Cloud Audit Logs to track these scans, and use Logs Explorer to identify vulnerabilities.
Configure Artifact Registry to automatically trigger vulnerability scans for new image tags, and view scan results. Use Cloud Audit Logs to track image tag creation events.

questions.explanation:
Artifact Analysis automatically scans container images pushed to Artifact Registry and continuously updates their vulnerability metadata as new vulnerability information becomes available. Artifact Registry upload operations generate Cloud Audit Logs, whose caller identity identifies the principal that performed the upload. Existing images require initial scanning coverage, while continuous analysis keeps scanned-image findings current.

**Learn more:** [Artifact analysis and vulnerability scanning](https://cloud.google.com/artifact-registry/docs/analysis) · [Artifact Registry audit logging](https://cloud.google.com/artifact-registry/docs/audit-logging)

questions.domain: Optimizing performance and cost
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are configuring the frontend tier of an application deployed on Google Cloud. The frontend tier runs on nginx and is deployed by using a managed instance group, with an Envoy-based external HTTP(S) load balancer in front of it. The application is deployed entirely in the `europe-west2` region and serves only users located in the United Kingdom. You need to select the most cost-effective network tier and load-balancing configuration. What should you use?

options.text: Premium Tier with a global load balancer
Premium Tier with a regional load balancer
Standard Tier with a global load balancer
Standard Tier with a regional load balancer

questions.explanation:
A regional external Application Load Balancer can use the Standard Network Service Tier, which provides lower outbound data-transfer charges. Because all backends are in `europe-west2` and the application serves only United Kingdom users, global load balancing and Premium Tier are unnecessary for this deployment.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Load Balancing pricing](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/pricing) · [Choose a load balancer](https://docs.cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/choosing-load-balancer)

questions.domain: Applying site reliability engineering practices

options.text: Add more serving capacity to all of your application's zones.
Have more frequent or potentially risky application releases.
Tighten the SLO match the application's observed reliability.
Implement and measure additional Service Level Indicators (SLIs) fro the application.
Announce planned downtime to consume more error budget, and ensure that users are not depending on a tighter SLO.

questions.explanation: Since the SLO has already been confirmed as appropriate by stakeholders, but the error budget is barely being consumed, the recommended approach in SRE practice is to intentionally use more of the available error budget rather than making the SLO stricter. This can be done by increasing release cadence or accepting more risk in releases (consuming budget through planned engineering velocity), or by scheduling planned maintenance/downtime that consumes budget in a controlled way while confirming users aren't relying on a tighter reliability guarantee than the SLO promises. Both approaches let the error budget's actual usage better reflect the agreed SLO without compromising business needs, and they preserve room for innovation and velocity rather than locking in unnecessarily high reliability.

Your company plans to implement a Cloud Deploy CD pipeline for a web service deployed to GKE. The web service currently has no automated testing. The Quality Assurance team must manually validate all new web-service releases before any production traffic is handled. You need to design the CD pipeline. What should you do?

options.text: Create a single pipeline stage, and use a standard deployment strategy.
Create a single pipeline stage, and use a canary deployment strategy.
Create two pipeline stages, and use a canary deployment strategy.
Create two pipeline stages, and use a standard deployment strategy.

questions.explanation:
A two-stage pipeline separates manual QA validation from the production deployment, so a release can be approved after QA and before promotion to production. Cloud Deploy can require approval before promotion to a target. A canary deployment progressively routes a portion of traffic to the new version, which would expose production traffic before the required manual validation; a standard deployment is therefore the suitable strategy after the QA gate.

**Learn more:** [Overview of Cloud Deploy](https://docs.cloud.google.com/deploy/docs/overview) · [Use a canary deployment strategy](https://docs.cloud.google.com/deploy/docs/deployment-strategies/canary)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You manage your company’s main revenue-generating application. An error-budget policy is in place that freezes production deployments when the application is nearing an SLO breach. Several issues have occurred recently, and the application has used up its error budget. You need to deploy a new application release containing a feature that your largest customer urgently requires. You have been informed that the release passed all unit tests. What should you do?

options.text: Delay the deployment of the feature until the error budget is replenished.
Re-run the unit tests, and start the deployment of the feature if the tests pass.
Start the deployment of the feature immediately.

options.text: Push the images to Google Container Registry (GCR) using the gcr.io hostname.

You are responsible for creating and updating the Terraform templates that define your infrastructure. Because two new engineers will also work on the same code, you need to establish a process and adopt a tool that prevents team members from overwriting one another’s code. You also need to ensure that all updates are included in the latest version. What should you do?

options.text: ג€¢ Store your code in a Git-based version control system. ג€¢ Establish a process that allows developers to merge their own changes at the end of each day. ג€¢ Package and upload code to a versioned Cloud Storage basket as the latest master version.

ג€¢ Store your code in a Git-based version control system. ג€¢ Establish a process that includes code reviews by peers and unit testing to ensure integrity and functionality before integration of code. ג€¢ Establish a process where the fully integrated code in the repository becomes the latest master version.

ג€¢ Store your code as text files in Google Drive in a defined folder structure that organizes the files. ג€¢ At the end of each day, confirm that all changes have been captured in the files within the folder structure. ג€¢ Rename the folder structure with a predefined naming convention that increments the version.

ג€¢ Store your code as text files in Google Drive in a defined folder structure that organizes the files. ג€¢ At the end of each day, confirm that all changes have been captured in the files within the folder structure and create a new .zip archive with a predefined naming convention. ג€¢ Upload the .zip archive to a versioned Cloud Storage bucket and accept it as the latest version.

questions.explanation:
Terraform infrastructure code should be stored in a Git-based version-control repository. Developers work in branches and integrate completed changes through reviewed pull requests, with testing performed before merging. The protected integrated main branch represents the latest approved code, providing a single authoritative version while preserving history and handling concurrent changes.

**Learn more:** [Best practices for version control | Terraform on Google Cloud](https://docs.cloud.google.com/docs/terraform/best-practices/version-control) · [Managing infrastructure as code with Terraform, Cloud Build, and GitOps](https://docs.cloud.google.com/docs/terraform/resource-management/managing-infrastructure-as-code)

You are deploying a Cloud Build job that deploys Terraform code whenever a Git branch is updated. During testing, you notice that the job fails and see the following error in the build logs:  
  
```text  
Initializing the backend...  
  
Error: Failed to get existing workspaces: querying Cloud Storage failed: googleapi: Error 403  
```  
  
You need to resolve the issue by following Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Change the Terraform code to use local state.
Create a storage bucket with the name specified in the Terraform configuration.
Grant the roles/owner Identity and Access Management (IAM) role to the Cloud Build service account on the project.
Grant the roles/storage.objectAdmin Identity and Access Management (1AM) role to the Cloud Build service account on the state file bucket.

questions.explanation:
A Terraform Cloud Storage backend must list and manage its state objects. Granting the Cloud Build service account `roles/storage.objectAdmin` on the state-file bucket provides the required object permissions at the bucket scope, following least privilege rather than assigning the broad Project Owner role. Google Cloud IAM documentation lists Storage Object Admin as granting the relevant Cloud Storage object permissions.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Storage roles and permissions](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/roles-permissions/storage) · [Managing infrastructure as code with Terraform, Cloud Build, and GitOps](https://cloud.google.com/docs/terraform/resource-management/managing-infrastructure-as-code)

questions.domain: Applying site reliability engineering practices
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are responsible for a service that has a clearly defined Service Level Objective (SLO). Over the past 6 months, the service has consistently met this SLO, and customer satisfaction has remained consistently high throughout that period. Most of the operational tasks for this service are automated, and only a few repetitive tasks occur with any frequency. Following site reliability engineering best practices, you want to optimize the balance between reliability and deployment velocity. What should you do? (Choose two.)

options.text: Make the service's SLO more strict.
Increase the service's deployment velocity and/or risk.
Shift engineering time to other services that need more reliability.
Get the product team to prioritize reliability work over new features.
Change the implementation of your Service Level Indicators (SLIs) to increase coverage.

questions.explanation:
When a service consistently exceeds its SLO, its error budget is under-consumed, indicating that engineering effort devoted to reliability could instead be redirected toward increasing feature velocity or supporting other services. SRE best practice treats an unused error budget as a resource to be spent: teams should take on more deployment risk/velocity since the budget allows for it, and engineers can be reassigned to services whose reliability needs are greater, thereby optimizing the overall balance of reliability and velocity across the organization. Tightening the SLO or prioritizing further reliability work is unwarranted since reliability targets are already being exceeded, and modifying SLI coverage does not address the velocity/reliability trade-off described.

**Learn more:** [Implementing SLOs - Google SRE Workbook](https://sre.google/workbook/implementing-slos/) · [Service Level Objectives - Google SRE Book](https://sre.google/sre-book/service-level-objectives/)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are designing a containerized CI pipeline to reduce dependence on public upstream container registries while improving build reproducibility and security. You need to design a pipeline that caches all containerized dependencies while minimizing the manual work and maintenance required. What should you do?

options.text: 1. Create a remote Docker repository for each upstream registry in Artifact Registry.2. Access the container images in the CI pipeline through the remote repository.
1. Create a standard Docker repository for each upstream registry in Artifact Registry.2. Upload the containers used in the build pipelines to the appropriate repositories.

1. Create a standard Docker repository for each upstream registry in Artifact Registry.2. Create a central virtual Docker repository to serve the standard repositories.3. Access the container images in the CI pipeline through the central repository.

1. Create a remote Docker repository for each upstream registry in Artifact Registry.2. Create a central virtual Docker repository to serve the remote repositories.3. Access the container images in the CI pipeline through the central repository.

questions.explanation:
Artifact Registry remote Docker repositories act as pull-through proxies for upstream registries: Artifact Registry fetches and caches an image when it is first requested, then serves the cached copy for later requests. A virtual Docker repository provides a single access point across multiple remote repositories, allowing the CI pipeline to use one central registry endpoint while avoiding manual uploads and maintenance of copied images.

**Learn more:** [Remote repositories overview | Artifact Registry](https://cloud.google.com/artifact-registry/docs/repositories/remote-overview) · [Virtual repositories overview | Artifact Registry](https://cloud.google.com/artifact-registry/docs/repositories/virtual-overview)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have a pool of application servers running on Compute Engine. You need a secure solution that requires the least configuration and lets developers easily access application logs for troubleshooting. How would you implement this solution on GCP?

options.text: ג€¢ Deploy the Stackdriver logging agent to the application servers. ג€¢ Give the developers the IAM Logs Viewer role to access Stackdriver and view logs.
ג€¢ Deploy the Stackdriver logging agent to the application servers. ג€¢ Give the developers the IAM Logs Private Logs Viewer role to access Stackdriver and view logs.
ג€¢ Deploy the Stackdriver monitoring agent to the application servers. ג€¢ Give the developers the IAM Monitoring Viewer role to access Stackdriver and view metrics.

ג€¢ Install the gsutil command line tool on your application servers. ג€¢ Write a script using gsutil to upload your application log to a Cloud Storage bucket, and then schedule it to run via cron every 5 minutes. ג€¢ Give the developers the IAM Object Viewer access to view the logs in the specified bucket.

questions.explanation:
The Compute Engine logging agent sends application logs to Cloud Logging, and the Logs Viewer role provides read-only access to view standard logs. This is the lowest-configuration, least-privilege option for developer troubleshooting. The Private Logs Viewer role is only necessary when access to private logs, such as Data Access audit logs, is required.

**Learn more:** [Access control with IAM | Cloud Logging](https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/access-control)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You recently migrated an ecommerce application to Google Cloud and now need to ready it for the upcoming peak-traffic season. You want to follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do first to prepare for the busy season?

options.text: Migrate the application to Cloud Run, and use autoscaling.
Create a Terraform configuration for the application's underlying infrastructure to quickly deploy to additional regions.
Load test the application to profile its performance for scaling.
Pre-provision the additional compute power that was used last season, and expect growth.

questions.explanation:
Load testing under expected peak conditions establishes whether the application can scale successfully and exposes performance bottlenecks and scaling limits. Those results inform subsequent capacity, quota, and autoscaling decisions.

**Learn more:** [Conduct load testing | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/support/docs/peak-events/conduct-load-testing) · [Plan resource allocation | Google Cloud Architecture Center](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/framework/performance-optimization/plan-resource-allocation)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company has recently encountered several production service issues. You need to create a Cloud Monitoring dashboard to troubleshoot them, and you want to use that dashboard to differentiate failures in your own service from those caused by a Google Cloud service that you use. What should you do?

options.text: Create a log-based metric to track cloud service errors, and display the metric on the dashboard.
Create a logs widget to display system errors from Cloud Logging on the dashboard.
Create an alerting policy for the system error metrics.
Enable Personalized Service Health annotations on the dashboard.

questions.explanation:
Personalized Service Health annotations mark periods of relevant Google Cloud service disruption directly on Cloud Monitoring dashboard charts. This correlates service-health incidents with the dashboard’s operational data, helping distinguish a Google Cloud service failure from an issue in the company’s own service.

**Learn more:** [Show events on a dashboard | Cloud Monitoring](https://docs.cloud.google.com/monitoring/dashboards/show-events) · [Personalized Service Health overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/service-health/docs/overview)

Your company processes IoT data at scale using Pub/Sub, the App Engine standard environment, and an application written in Go. You have observed that performance degrades inconsistently during peak load, but you could not reproduce the issue on your workstation. You need to continuously monitor the production application to identify slow paths in the code while minimizing performance impact and management overhead. What should you do?

options.text: Use Cloud Monitoring to assess the App Engine CPU utilization metric.
Install a continuous profiling tool into Compute Engine. Configure the application to send profiling data to the tool.
Periodically run the go tool pprof command against the application instance. Analyze the results by using flame graphs.
Configure Cloud Profiler, and initialize the cloud.google.com/go/profiler library in the application.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Profiler supports Go applications running in the App Engine standard environment and is initialized by importing and starting `cloud.google.com/go/profiler` in the application. It continuously gathers production profile data with low overhead, including CPU and heap profiles, so code-level slow paths can be analyzed without operating separate profiling infrastructure. [Profiling Go applications](https://docs.cloud.google.com/profiler/docs/profiling-go)

**Learn more:** [Profiling Go applications](https://docs.cloud.google.com/profiler/docs/profiling-go) · [Cloud Profiler overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/profiler/docs/about-profiler)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are developing a strategy to monitor your Google Cloud Platform (GCP) projects in production by using Stackdriver Workspaces. A requirement is to quickly identify and respond to production-environment issues without false alerts from development and staging projects. You also want to follow the principle of least privilege when giving relevant team members access to Stackdriver Workspaces. What should you do?

options.text: Grant relevant team members read access to all GCP production projects. Create Stackdriver workspaces inside each project.
Grant relevant team members the Project Viewer IAM role on all GCP production projects. Create Stackdriver workspaces inside each project.
Choose an existing GCP production project to host the monitoring workspace. Attach the production projects to this workspace. Grant relevant team members read access to the Stackdriver Workspace.

Create a new GCP monitoring project and create a Stackdriver Workspace inside it. Attach the production projects to this workspace. Grant relevant team members read access to the Stackdriver Workspace.

questions.explanation:
A dedicated monitoring project can host a Workspace whose monitoring scope contains only the production projects, keeping development and staging telemetry out of the production monitoring view. Granting the team read access to that Workspace provides access to the centralized production monitoring data without granting broad read access across every production project. Cloud Monitoring identifies the host as the scoping project and supports viewing monitored-project time-series data through appropriate Monitoring access on that project.

**Learn more:** [Metrics scopes overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/monitoring/settings) · [Control access with IAM](https://docs.cloud.google.com/monitoring/access-control)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are designing a system with three distinct environments: development, quality assurance (QA), and production. Terraform will deploy each environment, and each includes a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster so application teams can deploy their applications. Anthos Config Management will be used and templated to deploy infrastructure-level resources to every GKE cluster. All users, such as infrastructure operators and application owners, will use GitOps. How should you organize your source-control repositories for both Infrastructure as Code (IaC) and application code?

options.text: • Cloud Infrastructure (Terraform) repository is shared: different directories are different environments• GKE Infrastructure (Anthos Config Management Kustomize manifests) repository is shared: different overlay directories are different environments• Application (app source code) repositories are separated: different branches are different features

• Cloud Infrastructure (Terraform) repository is shared: different directories are different environments• GKE Infrastructure (Anthos Config Management Kustomize manifests) repositories are separated: different branches are different environments• Application (app source code) repositories are separated: different branches are different features

• Cloud Infrastructure (Terraform) repository is shared: different branches are different environments• GKE Infrastructure (Anthos Config Management Kustomize manifests) repository is shared: different overlay directories are different environments• Application (app source code) repository is shared: different directories are different features

• Cloud Infrastructure (Terraform) repositories are separated: different branches are different environments• GKE Infrastructure (Anthos Config Management Kustomize manifests) repositories are separated: different overlay directories are different environments• Application (app source code) repositories are separated: different branches are different

questions.explanation:
Terraform configurations can share a repository while using separate environment directories to keep development, QA, and production root configurations and state isolated. Config Sync supports a shared Kustomize configuration source with common base manifests and environment-specific overlays. Application code should remain in separate repositories by application or team, with branches used for feature development, so ownership and delivery workflows remain independent.

**Learn more:** [Best practices for root modules | Terraform on Google Cloud](https://docs.cloud.google.com/docs/terraform/best-practices/root-modules) · [Using Config Sync in multiple environments with automated rendering](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/config-sync/docs/tutorials/multiple-environments-config-sync)

A third-party application requires a service account key to function correctly. When you attempt to export the key from your cloud project, you get this error: “The organization policy constraint iam.disableServiceAccounKeyCreation is enforced.” You must make the third-party application work while adhering to Google-recommended security practices.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Enable the default service account key, and download the key.
Remove the iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation policy at the organization level, and create a key.
Disable the service account key creation policy at the project's folder, and download the default key.
Add a rule to set the iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation policy to off in your project, and create a key.

questions.explanation:
Service account keys are long-lived credentials and should remain disabled broadly. When a key is genuinely necessary, Google recommends disabling enforcement of `iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation` only for the required project, creating a least-scope exception while preserving the organization-wide control for other projects.

**Learn more:** [Troubleshoot organization policy errors for service accounts](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/troubleshoot-org-policies) · [Best practices for managing service account keys](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/best-practices-for-managing-service-account-keys)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You release a new version of an internal application during a weekend maintenance window, when user traffic is minimal. After the window closes, you discover that one of the new features is not working as expected in the production environment. Following an extended outage, you roll back the new release and deploy a fix.  
  
You want to change your release process to reduce mean time to recovery and avoid extended outages in the future. What should you do? (Choose two.)

options.text: Before merging new code, require 2 different peers to review the code changes.
Adopt the blue/green deployment strategy when releasing new code via a CD server.
Integrate a code linting tool to validate coding standards before any code is accepted into the repository.
Require developers to run automated integration tests on their local development environments before release.
Configure a CI server. Add a suite of unit tests to your code and have your CI server run them on commit and verify any changes.

questions.explanation:
Blue/green deployment keeps the previously working production environment available while the new version is validated, enabling traffic to be switched back rapidly if the release fails. Automated unit tests run by a CI server on every commit provide consistent, immediate validation of changes, so defects are detected before they reach production and fixes can move through a repeatable pipeline quickly.

**Learn more:** [Deploying .NET apps on Google Cloud — Blue-Green strategy](https://docs.cloud.google.com/dotnet/docs/deploy-dotnet-applications) · [Cloud Run adds support for gradual rollouts and rollbacks](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/serverless/cloud-run-now-supports-gradual-rollouts-and-rollbacks)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are designing the deployment and testing strategies for a CI/CD pipeline in Google Cloud. You must be able to:  
  
- Reduce the complexity of release deployments and minimize the time needed for deployment rollbacks.  
- Test actual production traffic while gradually increasing the number of users affected.  
  
You want to choose a deployment and testing strategy that fulfills these requirements. What should you do?

options.text: Recreate deployment and canary testing
Blue/green deployment and canary testing
Rolling update deployment and A/B testing
Rolling update deployment and shadow testing

questions.explanation:
A blue/green deployment keeps the prior production version available while the new version is deployed separately, so releases and rollbacks can be performed by switching traffic between versions. Canary testing progressively directs a controlled, increasing percentage of real production traffic to the new version, limiting the initial impact while validating it with real users.

**Learn more:** [Use a deployment strategy — Cloud Deploy](https://docs.cloud.google.com/deploy/docs/deployment-strategies) · [Use a canary deployment strategy — Cloud Deploy](https://docs.cloud.google.com/deploy/docs/deployment-strategies/canary)

You need to determine the root cause and implement a solution in your CI/CD workflow to keep this issue from happening again. What should you do?

options.text: Use a canary deployment strategy.
Implement static code analysis in the CI pipeline.
Run integration tests in the CI pipeline.
Enable Cloud Audit Logs for the deployment.

questions.explanation: Integration tests can run the application in a deployment-like environment and verify that the container starts with all required environment variables and dependent configuration present. This detects missing runtime configuration before deployment.

options.text: Use Google Cloud Deploy to deploy the network policies and the DaemonSet. Use Cloud Monitoring to trigger an alert if the network policies and DaemonSet drift from your source in the repository.

Use Google Cloud Deploy to deploy the DaemonSet and use Policy Controller to configure the network policies. Use Cloud Monitoring to detect drifts from the source in the repository and Cloud Functions to correct the drifts.
Use Cloud Build to render and deploy the network policies and the DaemonSet. Set up Config Sync to sync the configurations for the three environments.
Use Cloud Build to render and deploy the network policies and the DaemonSet. Set up a Policy Controller to enforce the configurations for the three environments.

questions.explanation:
Config Sync continuously reconciles cluster state with configurations stored in a Git repository, preventing configuration drift across a fleet. It can manage standard GKE objects, including NetworkPolicy resources and DaemonSet resources, making it the appropriate mechanism to install and keep these common configurations consistent across development, staging, and production. Cloud Build can render the configuration before it is synchronized. Policy Controller supplies admission-policy guardrails, rather than deploying the NetworkPolicy and DaemonSet manifests.

**Learn more:** [Config Sync overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/config-sync/docs/overview) · [Safe rollouts with Config Sync](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/config-sync/docs/tutorials/safe-rollouts-with-config-sync)

questions.question: You deploy your application with Spinnaker and have added a canary deployment stage to the pipeline. The application uses an in-memory cache that loads objects at startup. You want to automate a comparison of the canary version with the production version. How should you configure the canary analysis?

options.text: Compare the canary with a new deployment of the current production version.
Compare the canary with a new deployment of the previous production version.
Compare the canary with the existing deployment of the current production version.
Compare the canary with the average performance of a sliding window of previous production versions.

questions.explanation: A newly deployed instance of the current production version provides a baseline with the same startup-time in-memory-cache behavior as the canary. Comparing against an already running production deployment would confound the analysis because its cache is already warm.

questions.question: You deploy your application with Spinnaker and have added a canary deployment stage to the pipeline. The application uses an in-memory cache that loads objects at startup. You want to automate a comparison of the canary version with the production version. How should you configure the canary analysis?

options.text: Create an organization-level aggregated sink with a siem log bucket as the destination. Set an inclusion filter to include all logs.
Create a folder-level aggregated sink with a siem Pub/Sub topic as the destination. Set an inclusion filter to include all logs. Repeat for each folder.
Create an organization-level aggregated sink with a siem Pub/Sub topic as the destination. Set an inclusion filter to include all logs.
Create a project-level logging sink with a siem Pub/Sub topic as the destination. Set an inclusion filter to include all logs. Repeat for each project.

questions.explanation:
An organization-level aggregated sink routes log entries from the organization and all of its child resources, including projects added in the future. Routing that sink to a Pub/Sub topic supplies the SIEM’s required ingestion mechanism, and an inclusion filter for all logs ensures comprehensive coverage.

**Learn more:** [Collate and route organization- and folder-level logs to supported destinations](https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/export/aggregated_sinks) · [Aggregated sinks overview](https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/export/aggregated_sinks_overview)

questions.domain: Optimizing performance and cost
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are deploying a new web application on Cloud Run in your Google Cloud project. You anticipate traffic ranging from 10 requests per second during off-peak periods to 1000 requests per second at peak times. You want to use autoscaling to handle these traffic changes efficiently while ensuring the autoscaler does not exceed your project's resource quotas. What should you do?

options.text: Manually adjust the number of instances based on observed traffic patterns throughout the day.
Define appropriate resource limits for the Cloud Run service, and ensure your project has sufficient resource quotas to accommodate the desired scaling range.
Configure the autoscaler to scale based on CPU utilization with a target of 80%.
Configure the autoscaler to scale based on request count, with a target of 500 requests per instance.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Run scales instances automatically to meet traffic demand, but the number of instances that can be used is constrained by the project and region's available CPU and memory quotas relative to each instance's resource configuration. Define suitable service resource and scaling limits, and ensure the project has enough quota for the intended scaling range.

**Learn more:** [About maximum instances](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/configuring/max-instances-limits) · [Cloud Run quotas and limits](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/quotas)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are deploying a containerized application on Cloud Run. The application requires a password to connect to the database and retrieve data. To satisfy your company’s security requirements, the password must rotate every week. You need to implement a password-rotation policy that is easy to manage. What should you do?

options.text: 1. Deploy the container to Cloud Run.2. Create a new container each week with the new database password set as an environment variable in a Dockerfile.3. Deploy the new container to Cloud Run, and migrate the traffic to the new version.

1. Create a secret in Secret Manager to hold the password.2. Deploy the container to Cloud Run, and use the latest version of the secret as an environment variable.3. Create a new version of the secret with the new password in Secret Manager each week.

1. Deploy the container to Cloud Run.2. Create a new container each week with the new database password set as a secret during the build phase.3. Deploy the new container to Cloud Run, and migrate the traffic to the new version.

1. Create a secret in Secret Manager to hold the password.2. Deploy the container to Cloud Run, and use the latest version of the secret as a mounted volume.3. Create a new version of the secret in Secret Manager each week.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Run recommends storing passwords in Secret Manager. When a secret is mounted as a volume and references `latest`, Cloud Run fetches the latest Secret Manager value when the volume is read, which works well for secret rotation. Adding a new secret version each week avoids rebuilding and redeploying the container; the application can read the updated mounted secret value.

**Learn more:** [Configure secrets for services](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/configuring/services/secrets)

You work for a global organization and operate a service with a 99% availability target and limited engineering resources.  
  
For the current calendar month, you observe that the service has achieved 99.5% availability. You must ensure that the service meets its defined availability goals and can respond to business changes, including the upcoming launch of new features.  
  
You also need to reduce technical debt while minimizing operational costs. You want to follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Add N+1 redundancy to your service by adding additional compute resources to the service.
Identify, measure, and eliminate toil by automating repetitive tasks.
Define an error budget for your service level availability and minimize the remaining error budget.
Allocate available engineers to the feature backlog while you ensure that the service remains within the availability target.

questions.explanation:
A 99% availability SLO permits a 1% error budget. With 99.5% availability for the current month, the service remains within its SLO, so engineering capacity can be directed toward feature work while availability continues to be monitored and kept within the target. Google SRE uses error budgets to balance service reliability with innovation; reliability work and release restrictions become the priority when the error budget is exhausted.

**Learn more:** [Google SRE: Production Services Best Practices](https://sre.google/sre-book/service-best-practices/) · [Set realistic targets for reliability | Google Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/architecture/framework/reliability/choose-slos)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are creating a centralized platform for monitoring your applications. The applications currently run on Kubernetes clusters on-premises and in the cloud across multiple Google Cloud projects. You want developers to monitor both infrastructure and application metrics with OpenTelemetry across on-premises and Google Cloud environments. At the same time, you want operations to remain easy to support and all metrics integrated in one place. What should you do?

options.text: Implement a sidecar OpenTelemetry Collector alongside each Pod in all Kubernetes clusters (on-premises and GKE). Configure these collectors to export Prometheus-formatted metrics. Use dedicated Prometheus instances in each Kubernetes cluster and Thanos in a central GKE cluster. Install Grafana on a GKE cluster, and use Grafana to monitor the applications.
Create a scoping project and add all the Google Cloud projects to it. Use Bindplane to streamline OpenTelemetry metric collection for the on-premises Kubernetes clusters into Cloud Monitoring.

Create a new Google Cloud project to use as a scoping project and add all the other Google Cloud projects to it. Instrument the applications running on-premises to export the metrics to Cloud Monitoring as user-defined metrics. Use Cloud Monitoring to monitor the applications.

Enable Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus collections by using the OpenTelemetry Collector on the Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) clusters, and enable non-managed Prometheus for the on-premises Kubernetes clusters. Install Grafana on a GKE cluster, and use Grafana to monitor the applications.

questions.explanation:
A Cloud Monitoring metrics scope, hosted by a scoping project, lets queries view metric data from multiple Google Cloud projects in one place. Bindplane is an OpenTelemetry-native pipeline that simplifies deployment and management of collectors in hybrid and on-premises environments and sends their metrics to Cloud Monitoring, where they can be viewed with other monitored systems. This combines multi-project visibility with centrally managed hybrid telemetry collection.

**Learn more:** [Configuring your metrics scopes](https://docs.cloud.google.com/stackdriver/docs/managed-prometheus/best-practices/config) · [Collect on-premises and hybrid-cloud metrics with Bindplane](https://docs.cloud.google.com/monitoring/bindplane/collecting-on-prem-hybrid?hl=en)

Your organization needs to gather system logs for generating dashboards in Cloud Operations for its Google Cloud project. You must configure all existing and future Compute Engine instances to collect the system logs, while ensuring that the Ops Agent stays up to date. What should you do?

options.text: Use the gcloud CLI to install the Ops Agent on each VM listed in the Cloud Asset Inventory,
Select all VMs with an Agent status of Not detected on the Cloud Operations VMs dashboard. Then select Install agents.
Use the gcloud CLI to create an Agent Policy.
Install the Ops Agent on the Compute Engine image by using a startup script

questions.explanation:
An Ops Agent policy manages agent installation across Compute Engine VMs that match its filters, including both existing and future instances. The policy can also enable automatic upgrades, keeping the Ops Agent current while collecting logs for Cloud Operations.

**Learn more:** [Use agent policies (GA)](https://docs.cloud.google.com/stackdriver/docs/solutions/agents/ops-agent/agent-policies) · [gcloud compute instances ops-agents policies create](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/compute/instances/ops-agents/policies/create)
