questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You manage a critical user-facing application and configured a service level objective (SLO) in Cloud Monitoring to measure 99% availability across a 30-day rolling window. Recently, a series of minor issues has increased latency, causing the error budget to be consumed faster. You need proactive notification when the service risks violating its SLO before the error budget is completely exhausted. What should you do?

options.text: Configure a log-based metric in Cloud Monitoring that tracks the rate of application error logs. Create an alerting policy on this metric that triggers when the error rate shows a significant anomalous deviation from its historical baseline.
Create a custom dashboard in Cloud Monitoring that visualizes the SLO compliance percentage and the remaining error budget. Configure the dashboard to send a scheduled daily report through email.

In Cloud Monitoring, create an alerting policy based on the SLO’s error budget burn rate. Configure the alert to trigger when the current consumption rate is projected to exhaust the budget before the end of the 30-day compliance period.
In Metrics Explorer, create an alerting policy based on the average request latency for the application’s load balancer. Configure the alert to trigger if latency exceeds a predefined threshold.

questions.explanation:
An SLO error-budget burn-rate alert monitors the rate at which the budget is consumed. A slow-burn policy can be configured to notify when the sustained rate would exhaust the error budget before the compliance period ends, allowing intervention before the SLO is violated.

**Learn more:** [Alerting on your burn rate | Google Cloud Observability](https://cloud.google.com/stackdriver/docs/solutions/slo-monitoring/alerting-on-budget-burn-rate) · [Using microservice dashboards | Google Cloud Observability](https://cloud.google.com/stackdriver/docs/solutions/slo-monitoring/ui/svc-dashboard)

Your company is preparing a large holiday-season marketing event for an online retailer. You expect your web application to receive a high volume of traffic over a short time period. You must ready the application for possible failures during the event. What should you do? (Choose two.)

options.text: Configure Anthos Service Mesh on the application to identify issues on the topology map.
Ensure that relevant system metrics are being captured with Cloud Monitoring, and create alerts at levels of interest.
Review your increased capacity requirements and plan for the required quota management.
Monitor latency of your services for average percentile latency.
Create alerts in Cloud Monitoring for all common failures that your application experiences.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Monitoring metrics and alerting policies provide operational visibility and notifications when defined conditions are met. Google Cloud quotas can block requests or resource use when exceeded, so projected capacity must be reviewed and quota adjustments planned before a traffic surge.

**Learn more:** [Alerting overview | Cloud Monitoring](https://docs.cloud.google.com/monitoring/alerts?hl=en) · [Cloud Quotas overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/docs/quotas/overview)

You are designing a new Google Cloud organization for a client. The client is concerned about risks associated with long-lived credentials created in Google Cloud. You need to design a solution that completely eliminates the risks associated with using JSON service account keys while minimizing operational overhead. What should you do?

options.text: Apply the constraints/iam.disableServiceAccountKevCreation constraint to the organization.
Use custom versions of predefined roles to exclude all iam.serviceAccountKeys.* service account role permissions.
Apply the constraints/iam.disableServiceAccountKeyUpload constraint to the organization.
Grant the roles/iam.serviceAccountKeyAdmin IAM role to organization administrators only.

questions.explanation:
Enforcing the organization policy that disables service account key creation prevents user-managed external service account keys, including JSON keys, from being created throughout the organization’s governed resource hierarchy. This centrally eliminates new long-lived service account credentials without requiring ongoing custom-role maintenance. Disabling key upload addresses only external public-key uploads, not JSON key creation.

**Learn more:** [Restricting service account usage](https://cloud.google.com/resource-manager/docs/organization-policy/restricting-service-accounts) · [Organization policy constraints](https://cloud.google.com/organization-policy/reference/org-policy-constraints)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are developing an ecommerce web application that will be deployed to Google Cloud. You must periodically test the production checkout process to verify that it works and to ensure you receive automated notifications when failures occur. You also need to minimize administrative effort and follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Use Workflows to create a workflow verifying the functionality, and trigger the workflow periodically by using Cloud Tasks.
Implement a Cloud Run function for synthetic monitoring with an alerting policy.
Create an alerting policy in Cloud Logging to monitor for failed logs during the checkout process.
Configure an uptime check with an alerting policy.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud synthetic monitoring supports scripted tests for multi-step web workflows such as an ecommerce checkout process. It deploys and periodically runs a dedicated 2nd generation Cloud Run function, and an alerting policy can notify operators when a test fails. Uptime checks are intended for endpoint availability and response validation, not full checkout-flow testing.

**Learn more:** [Synthetic monitoring overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/monitoring/uptime-checks/introduction) · [Create a synthetic monitor](https://docs.cloud.google.com/monitoring/synthetic-monitors/create)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You support a high-traffic web application that uses a microservice architecture. The application's home page shows multiple widgets with content such as current weather, stock prices, and news headlines. The main serving thread calls a dedicated microservice for every widget and then renders the homepage for the user. The microservices occasionally fail; when this occurs, the serving thread delivers the homepage with some content missing. Application users are unhappy when this degraded mode happens too often, but they prefer receiving some content to receiving none at all. You want to define a Service Level Objective (SLO) so the user experience does not degrade excessively. Which Service Level Indicator (SLI) should be used to measure this?

options.text: A quality SLI: the ratio of non-degraded responses to total responses.
An availability SLI: the ratio of healthy microservices to the total number of microservices.
A freshness SLI: the proportion of widgets that have been updated within the last 10 minutes.
A latency SLI: the ratio of microservice calls that complete in under 100 ms to the total number of microservice calls.

questions.explanation:
A quality SLI measures the proportion of user responses served in an undegraded state. It directly captures the missing-widget experience caused by failed optional microservices while recognizing that the homepage itself can still be served.

**Learn more:** [Google SRE Workbook: Implementing SLOs](https://sre.google/workbook/implementing-slos/)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to deploy a new service to production. The service must automatically scale with a Managed Instance Group (MIG) and be deployed across multiple regions. Each instance requires a large number of resources, and you need to plan for capacity. What should you do?

options.text: Use the n1-highcpu-96 machine type in the configuration of the MIG.
Monitor results of Stackdriver Trace to determine the required amount of resources.
Validate that the resource requirements are within the available quota limits of each region.
Deploy the service in one region and use a global load balancer to route traffic to this region.

questions.explanation:
Compute Engine VM resource quotas, including CPU quota, are managed per region. A managed instance group needs available quota for the resources used by its instances and for the instance-group resource itself; therefore, verify that each deployment region has sufficient quota before relying on autoscaling.

**Learn more:** [Allocation quotas | Compute Engine | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/resource-usage) · [About regional MIGs | Compute Engine | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instance-groups/regional-migs)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are planning how to display Cloud Monitoring metrics for your organization’s Google Cloud projects. Your organization has three folders and six projects:  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783848186639-lysy5za6.png)  
  
You want to configure Cloud Monitoring dashboards so they display metrics only from projects within a single folder. You must ensure the dashboards do not show metrics from projects in the other folders. You want to follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Create a single new scoping project.
Create new scoping projects for each folder.
Use the current app-one-prod project as the scoping project.
Use the current app-one-dev, app-one-staging, and app-one-prod projects as the scoping project for each folder.

questions.explanation:
A metrics scope defines the set of project time-series data that Cloud Monitoring dashboards can chart. Creating a separate new scoping project for each folder lets each scope include only the projects in that folder, preventing dashboards from displaying metrics from the other folders. Google recommends using a new project, or one with no resources, as a scoping project so its own resource metrics do not complicate dashboards or require exclusion filters.

**Learn more:** [Metrics scopes overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/monitoring/settings?hl=en) · [Configure a metrics scope](https://docs.cloud.google.com/monitoring/settings/multiple-projects)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are building a Node.js utility on a Cloud Workstations workstation by using Code OSS. The utility is a simple web page, and you have already verified that all required firewall rules are in place. You tested the application by starting it on port 3000 on your Cloud Workstations workstation, but now need to access the web page from your local machine. You must follow Google-recommended security practices. What should you do?

options.text: Use a browser running on a bastion host VM.
Run the gcloud compute start-iap-tunnel command to the Cloud Workstations VM.
Allow public IP addresses in the Cloud Workstations configuration.
Click the preview link in the Code OSS panel.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Workstations provides built-in browser access to HTTP services running on a workstation. The Code OSS preview link opens the workstation service through the managed, authenticated web-preview path, which is protected by IAM; port 3000 is within the default browser-accessible port range.

**Learn more:** [Access HTTP servers running on a workstation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/workstations/docs/access-http-servers-running-on-workstations?hl=en) · [Cloud Workstations product overview](https://cloud.google.com/workstations?hl=en)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have several applications exposed through a load balancer, and you are monitoring requests blocked by Google Cloud Armor. You need to create a dashboard to monitor requests for `https://mountkirk.com/api` only. You want to identify the parameters being blocked. What should you do?

options.text: 1. Create a log-based counter metric with filters for configuredAction=ALLOW and requestUrl=~

1. Create a log-based metric with the Boolean metric type with the filter configuredAction=BLOCKED.2. Create a dashboard in Cloud Monitoring with the new metric, with an aggregation on matchedFieldName.
1. Create a log-based counter metric with filters for configuredAction=BLOCKED and requestUrl=~
1. Create a dashboard in Cloud Monitoring by using the networksecurity.googleapis.com metric with the https/request_count type.2. Filter the blocked parameter as true.

questions.explanation:
A counter log-based metric counts Cloud Armor request-log entries that match its filter. Filtering for blocked actions and the specified request URL isolates blocked requests to that API, while aggregation on `matchedFieldName` separates the metric data by the parameter that matched the blocking rule. Cloud Logging supports counter metrics with filters and user-defined labels that can be charted and aggregated in Cloud Monitoring.

**Learn more:** [Configure counter metrics | Cloud Logging](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/logs-based-metrics/counter-metrics) · [Configure labels on log-based metrics | Cloud Logging](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/logs-based-metrics/labels)

Your organization relies on a change advisory board (CAB) to approve every change to an existing service. You want to revise this process so it removes any negative effect on software delivery performance. What should you do? (Choose two.)

options.text: Replace the CAB with a senior manager to ensure continuous oversight from development to deployment.
Let developers merge their own changes, but ensure that the team's deployment platform can roll back changes if any issues are discovered.
Move to a peer-review based process for individual changes that is enforced at code check-in time and supported by automated tests.
Batch changes into larger but less frequent software releases.
Ensure that the team's development platform enables developers to get fast feedback on the impact of their changes.

questions.explanation:
High-performing software delivery replaces heavyweight change-approval processes with peer review supported by automated testing, allowing controls to occur during code integration without a CAB bottleneck. Development platforms should also provide rapid feedback about the effects of changes so developers can detect and address issues early.

**Learn more:** [DevOps capabilities](https://cloud.google.com/architecture/devops) · [Patterns for scalable and resilient apps](https://cloud.google.com/architecture/scalable-and-resilient-apps)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You support a trading application written in Python and hosted on App Engine flexible environment. You want to customize the error information being sent to Stackdriver Error Reporting. What should you do?

options.text: Install the Stackdriver Error Reporting library for Python, and then run your code on a Compute Engine VM.
Install the Stackdriver Error Reporting library for Python, and then run your code on Google Kubernetes Engine.
Install the Stackdriver Error Reporting library for Python, and then run your code on App Engine flexible environment.
Use the Stackdriver Error Reporting API to write errors from your application to ReportedErrorEvent, and then generate log entries with properly formatted error messages in Stackdriver Logging.

questions.explanation:
Error Reporting is automatically enabled for App Engine flexible environment applications with no additional setup required, since messages written to stderr are automatically captured. To customize the error information that gets sent to Error Reporting (rather than relying solely on the default stderr capture), Google Cloud provides language-specific instrumentation client libraries, including one for Python (google-cloud-error-reporting), which lets you programmatically report exceptions and custom error details via methods such as report_exception() and report(). This library can be installed and used directly within the existing App Engine flexible environment deployment — there is no requirement to move the workload to Compute Engine or Google Kubernetes Engine to achieve this customization.

**Learn more:** [Setting up on App Engine flexible environment | Error Reporting | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/error-reporting/docs/setup/app-engine-flexible-environment) · [Instrument Python apps for Error Reporting | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/error-reporting/docs/setup/python)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You support a multi-region web service running on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) behind a Global HTTP/S Cloud Load Balancer (CLB). For legacy reasons, user requests initially pass through a third-party Content Delivery Network (CDN), which then directs traffic to the CLB. You have already implemented an availability Service Level Indicator (SLI) at the CLB level. However, you want to expand coverage for a potential load-balancer misconfiguration, CDN failure, or another global networking catastrophe. Where should this new SLI be measured? (Choose two.)

options.text: Your application servers' logs.
Instrumentation coded directly in the client.
Metrics exported from the application servers.
GKE health checks for your application servers.
A synthetic client that periodically sends simulated user requests.

questions.explanation:
Client-side instrumentation measures real users’ end-to-end availability across the CDN, load balancer, and application path. An external synthetic client independently sends simulated requests through that same path, detecting CDN, load-balancer, and global network failures that can prevent requests from ever reaching the load balancer. Google SRE guidance identifies client-side instrumentation and black-box monitoring as SLI sources, and recommends black-box monitoring to catch failures in network layers, caches, and proxies outside the microservice.

**Learn more:** [Google SRE Workbook: Implementing SLOs](https://sre.google/workbook/implementing-slos/) · [Google SRE Workbook: SLO Engineering Case Studies](https://sre.google/workbook/slo-engineering-case-studies/)

questions.domain: Bootstrapping and maintaining a Google Cloud organization
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company keeps a large amount of rarely accessed data in Cloud Storage. Projects in the company's CustomerService folder access Cloud Storage often but retain very little data. You want to enable Data Access audit logging throughout the company to identify data-usage patterns. You need to exclude projects in the CustomerService folder from Data Access audit logging. What should you do?

options.text: Enable Data Access audit logging for Cloud Storage at the organization level, and configure exempted principals to include users of the CustomerService folder.
Enable Data Access audit logging for Cloud Storage at the organization level, with no additional configuration.
Enable Data Access audit logging for Cloud Storage for all projects and folders other than the CustomerService folder.
Enable Data Access audit logging for Cloud Storage for all projects and folders, and configure exempted principals to include users of the CustomerService folder.

questions.explanation:
Data Access audit-log configuration is inherited through the Google Cloud resource hierarchy. A project or folder cannot disable a log type that its parent organization or folder has enabled. Exempted principals only suppress logging for named identities; they do not exclude an entire folder of projects. Enabling Cloud Storage Data Access audit logging on every applicable project and folder except the CustomerService folder preserves logging for the rest of the company while excluding that folder's projects.

**Learn more:** [Enable Data Access audit logs](https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/audit/configure-data-access)

questions.domain: Optimizing performance and cost
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You use Cloud Build to build your application. You want to reduce the build time while minimizing cost and development effort. What should you do?

options.text: Use Cloud Storage to cache intermediate artifacts.
Run multiple Jenkins agents to parallelize the build.
Use multiple smaller build steps to minimize execution time.
Use larger Cloud Build virtual machines (VMs) by using the machine-type option.

questions.explanation:
Caching intermediate build artifacts (such as dependency directories or Docker layers) in a Cloud Storage bucket lets subsequent builds reuse prior results instead of rebuilding everything from scratch, which meaningfully shortens build times. This approach uses inexpensive Cloud Storage rather than provisioning larger, more expensive Cloud Build VMs, and it requires only a small addition to the build configuration (copying artifacts to and from the bucket), so it minimizes both cost and development effort compared to alternatives like upgrading machine types (which increases cost), using Jenkins agents (not applicable to Cloud Build and adds operational overhead), or arbitrarily splitting build steps (which doesn't inherently reduce total execution time).

**Learn more:** [Best practices for speeding up builds | Cloud Build | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/build/docs/optimize-builds/speeding-up-builds)

questions.domain: Implementing observability practices and troubleshooting issues
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company has a Google Cloud resource hierarchy that contains folders for production, test, and development. Your cyber security team needs to assess the company's Google Cloud security posture to speed up security-issue identification and remediation. You must centralize logs generated by Google Cloud services from all projects only within the production folder, enabling alerting and near-real-time analysis. What should you do?

options.text: Enable the Workflows API and route all the logs to Cloud Logging.
Create a central Cloud Monitoring workspace and attach all related projects.
Create an aggregated log sink associated with the production folder that uses a Pub/Sub topic as the destination.
Create an aggregated log sink associated with the production folder that uses a Cloud Logging bucket as the destination.

questions.explanation:
An aggregated sink configured on the production folder routes log entries from that folder and all of its child resources, including its projects. Using a Pub/Sub topic as the destination delivers the routed log entries in near real time, allowing downstream alerting and security-analysis systems to consume them.

**Learn more:** [Collate and route organization- and folder-level logs to supported destinations](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/export/aggregated_sinks) · [View logs routed to Pub/Sub](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/export/pubsub)

questions.domain: Bootstrapping and maintaining a Google Cloud organization
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company is developing an AI-powered Java web application. You need to provide your developers with a secure, managed, cloud-based Java integrated development environment (IDE). You must make sure the necessary GPUs are attached to their development instances and want to follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Create a dedicated Google Cloud project for development with sufficient GPU quota. Grant developers access to use Cloud Shell Editor within the project.
Use Cloud Workstations to create a dedicated workstation with an attached GPU for each developer. Grant the Cloud Workstations User role to the users.
Create a separate Google Cloud project with a GPU-equipped VM for each developer, and grant each developer Editor access to their project.
Deploy a GKE cluster with GPUs attached. Create a namespace for each developer, and grant the namespace access to the corresponding developer.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Workstations provides managed cloud development environments and supports GPUs configured for each workstation. Google Cloud Workstations attaches the configured GPUs and installs the required device drivers, while the Cloud Workstations User role grants developers runtime access to their assigned workstations.

**Learn more:** [Available GPUs | Cloud Workstations](https://docs.cloud.google.com/workstations/docs/available-gpus?hl=en) · [Access control with IAM | Cloud Workstations](https://docs.cloud.google.com/workstations/docs/access-control)

questions.domain: Building and implementing CI/CD pipelines, including continuous testing, for application, infrastructure, and machine learning workloads
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are setting up a CI pipeline. Its build step for integration testing needs access to APIs within your private VPC network. Your security team requires that API traffic not be exposed publicly. You need to implement a solution that minimizes management overhead. What should you do?

options.text: Use Cloud Build private pools to connect to the private VPC.
Use Spinnaker for Google Cloud to connect to the private VPC.
Use Cloud Build as a pipeline runner. Configure Internal HTTP(S) Load Balancing for API access.
Use Cloud Build as a pipeline runner. Configure External HTTP(S) Load Balancing with a Google Cloud Armor policy for API access.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Build private pools are fully managed, customer-specific worker pools that can connect privately to a VPC. Configuring a private connection enables the build workers and VPC resources to communicate exclusively through internal IP addresses, avoiding public API exposure while requiring no self-managed build infrastructure.

**Learn more:** [Private pools overview | Cloud Build](https://docs.cloud.google.com/build/docs/private-pools/private-pools-overview) · [Set up environment to use private pools in a VPC network | Cloud Build](https://docs.cloud.google.com/build/docs/private-pools/set-up-private-pool-to-use-in-vpc-network)

questions.domain: Optimizing performance and cost
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are working with a government agency that requires application logs to be archived for seven years. You need to configure Stackdriver to export and store the logs while minimizing storage costs. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Cloud Storage bucket and develop your application to send logs directly to the bucket.
Develop an App Engine application that pulls the logs from Stackdriver and saves them in BigQuery.
Create an export in Stackdriver and configure Cloud Pub/Sub to store logs in permanent storage for seven years.
Create a sink in Stackdriver, name it, create a bucket on Cloud Storage for storing archived logs, and then select the bucket as the log export destination.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Logging (formerly Stackdriver Logging) lets you create export sinks that route log entries to supported destinations such as Cloud Storage, BigQuery, or Pub/Sub. For long-term, low-cost archival like a seven-year retention requirement, exporting to a Cloud Storage bucket (especially using a cost-optimized storage class such as Coldline or Archive) is the cheapest and most appropriate option. The correct workflow is to create a sink in Cloud Logging, give it a name, create (or select) a Cloud Storage bucket to hold the archived logs, and configure that bucket as the sink's export destination. This built-in export mechanism is designed specifically for this purpose, unlike manually coding an application to write logs directly to storage, routing through BigQuery (which is costlier for pure archival), or using Pub/Sub (a messaging/streaming service, not a long-term storage destination).

**Learn more:** [Configure and manage sinks | Cloud Logging](https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/export/configure_export_v2) · [Overview of logs export | Cloud Logging](https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/export)

questions.domain: Optimizing performance and cost
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You must deploy a new service to production. The service must automatically scale with a managed instance group and be deployed across multiple regions. Each instance requires a large number of resources, and capacity planning is needed. What should you do?

options.text: Monitor results of Cloud Trace to determine the optimal sizing.
Use the n2-highcpu-96 machine type in the configuration of the managed instance group.
Deploy the service in multiple regions and use an internal load balancer to route traffic.
Validate that the resource requirements are within the available project quota limits of each region.

questions.explanation:
Compute Engine VM, CPU, and managed instance group allocation quotas are regional. An autoscaling managed instance group with resource-intensive instances can fail to scale or deploy if the project lacks sufficient quota in any target region, so the resource requirements must be validated against the available project quota limits in each region.

**Learn more:** [Compute Engine allocation quotas](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/resource-usage) · [Compute Engine quota and limits overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/quotas-limits)

questions.domain: Applying site reliability engineering practices
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are leading a DevOps project for your organization. The DevOps team is responsible for managing the service infrastructure and for being on-call for incidents. The Software Development team is responsible for writing, submitting, and reviewing code. Neither team has published any SLOs.  
  
You want to create a new joint-ownership model for a service between the DevOps team and the Software Development team. Which responsibilities should be assigned to each team in the new joint-ownership model?

options.text: ![](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1785600122013-d1kya5sd.png)
![](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1785600124669-3ni6sd0k.png)
![](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1785600127817-kt3vywk3.png)
![](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1785600130388-e56q3veq.png)

questions.explanation:
A joint-ownership model keeps service-infrastructure management with the DevOps team while sharing code reviews, incident on-call coverage, and SLO adoption and publication across both teams. Including developers in on-call rotations connects them to the operational consequences of their code, and shared SLOs provide a common reliability language and accountability across development and operations.

**Learn more:** [Google SRE: Production Services Best Practices](https://sre.google/sre-book/service-best-practices/) · [Google SRE: SLO Implementation—Evernote and Home Depot](https://sre.google/workbook/slo-engineering-case-studies/)

questions.domain: Building and implementing CI/CD pipelines, including continuous testing, for application, infrastructure, and machine learning workloads
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company operates applications in Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) that are deployed using a GitOps methodology. Application developers frequently create cloud resources that support their applications. You want to enable developers to manage infrastructure as code while following Google-recommended practices. You must ensure that the infrastructure-as-code configuration is periodically reconciled to prevent configuration drift. What should you do?

options.text: Install and configure Config Connector in Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE).
Configure Cloud Build with a Terraform builder to execute terraform plan and terraform apply commands.
Create a Pod resource with a Terraform docker image to execute terraform plan and terraform apply commands.
Create a Job resource with a Terraform docker image to execute terraform plan and terraform apply commands.

questions.explanation:
Config Connector lets teams manage Google Cloud resources declaratively through Kubernetes custom resources in GKE, aligning infrastructure definitions with a GitOps workflow. Its controllers reconcile the actual environment with the declared desired state at updates and on a periodic interval, which detects and corrects configuration drift.

**Learn more:** [Config Connector overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/config-connector/docs/overview) · [Config Connector reconciliation strategy](https://docs.cloud.google.com/config-connector/docs/concepts/reconciliation)

questions.domain: Building and implementing CI/CD pipelines, including continuous testing, for application, infrastructure, and machine learning workloads

options.text: Upgrade your on-premises VMs to have faster CPUs and more memory.
Implement a blue-green deployment strategy for your on-premises VMs.
Increase the number of Jenkins executor threads.
Configure Jenkins to use an artifact repository in your on-premises environment.

questions.explanation:
A Jenkins executor is a slot for executing tasks, and the number of executors on a node determines how many tasks or Pipeline stages can run concurrently. Increasing the executor count increases available deployment execution slots, reducing queueing delay before on-premises deployments begin.

**Learn more:** [Jenkins: Managing Nodes](https://www.jenkins.io/doc/book/managing/nodes/) · [Jenkins: Executor Starvation](https://www.jenkins.io/doc/book/using/executor-starvation/)

You have multiple applications running on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) and Cloud Run. You plan to use BigQuery as the central repository for logs. You need to centralize log collection and analysis to obtain a comprehensive view of your system’s health and performance while minimizing configuration complexity and costs. What should you do?

options.text: Configure each application to write logs directly to BigQuery by using the BigQuery API.
Use Datadog to collect logs from GKE and Cloud Run, then forward the logs to BigQuery.
Configure Cloud Logging to collect logs from GKE and Cloud Run, and create a sink to export the logs to BigQuery.
Manually download log files from GKE and Cloud Run, then upload them to BigQuery by using the Google Cloud console.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Logging centrally collects Google Cloud workload logs, and a log sink can route the relevant log entries to a write-enabled BigQuery dataset for analysis. This managed approach avoids adding logging code to every application or operating and paying for a separate log-collection platform.

**Learn more:** [Route logs to supported destinations](https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/export/configure_export_v2) · [View logs routed to BigQuery](https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/export/bigquery)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You recently created a project to deploy multiple applications on Compute Engine VM instances across multiple regions.  
  
Although you expect the total number of instances not to decrease, you anticipate needing to change the allocation of instances among regions in the future. You want to minimize running costs for this multi-year project. What should you do?

options.text: Create a resource-based committed use discount for a 3-year term.
Create a compute flexible committed use discount for a 3-year term with reservations.
Create a compute flexible committed use discount for a 3-year term.
Create a resource-based committed use discount for a 1-year term.

questions.explanation:
A 3-year compute flexible committed use discount provides the longer-term commitment savings while allowing eligible Compute Engine usage to shift across regions. Resource-based CUDs are tied to a specific region, whereas compute flexible CUDs are not restricted to a single project, region, or machine configuration. Reservations provide capacity assurance, not the needed regional cost flexibility.

**Learn more:** [Committed use discounts (CUDs) for Compute Engine](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/committed-use-discounts-overview)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company permits teams to self-manage Google Cloud projects, including project-level Identity and Access Management (IAM). You are concerned that the team responsible for the Shared VPC project could accidentally delete that project, so a lien has been applied to it. You need to design a solution that limits Shared VPC project deletion to users who have the `resourcemanager.projects.updateLiens` permission at the organization level. What should you do?

options.text: Instruct teams to only perform IAM permission management as code with Terraform.
Enable VPC Service Controls for the container.googleapis.com API service.
Revoke the resourcemanager.projects.updateLiens permission from all users associated with the project.
Enable the compute.restrictXpnProjectLienRemoval organization policy constraint.

questions.explanation:
Enforcing the `compute.restrictXpnProjectLienRemoval` organization policy constraint restricts removal of a Shared VPC host-project lien to principals whose lien-related permissions are granted at the organization level. Since the lien must be removed before the project can be deleted, this prevents project-level administrators from removing the lien and accidentally deleting the Shared VPC host project.

**Learn more:** [Provision Shared VPC](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/provisioning-shared-vpc) · [Organization policy constraints for Cloud Load Balancing](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/org-policy-constraints)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are operating a web application deployed in a Compute Engine managed instance group. Ops Agent is installed on every instance. You recently identified suspicious activity originating from a particular IP address. You need to configure Cloud Monitoring to display the number of requests from that IP address with minimal operational overhead. What should you do?

options.text: Configure the Ops Agent with a logging receiver. Create a logs-based metric.B Create a script to scrape the web server log. Export the IP address request metrics to the Cloud Monitoring API.
Update the application to export the IP address request metrics to the Cloud Monitoring API.
Configure the Ops Agent with a metrics receiver.

questions.explanation:
Ops Agent logging receivers collect web server log entries and send them to Cloud Logging. A user-defined logs-based counter metric can filter those entries for the specified client IP address and is available in Cloud Monitoring for charting. This uses the existing logs and avoids maintaining a scraper or modifying the application.

**Learn more:** [Configure the Ops Agent](https://cloud.google.com/monitoring/agent/ops-agent/configuration) · [Log-based metrics overview](https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/logs-based-metrics)

Your company applies Site Reliability Engineering principles. You are preparing a postmortem for an incident caused by a software change that severely impacted users. You want to avoid severe incidents in the future. What should you do?

options.text: Identify engineers responsible for the incident and escalate to their senior management.
Ensure that test cases that catch errors of this type are run successfully before new software releases.
Follow up with the employees who reviewed the changes and prescribe practices they should follow in the future.
Design a policy that will require on-call teams to immediately call engineers and management to discuss a plan of action if an incident occurs.

questions.explanation:
SRE postmortems should produce blameless, system-focused preventative actions. Requiring successful execution of test cases that detect this class of error before releases improves the release process and reduces the likelihood that the same software defect reaches users.

**Learn more:** [Google SRE Workbook: Postmortem Culture](https://sre.google/workbook/postmortem-culture/) · [Google SRE Book: Postmortem Culture: Learning from Failure](https://sre.google/sre-book/postmortem-culture/)

You support a production service running on one Compute Engine instance. You regularly spend time recreating the service by deleting a crashing instance and creating a replacement from the relevant image. You want to reduce the time spent on manual operations while following Site Reliability Engineering principles. What should you do?

options.text: File a bug with the development team so they can find the root cause of the crashing instance.
Create a Managed instance Group with a single instance and use health checks to determine the system status.
Add a Load Balancer in front of the Compute Engine instance and use health checks to determine the system status.
Create a Stackdriver Monitoring dashboard with SMS alerts to be able to start recreating the crashed instance promptly after it was crashed.

questions.explanation:
A single-instance managed instance group (MIG) maintains the desired VM count using its instance template. An application-based health check can mark an unresponsive VM unhealthy, and the MIG autoheals it by automatically recreating the VM. This provides automated recovery instead of repeated manual replacement.

**Learn more:** [Set up an application-based health check and autohealing](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instance-groups/autohealing-instances-in-migs) · [Basic scenarios for creating managed instance groups (MIGs)](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instance-groups/creating-groups-of-managed-instances)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are investigating slow Apigee responses for API requests to the orders proxy in the Production environment. The proxy uses multiple services running in Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) with Cloud Service Mesh. You need to identify the root cause of the latency issues without affecting the performance of the other exposed services. What should you do?

options.text: Enable distributed tracing in the Production environment. Use Cloud Trace to check each span, and identify the service causing increased latency.
Use Cloud Monitoring with the Apigee target latencies metric to identify the service causing increased latency.
Use Cloud Logging to view the logs from different backends to identify the service causing increased latency.
Enable distributed tracing on Apigee with the configuration to trace only the orders proxy. Use Cloud Trace to check each span, and identify the service causing increased latency.

questions.explanation:
Apigee distributed tracing sends request-flow data to Cloud Trace, where spans expose the timing of individual flow steps and participating services. Tracing has a performance cost, but Apigee supports trace-configuration overrides for a specific API proxy so that troubleshooting can be limited to the orders proxy rather than applied to all proxies in the Production environment.

**Learn more:** [Enabling distributed tracing | Apigee](https://docs.cloud.google.com/apigee/docs/api-platform/develop/enabling-distributed-trace)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You use Cloud Build to build and deploy your application. You want to securely incorporate database credentials and other application secrets into the build pipeline, while also minimizing development effort. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Cloud Storage bucket and use the built-in encryption at rest. Store the secrets in the bucket and grant Cloud Build access to the bucket.
Encrypt the secrets and store them in the application repository. Store a decryption key in a separate repository and grant Cloud Build access to the repository.
Use client-side encryption to encrypt the secrets and store them in a Cloud Storage bucket. Store a decryption key in the bucket and grant Cloud Build access to the bucket.
Use Cloud Key Management Service (Cloud KMS) to encrypt the secrets and include them in your Cloud Build deployment configuration. Grant Cloud Build access to the KeyRing.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud recommends using Cloud Key Management Service (Cloud KMS) to encrypt sensitive values such as database credentials, then storing the resulting ciphertext directly in the Cloud Build configuration file (cloudbuild.yaml). During the build, a Cloud Build step decrypts the secret using the same KMS key, provided that the Cloud Build service account has been granted the Cloud KMS CryptoKey Decrypter role on the appropriate KeyRing/CryptoKey. This approach requires no additional storage infrastructure, uses Google-managed key rotation and access control, and integrates natively with Cloud Build, thereby minimizing development and operational effort compared to manually managing encryption keys and secret files in Cloud Storage or separate repositories.

**Learn more:** [Encrypting and Decrypting Secrets in Cloud Build](https://cloud.google.com/build/docs/securing-builds/use-encrypted-credentials)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an application running on Cloud Run. You want to use live production traffic to test a new application version while allowing the quality assurance team to carry out manual testing. You need to limit the potential impact of issues while the new version is being tested, and you must be able to roll back to a prior application version if necessary. How should you deploy the new version? (Choose two.)

options.text: Deploy the application as a new Cloud Run service.
Deploy a new Cloud Run revision with a tag and use the --no-traffic option.
Deploy a new Cloud Run revision without a tag and use the --no-traffic option.
Deploy the new application version and use the --no-traffic option. Route production traffic to the revision’s URL.
Deploy the new application version, and split traffic to the new version.

questions.explanation:
A new Cloud Run revision deployed with both a tag and `--no-traffic` can be manually tested at its tag-specific URL without receiving production traffic. Traffic splitting can then direct a limited percentage of live production requests to that revision while the prior revision continues serving the rest; traffic can be reassigned to the prior revision to roll back. [Cloud Run rollouts, rollbacks, and traffic migration](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/rollouts-rollbacks-traffic-migration)

**Learn more:** [Cloud Run rollouts, rollbacks, and traffic migration](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/rollouts-rollbacks-traffic-migration)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are accountable for the reliability of a custom-built, distributed file-storage service used internally by your company. The service processes thousands of file uploads and downloads each day. You must define a service level indicator (SLI) to measure the reliability of service use and configure alerts for potential problems. Which SLI should you use to measure service reliability?

options.text: Average request latency of API calls (e.g., get, put, list)
Number of successful file uploads and downloads per minute
Average size of objects stored in your service
Ratio of successful API calls to the total number of attempted API calls

questions.explanation: A reliability SLI should measure whether requested file-storage operations succeed. The ratio of successful API calls to total attempted API calls provides the operation success rate, capturing failures across uploads, downloads, and other API requests. Average latency measures performance, successful operations per minute measures traffic volume, and average object size does not measure service reliability.

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company is building a new cloud-native Google Cloud organization. You anticipate that this Google Cloud organization will initially be used by a small number of departments and later grow to support a large number of departments. Each department runs many applications of varying sizes. You must design the VPC network architecture.  
  
Your solution must minimize management effort while remaining flexible enough for development teams to rapidly adapt to their changing needs. What should you do?

options.text: Create a separate VPC for each department, and connect the VPCs with VPC Network Peering.
Create a separate VPC for each department. Use Private Service Connect to connect the VPCs.
Create a separate VPC for each application. Use Private Service Connect to connect the VPCs.
Create a separate VPC for each department, and connect the VPCs with Cloud VPN.

questions.explanation:
Creating a VPC network for each autonomous department gives that department an independent network boundary that can scale with its applications. VPC Network Peering provides private internal-IP connectivity between VPC networks with low management overhead, while preserving each VPC's separate administration and firewall controls. Private Service Connect is for publishing and consuming services privately, and Cloud VPN introduces tunnel administration and bandwidth constraints that are unnecessary for this intra-cloud VPC connectivity pattern.

**Learn more:** [Best practices and reference architectures for VPC design](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/best-practices-vpc-design) · [VPC Network Peering](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/vpc-peering)

Your organization has recently adopted a container-based workflow for application development. Your team develops many applications that are continuously deployed through an automated build pipeline to a Kubernetes cluster in the production environment. The security auditor is concerned that developers or operators might bypass automated testing and deploy code changes to production without approval. What should you do to enforce approvals?

options.text: Configure the build system with protected branches that require pull request approval.
Use an Admission Controller to verify that incoming requests originate from approved sources.
Leverage Kubernetes Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) to restrict access to only approved users.
Enable binary authorization inside the Kubernetes cluster and configure the build pipeline as an attestor.

questions.explanation:
Binary Authorization enforces deployment-time constraints by requiring a trusted attestation for each container image. When the automated build pipeline is configured as an attestor, only images that the pipeline has signed after completing the required process are permitted to deploy; unattested images are blocked.

**Learn more:** [Binary Authorization attestations overview](https://cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/attestations) · [Create a Binary Authorization attestation in a Cloud Build pipeline](https://cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/cloud-build)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your application services are running in Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). You want to ensure that only images from your centrally managed Google Container Registry (GCR) image registry in the `altostrat-images` project can be deployed to the cluster, while minimizing development time. What should you do?

options.text: Create a custom builder for Cloud Build that will only push images to gcr.io/altostrat-images.
Use a Binary Authorization policy that includes the whitelist name pattern gcr.io/altostrat-images/.
Add logic to the deployment pipeline to check that all manifests contain only images from gcr.io/altostrat-images.
Add a tag to each image in gcr.io/altostrat-images and check that this tag is present when the image is deployed.

questions.explanation:
Binary Authorization enforces image admission policies for GKE. Its policy supports allowlisting container images by `namePattern`; with other images denied by the admission rule, the `gcr.io/altostrat-images/` registry path can be the permitted deployment source. This provides cluster-side enforcement rather than relying on build or deployment-pipeline logic. [Google Cloud Binary Authorization policy YAML reference](https://docs.cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/policy-yaml-reference)

**Learn more:** [Google Cloud Binary Authorization policy YAML reference](https://docs.cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/policy-yaml-reference) · [Google Cloud Binary Authorization concepts](https://docs.cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/key-concepts)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are developing and operating client applications in Cloud Run and Cloud Functions. Your client requires all logs to remain available for one year so that the client can import them into its logging service. You must minimize the required code changes. What should you do?

options.text: Update all images in Cloud Run and all functions in Cloud Functions to send logs to both Cloud Logging and the client's logging service. Ensure that all the ports required to send logs are open in the VPC firewall.
Create a Pub/Sub topic, subscription, and logging sink. Configure the logging sink to send all logs into the topic. Give your client access to the topic to retrieve the logs.
Create a storage bucket and appropriate VPC firewall rules. Update all images in Cloud Run and all functions in Cloud Functions to send logs to a file within the storage bucket.

Create a logs bucket and logging sink. Set the retention on the logs bucket to 365 days. Configure the logging sink to send logs to the bucket. Give your client access to the bucket to retrieve the logs.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Logging can route logs from Cloud Run and Cloud Functions to a user-defined log bucket through a logging sink without application changes. Log-bucket retention is configurable from 1 to 3,650 days, so setting it to 365 days preserves the logs for one year; granting the client appropriate access lets it retrieve them for import into its logging service.

**Learn more:** [Configure log buckets](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/buckets) · [Route log entries](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/routing/overview)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You experienced a major service outage that impacted all service users for several hours. After several hours of incident management, the service returned to normal and user access was restored. Following Site Reliability Engineering recommended practices, you must provide an incident summary to the relevant stakeholders. What should you do first?

options.text: Call individual stakeholders to explain what happened.
Develop a post-mortem to be distributed to stakeholders.
Send the Incident State Document to all the stakeholders.
Require the engineer responsible to write an apology email to all stakeholders.

questions.explanation:
A major, prolonged, user-affecting outage should be documented through a blameless postmortem. A postmortem records the incident’s impact, mitigation or resolution, root causes, and follow-up actions to prevent recurrence, and it is reviewed and shared with stakeholders. The Incident State Document is the living record used during active incident response.

**Learn more:** [Postmortem Culture: Learning from Failure](https://sre.google/sre-book/postmortem-culture/) · [Incident Management Guide](https://sre.google/resources/practices-and-processes/incident-management-guide/)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are on call for an infrastructure service with many dependent systems. An alert indicates that the service is failing to serve most requests, affecting all of its dependent systems and hundreds of thousands of users. Under your Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) incident-management protocol, you declare yourself Incident Commander (IC) and bring in two experienced teammates as Operations Lead (OL) and Communications Lead (CL). What should you do next?

options.text: Look for ways to mitigate user impact and deploy the mitigations to production.
Contact the affected service owners and update them on the status of the incident.
Establish a communication channel where incident responders and leads can communicate with each other.
Start a postmortem, add incident information, circulate the draft internally, and ask internal stakeholders for input.

questions.explanation:
An incident response needs an established shared communication channel to coordinate responders, communicate current state, and maintain control of the response. With the IC, OL, and CL roles assigned, that channel gives the OL a coordinated path for mitigation work and the CL a reliable means to manage updates to responders and stakeholders. [Google SRE Workbook: Incident Response](https://sre.google/workbook/incident-response/)

**Learn more:** [Google SRE Workbook: Incident Response](https://sre.google/workbook/incident-response/) · [Google SRE Book: Managing Incidents](https://sre.google/sre-book/managing-incidents/)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization has recently moved to a container-based workflow for application development. Your team builds many applications that are continuously deployed through an automated build pipeline into production. A recent security audit found that the code being pushed to production may contain vulnerabilities, and that your existing tooling for virtual machine (VM) vulnerabilities is no longer applicable to this containerized environment. You need to ensure the security and patch level of all code running through the pipeline. What should you do?

options.text: Set up Container Analysis to scan and report Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures.
Configure the containers in the build pipeline to always update themselves before release.
Reconfigure the existing operating system vulnerability software to exist inside the container.
Implement static code analysis tooling against the Docker files used to create the containers.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud's Container Analysis (part of Artifact Analysis) automatically scans container images uploaded to Artifact Registry or Container Registry, extracting package information and cross-referencing it against vulnerability databases (such as the National Vulnerability Database) to identify Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs), including severity and CVSS scores, and fix availability. This continuous scanning keeps vulnerability metadata current as new CVEs are published, giving visibility into the security and patch level of every image moving through the build pipeline—something VM-focused vulnerability tools cannot provide for containerized workloads. This makes it the appropriate solution, unlike self-updating containers (no reporting/visibility), reusing VM tooling inside containers (explicitly stated as inapplicable), or static analysis of Dockerfiles alone (doesn't detect vulnerabilities in installed packages within the built image).

**Learn more:** [Container scanning overview | Artifact Analysis | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/artifact-analysis/docs/container-scanning-overview) · [Artifact analysis and vulnerability scanning | Artifact Registry | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/artifact-registry/docs/analysis)

questions.question: You support an application that runs on App Engine. The application is used worldwide and accessed from multiple device types. You need to determine the number of connections. You use Stackdriver Monitoring for App Engine. Which metric should you use?

options.text: flex/connections/current
tcp_ssl_proxy/new_connections
tcp_ssl_proxy/open_connections
flex/instance/connections/current

questions.explanation:
`appengine.googleapis.com/flex/connections/current` measures the current active connections for an App Engine flexible environment version. The instance-level metric is limited to a single App Engine flexible instance, while the TCP/SSL proxy metrics apply to TCP Proxy Load Balancing rather than App Engine application connections.\
\
**Learn more:** [Google Cloud metrics: A or B — App Engine metrics](https://docs.cloud.google.com/monitoring/api/metrics_gcp_a_b)

questions.question: You support an application that runs on App Engine. The application is used worldwide and accessed from multiple device types. You need to determine the number of connections. You use Stackdriver Monitoring for App Engine. Which metric should you use?

options.text: Confirm that the Stackdriver agent has been installed in the hosting virtual machine.
Confirm that your account has the proper permissions to use the Stackdriver dashboard.
Confirm that port 25 has been opened in the firewall to allow messages through to Stackdriver.
Confirm that the application is using the required client library and the service account key has proper permissions.

questions.explanation:
When logs from a newly deployed VM-based application do not appear in Stackdriver, the most common cause is that the Stackdriver Logging agent was never installed (or is not running) on the hosting virtual machine. The agent is responsible for collecting logs from the VM and forwarding them to Cloud Logging; without it, no application or system logs will be sent, regardless of IAM permissions or firewall rules for unrelated ports.

**Learn more:** [Installing the Logging agent](https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/agent/logging/installation)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are configuring connectivity between Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) clusters in separate VPCs. Nodes in Cluster A cannot reach nodes in Cluster B. You suspect the workload-access problem results from the network configuration. You must troubleshoot the problem but do not have execute access to workloads or nodes. You want to determine the layer where network connectivity is failing. What should you do?

options.text: Install a toolbox container on the node in Cluster Confirm that the routes to Cluster B are configured appropriately.
Use Network Connectivity Center to perform a Connectivity Test from Cluster A to Cluster B.
Use a debug container to run the traceroute command from Cluster A to Cluster B and from Cluster B to Cluster A. Identify the common failure point.
Enable VPC Flow Logs in both VPCs, and monitor packet drops.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud Connectivity Tests analyzes reachability between endpoints, including GKE clusters, by evaluating the expected packet-forwarding path and relevant VPC configuration such as routes and firewall rules. Its results identify where traffic is delivered or dropped without requiring interactive access to a node or workload.

**Learn more:** [Connectivity Tests overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-intelligence-center/docs/connectivity-tests/concepts/overview) · [Test connectivity within VPC networks](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-intelligence-center/docs/connectivity-tests/concepts/test-within-vpc-networks?hl=en)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company operates applications in Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). Application developers regularly create cloud resources to support those applications. You need to enable developers to manage infrastructure as code while following Google-recommended practices. You want to manage infrastructure as code by using Kubernetes Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs) and ensure that the selected setup is supported through the Google Cloud Support Portal. What should you do?

options.text: Configure Cloud Build with a Terraform builder to execute the terraform plan and terraform apply commands.
Install and configure Crossplane in GKE.
Configure a GitHub Action with a Terraform builder to execute the terraform plan and terraform apply commands as part of the pull request process.
Install and configure Config Connector in GKE.

questions.explanation:
Config Connector is a Google Cloud-supported Kubernetes add-on that provides CRDs and controllers for creating and managing Google Cloud resources from Kubernetes objects. Installing and configuring it in GKE meets the requirement for CRD-based infrastructure as code with Google Cloud support.

**Learn more:** [Config Connector overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/config-connector/docs/overview) · [Installing with the GKE add-on](https://docs.cloud.google.com/config-connector/docs/how-to/install-upgrade-uninstall)

questions.domain: Applying site reliability engineering practices
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization wants to adopt Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) culture and principles. Recently, a service you support experienced a limited outage. A manager from another team asks for a formal explanation of what occurred so they can implement remediations. What should you do?

options.text: Develop a postmortem that includes the root causes, resolution, lessons learned, and a prioritized list of action items. Share it with the manager only.
Develop a postmortem that includes the root causes, resolution, lessons learned, and a prioritized list of action items. Share it on the engineering organization's document portal.
Develop a postmortem that includes the root causes, resolution, lessons learned, the list of people responsible, and a list of action items for each person. Share it with the manager only.

Develop a postmortem that includes the root causes, resolution, lessons learned, the list of people responsible, and a list of action items for each person. Share it on the engineering organization's document portal.

questions.explanation:
SRE uses blameless postmortems to record the root causes, resolution, lessons learned, and prioritized corrective actions without assigning personal blame. Sharing the completed postmortem broadly through the engineering organization enables cross-team learning and helps prevent recurrence.

**Learn more:** [Google SRE: Postmortem Culture—Learning from Failure](https://sre.google/sre-book/postmortem-culture/) · [Google SRE Workbook: Postmortem Practices for Incident Management](https://sre.google/workbook/postmortem-culture/)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are implementing a CI/CD pipeline for your application in your company’s multi-cloud environment. Your application is deployed using custom Compute Engine images and their equivalents in other cloud providers. You need to implement a solution that enables you to build and deploy the images to your current environment and that can adapt to future changes. Which solution stack should you use?

options.text: Cloud Build with Packer
Cloud Build with Google Cloud Deploy
Google Kubernetes Engine with Google Cloud Deploy
Cloud Build with kpt

questions.explanation:
Cloud Build can run the image-building pipeline, and Packer creates identical virtual-machine images for multiple platforms from a single source configuration. This makes Cloud Build with Packer suitable for producing custom Compute Engine images and corresponding images for other cloud providers while retaining portability as the environment evolves.

**Learn more:** [Building VM images using Packer](https://docs.cloud.google.com/build/docs/building/build-vm-images-with-packer) · [Packer builders overview](https://developer.hashicorp.com/packer/docs/builders)

options.text: Use Cloud Build to trigger a Spinnaker pipeline.
Use Cloud Pub/Sub to trigger a Spinnaker pipeline.
Use a custom builder in Cloud Build to trigger Jenkins pipeline.
Use Cloud Pub/Sub to trigger a custom deployment service running in Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE).

questions.explanation:
Spinnaker can subscribe to Google Pub/Sub messages and use them to trigger a pipeline. Its Pub/Sub integration explicitly supports messages that originate from Google Container Registry (GCR), so an image-update event can directly initiate deployment without custom deployment code or an additional CI/CD intermediary.

You built a serverless application using Cloud Run and deployed it to your production environment. You want to determine the application's resource utilization for cost optimization. What should you do?

options.text: Use Cloud Trace with distributed tracing to monitor the resource utilization of the application.
Use Cloud Profiler with Ops Agent to monitor the CPU and memory utilization of the application.
Use Cloud Monitoring to monitor the container CPU and memory utilization of the application.
Use Cloud Ops to create logs-based metrics to monitor the resource utilization of the application.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Monitoring provides Cloud Run’s built-in container CPU utilization and container memory utilization metrics. Monitoring those metrics shows whether allocated compute resources are over- or under-utilized, which supports cost optimization.

**Learn more:** [Monitor Health and Performance — Cloud Run](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/monitoring) · [Configure CPU limits for services — Cloud Run](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/configuring/services/cpu)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You created a Stackdriver CPU-utilization chart in a dashboard in your workspace project. You want to share the chart only with your Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) team while following the principle of least privilege. What should you do?

options.text: Share the workspace Project ID with the SRE team. Assign the SRE team the Monitoring Viewer IAM role in the workspace project.
Share the workspace Project ID with the SRE team. Assign the SRE team the Dashboard Viewer IAM role in the workspace project.
Click ג€Share chart by URLג€ and provide the URL to the SRE team. Assign the SRE team the Monitoring Viewer IAM role in the workspace project.
Click ג€Share chart by URLג€ and provide the URL to the SRE team. Assign the SRE team the Dashboard Viewer IAM role in the workspace project.

questions.explanation:
The Monitoring Viewer role (`roles/monitoring.viewer`) provides read-only access to Cloud Monitoring data and configurations, allowing recipients to view the chart without being able to modify Monitoring resources. The Dashboard Configuration Viewer role only permits access to dashboard configurations and does not include permission to read the underlying metric data. Sharing the chart URL directly with the SRE team scopes the sharing action to that chart.

**Learn more:** [Share a custom dashboard](https://cloud.google.com/monitoring/charts/share-dashboards) · [Control access with IAM](https://cloud.google.com/monitoring/access-control)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are configuring a CI/CD pipeline to containerize an application. You must make sure containers are pushed to Artifact Registry only when they contain no critical vulnerabilities. You also want to minimize the maintenance effort for the pipeline. What should you do?

options.text: Create a script using a VM to build and push the container to Artifact Registry. After pushing the container, use automatic scanning in Artifact Analysis to check for critical vulnerabilities. Delete the container if critical vulnerabilities are detected.
Use Cloud Build to build the container. Use On-Demand Scanning in Artifact Analysis to check for critical vulnerabilities before pushing the image to Artifact Registry.

Install Jenkins on a VM and create a pipeline to build the container. Use On-Demand Scanning in Artifact Analysis to check for critical vulnerabilities before pushing the container to Artifact Registry.

Use Cloud Build to build the container. After pushing the container to Artifact Registry, use automatic scanning in Artifact Analysis to check for critical vulnerabilities. Delete the container if critical vulnerabilities are detected.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Build provides the managed build pipeline with the least operational overhead. Artifact Analysis On-Demand Scanning can scan the built image before it is pushed and can cause the build to fail when it finds a vulnerability at the configured CRITICAL severity, preventing that image from being stored in Artifact Registry. Automatic scanning is triggered when images are pushed, so it cannot enforce this pre-push requirement.

**Learn more:** [Use On-Demand Scanning in your Cloud Build pipeline](https://docs.cloud.google.com/artifact-analysis/docs/ods-cloudbuild) · [Scan OS packages manually](https://docs.cloud.google.com/artifact-analysis/docs/scan-os-on-demand)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company operates a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster for each environment: staging and production. You need to configure cluster release channels in accordance with Google-recommended practices. You want to prioritize maximum cluster stability rather than access to the newest features. What should you do?

options.text: Configure the production cluster to use the Stable release channel, and configure the staging cluster to use the Regular release channel.
Configure the production cluster to use the Extended release channel, and configure the staging cluster to use the Rapid release channel.
Configure the production cluster to use the Stable release channel, and configure the staging cluster to use the Stable release channel.
Configure the production cluster to use the Regular release channel, and configure the staging cluster to use the Regular release channel.

questions.explanation:
The Stable channel prioritizes stability and receives versions only after validation in the Rapid and Regular channels, making it appropriate for a production cluster where maturity is the priority. Using the Regular channel in staging exposes that environment to releases earlier, allowing validation before they reach production. Extended is intended for long-term support of a Kubernetes minor version, not as the general choice for maximum release stability.

**Learn more:** [About release channels | Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE)](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/release-channels)

Your team operates a high-traffic application that produces several terabytes of logs each day. You need to lower Cloud Logging costs while keeping critical operational and security information. What should you do?

options.text: Configure exclusion filters for DEBUG logs, and configure export of ERROR logs to BigQuery.
Halve log retention period for the _Default logging bucket to 15 days.
Enable sampling for all log levels on the _Default logging bucket.
Create log-based metrics for key indicators, and configure logging exclusion filters for non- ERROR logs.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Logging exclusion filters reduce chargeable log volume by preventing matching entries from being routed to a sink. Excluding high-volume DEBUG logs preserves more valuable log levels, while routing ERROR logs to BigQuery retains critical error data for querying and analysis. Sampling every severity level or excluding all non-ERROR entries can discard important operational warnings and security records. The `_Default` log bucket has a fixed 30-day retention period.

**Learn more:** [Route log entries](https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/routing/overview) · [Cloud Logging LogExclusion reference](https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/reference/v2/rest/v2/billingAccounts.exclusions)

Your organization runs multiple Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) clusters in one project. You must design a highly available solution for collecting and querying both domain-specific workload metrics and default GKE metrics across every cluster, while keeping operational overhead to a minimum. What should you do?

options.text: Use Prometheus operator to install Prometheus in every cluster and scrape the metrics. Configure remote-write to one central Prometheus. Query the central Prometheus instance.
Enable managed collection on every GKE cluster. Query the metrics in BigQuery.

Use Prometheus operator to install Prometheus in every cluster and scrape the metrics. Ensure that a Thanos sidecar is enabled on every Prometheus instance. Configure Thanos in the central cluster. Query the central Thanos instance.
Enable managed collection on every GKE cluster. Query the metrics in Cloud Monitoring.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus managed collection collects Prometheus-compatible workload metrics without requiring self-managed Prometheus servers. GKE default system metrics and managed Prometheus metrics are available in Cloud Monitoring, which provides a centralized, highly available query and monitoring service across clusters in the project.

**Learn more:** [Collect Prometheus metrics from GKE](https://docs.cloud.google.com/monitoring/integrate/gke) · [Configure metrics collection](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/configure-metrics)
