questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your team is building a new application to deploy both within and outside Google Cloud Platform (GCP). You must gather detailed metrics, such as system resource utilization. You want to use centralized GCP services while minimizing the work needed to set up this collection system. What should you do?

options.text: Import the Stackdriver Profiler package, and configure it to relay function timing data to Stackdriver for further analysis.
Import the Stackdriver Debugger package, and configure the application to emit debug messages with timing information.
Instrument the code using a timing library, and publish the metrics via a health check endpoint that is scraped by Stackdriver.
Install an Application Performance Monitoring (APM) tool in both locations, and configure an export to a central data storage location for analysis.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Profiler uses a language-specific profiling agent to continuously collect low-overhead CPU-usage and memory-allocation data and analyze it in Google Cloud. It supports applications running outside Google Cloud as well as supported Google Cloud environments, so importing and configuring its package provides centralized resource-consumption analysis without building a custom metrics collection and export pipeline.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Profiler overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/profiler/docs/about-profiler)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are deploying an application on Cloud Run. The application needs a password to start. Your organization mandates that every password be rotated every 24 hours, and the application must use the newest password. You need to deploy the application without downtime. What should you do?

options.text: Store the password in Secret Manager and send the secret to the application by using environment variables.
Store the password in Secret Manager and mount the secret as a volume within the application.
Use Cloud Build to add your password into the application container at build time. Ensure that Artifact Registry is secured from public access.
Store the password directly in the code. Use Cloud Build to rebuild and deploy the application each time the password changes.

questions.explanation:
A Secret Manager secret mounted as a Cloud Run volume can use the `latest` version, and Cloud Run fetches the current secret value when the mounted volume is read. This lets the application access rotated credentials without rebuilding the container or deploying a replacement revision. Environment-variable secrets are retrieved before an instance starts and therefore do not update in already-running instances.

**Learn more:** [Configure secrets for Cloud Run services](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/configuring/services/secrets)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are deploying a new application on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) that handles personally identifiable information (PII). You need to configure Cloud Logging to collect application logs while ensuring sensitive user information is not exposed. What should you do?

options.text: Implement log sampling to reduce the volume of logs collected.
Configure Cloud Data Loss Prevention to scan logs in real-time and redact PII before it's stored in Cloud Logging.
Disable Cloud Logging for the application to prevent sensitive data from being logged.
Store all logs in an encrypted Cloud Storage bucket with restricted access.

questions.explanation:
Sensitive Data Protection (formerly Cloud Data Loss Prevention) can detect sensitive data in text and de-identify it by redacting or replacing detected values. Applying this protection to log content prevents PII from being retained in Cloud Logging while preserving useful application telemetry.

**Learn more:** [Redacting sensitive data from text | Sensitive Data Protection](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sensitive-data-protection/docs/redacting-sensitive-data)

questions.domain: Optimizing performance and cost
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are bringing your company’s marketing department onto Google Cloud. The marketing department will manage development, but you need to monitor all spending and receive an alert if the marketing budget is exceeded. What should you do?

options.text: Create all Google Cloud projects. Create one budget alert for each project with the total budget split by the number of projects as the limit.
Create all Google Cloud projects under a new marketing folder. Create one budget alert for each project with the total budget as the limit.
Create all Google Cloud projects under a new marketing folder. Create one budget alert at folder level with the total budget as the limit.
Create all the Google Cloud projects. Create one budget alert for each project with the total budget as the limit.

questions.explanation:
A Cloud Billing budget can be scoped to all projects under a folder by filtering on that folder as a resource ancestor. One budget at the marketing-folder level therefore monitors the combined costs of the marketing projects against the full marketing budget and can issue threshold alerts when that aggregate spending exceeds the limit.

**Learn more:** [Create, edit, or delete budgets and budget alerts](https://cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/budgets) · [gcloud billing budgets create reference](https://cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/billing/budgets/create)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are designing a new multi-tenant Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster for a customer. The customer is concerned about the risks of using long-lived credentials. The customer requires each GKE workload to have the minimum Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions, following the principle of least privilege (PoLP). You need to design an IAM impersonation solution that follows Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: 1. Create a Google service account.2. Create a node pool, and set the Google service account as the default identity.3. Ensure that workloads can only run on the designated node pool by using node selectors, taints, and tolerations.4. Repeat for each workload.
1. Create a Google service account.2. Create a node pool without taints, and set the Google service account as the default identity.3. Grant IAM permissions to the Google service account.

1. Create a Google service account.2. Create a Kubernetes service account in a Workload Identity-enabled cluster.3. Link the Google service account with the Kubernetes service account by using the roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser role and iam.gke.io/gcp-service-account annotation.4. Map the Kubernetes service account to the workload.5. Repeat for each workload.

1. Create a Google service account.2. Create a service account key for the Google service account.3. Create a Kubernetes secret with a service account key.4. Ensure that workload mounts the secret and set the GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS environment variable to point at the mount path.5. Repeat for each workload.

questions.explanation:
Workload Identity Federation for GKE avoids service-account key files and supports distinct, fine-grained identities and IAM authorization for individual workloads. In the IAM service-account impersonation approach, a Kubernetes service account receives `roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser` on the linked Google service account and is annotated with `iam.gke.io/gcp-service-account`; workloads using that Kubernetes service account can impersonate the Google service account. Creating a separate mapping and narrowly scoped IAM permissions for each workload enforces least privilege.

**Learn more:** [Authenticate to Google Cloud APIs from GKE workloads](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/workload-identity) · [About Workload Identity Federation for GKE](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/workload-identity)

Your company wants to centralize all monitoring and alerting capabilities. Its VPC network has an internally exposed webhook that can be called to trigger alerts. You need to integrate your Google Cloud alerts so they call this webhook. You want to minimize costs while following Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Configure a new Pub/Sub notification channel with a new topic. Create a pull subscription to consume the events.
Configure a new Pub/Sub notification channel with a new topic. Create a push subscription with the webhook as a subscriber to get the events.
Configure a new webhook notification channel. Edit your alerting policies to use the new notification channel to propagate the events.

Configure a new Pub/Sub notification channel with a new topic. Create a new Cloud Run function with direct VPC egress to write the events to the internal endpoint. Create a push subscription with the Cloud Run function as a subscriber to get the events.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Monitoring webhook notification channels support only public endpoints, and Pub/Sub cannot directly push messages to private VPC addresses. Publishing alerts to a Pub/Sub notification channel and delivering them to a Cloud Run function through a push subscription provides a managed integration point. The function can use direct VPC egress to call the internally exposed webhook.

**Learn more:** [Create and manage notification channels](https://docs.cloud.google.com/monitoring/support/notification-options) · [Create push subscriptions](https://docs.cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/create-push-subscription)

A new release of your containerized application has been tested and is ready for production deployment on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). You were unable to fully load-test the new release in your pre-production environment, and must ensure that the application has no performance problems after deployment. The deployment must be automated. What should you do?

options.text: Deploy the application through a continuous delivery pipeline by using canary deployments. Use Cloud Monitoring to look for performance issues, and ramp up traffic as supported by the metrics.

Deploy the application through a continuous delivery pipeline by using blue/green deployments. Migrate traffic to the new version of the application and use Cloud Monitoring to look for performance issues.
Deploy the application by using kubectl and use Config Connector to slowly ramp up traffic between versions. Use Cloud Monitoring to look for performance issues.

Deploy the application by using kubectl and set the spec.updateStrategy.type field to RollingUpdate. Use Cloud Monitoring to look for performance issues, and run the kubectl rollback command if there are any issues.

questions.explanation:
A canary deployment progressively directs a limited share of traffic to the new version while the existing version remains available. Monitoring performance during each increment allows traffic to be increased only when the metrics support it, limiting the impact of an undetected production performance problem. Cloud Deploy supports automated canary deployments to GKE through a delivery pipeline.

**Learn more:** [Canary deployments to GKE using service-based networking](https://docs.cloud.google.com/deploy/docs/deployment-strategies/canary/gke/service-networking) · [Use a canary deployment strategy](https://docs.cloud.google.com/deploy/docs/deployment-strategies/canary)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],As a Site Reliability Engineer, you support a Go application running in production on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). After deploying a new application version, you observe that it runs for approximately 15 minutes before restarting. You add Cloud Profiler to the application and observe that heap usage increases continuously until the application restarts. What should you do?

options.text: Increase the CPU limit in the application deployment.
Add high memory compute nodes to the cluster.
Increase the memory limit in the application deployment.
Add Cloud Trace to the application, and redeploy.

questions.explanation:
A container that continuously consumes heap memory can reach its configured memory limit, be terminated by the OOM killer, and then restart. Raising the deployment's container memory limit accommodates higher peak memory usage; node memory alone does not raise a container-level limit. The underlying memory leak should also be corrected.

**Learn more:** [Troubleshoot OOM events | Google Kubernetes Engine](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/troubleshooting/oom-events)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You manage a critical, high-traffic application running on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). You are preparing to release a new version of the application that includes significant changes to its payment-processing workflow. You need to implement a deployment strategy that minimizes risk and automatically rolls back if the release is unstable. What should you do?

options.text: Use Cloud Deploy to execute a canary deployment. Configure the delivery pipeline with a multi-phase canary deployment sequence, starting with a 5% traffic split. Define success criteria using application telemetry from Cloud Monitoring, and configure Cloud Deploy to automatically roll back the release if the new version fails verification.

Configure your GKE deployment manifest to use a blue-green strategy. Deploy the new version as a “green” deployment alongside the existing “blue” deployment. Once the “green” environment is live, update the service selector to gradually switch user traffic to the new version.

Edit the GKE Service manifest to include a new selector for the v2 pods Then, create a second GKE Deployment for the new version of the application. Slowly scale up the replica count of the new deployment while scaling down the old one to gradually shift traffic.

Configure the GKE Deployment to use the default rolling update strategy. Monitor logs and metrics in Cloud Monitoring during the update. If an issue is detected, use the kubectl rollout undo command to automatically revert the application to the previous stable version.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Deploy can perform a progressive, multi-phase canary deployment to GKE, initially exposing only a small percentage of traffic to the new version. Deploy analysis can assess application telemetry from Cloud Monitoring during canary phases, and a Cloud Deploy repair rollout automation can roll back to the most recently successful release after failed rollout repair attempts. This limits the impact of an unstable payment-processing release while providing automated recovery.

**Learn more:** [Use a canary deployment strategy](https://docs.cloud.google.com/deploy/docs/deployment-strategies/canary) · [Run analysis jobs in Cloud Deploy](https://docs.cloud.google.com/deploy/docs/analysis?hl=en)

questions.question: You manage production deployments to a set of Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) clusters. You need to ensure that only images successfully built by your trusted CI/CD pipeline are deployed to production. What should you do?

options.text: Enable Cloud Security Scanner on the clusters.
Enable Vulnerability Analysis on the Container Registry.
Set up the Kubernetes Engine clusters as private clusters.
Set up the Kubernetes Engine clusters with Binary Authorization.

questions.explanation:
Binary Authorization enforces deploy-time policies for GKE container images. It can require attestations from a trusted build or CI system, allowing verified images to deploy and denying images that lack the required attestation.\
\
**Learn more:** [Deploy only images built by Cloud Build](https://docs.cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/deploy-cloud-build) · [Binary Authorization overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/overview)

questions.question: You manage production deployments to a set of Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) clusters. You need to ensure that only images successfully built by your trusted CI/CD pipeline are deployed to production. What should you do?

options.text: Configure Prometheus cross-service federation for centralized data access.
Configure workload metrics within Cloud Operations for GKE.
Configure Prometheus hierarchical federation for centralized data access.
Configure Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus is a fully managed, multi-cloud and cross-project Prometheus solution. It sends metrics to Google’s globally scalable Monarch backend, where PromQL queries can retrieve and aggregate data across regions and projects. This provides global visibility while removing the need to operate and scale a centralized or hierarchical Prometheus federation deployment.

**Learn more:** [Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus](https://docs.cloud.google.com/stackdriver/docs/managed-prometheus) · [Query using the Prometheus API or UI](https://docs.cloud.google.com/stackdriver/docs/managed-prometheus/query-api-ui)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You use Terraform to manage infrastructure as code in a CI/CD pipeline. You observe that multiple copies of the full infrastructure stack exist in your Google Cloud project, with a new copy being created whenever a change is made to the existing infrastructure. You must optimize cloud spending by ensuring that only one instance of the infrastructure stack exists at any given time. You want to follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Create a new pipeline to delete old infrastructure stacks when they are no longer needed.
Confirm that the pipeline is storing and retrieving the terraform.tfstate file from Cloud Storage with the Terraform gcs backend.
Verify that the pipeline is storing and retrieving the terraform.tfstate file from a source control.
Update the pipeline to remove any existing infrastructure before you apply the latest configuration.

questions.explanation:
Terraform uses its state file to maintain the mapping between configuration and deployed resources. A CI/CD pipeline must use a shared remote state so each run recognizes and updates the existing resources rather than treating them as new. Google recommends the Cloud Storage state backend for Terraform on Google Cloud; it retrieves the latest state before commands and writes the updated state afterward.

**Learn more:** [Store Terraform state in a Cloud Storage bucket](https://docs.cloud.google.com/docs/terraform/resource-management/store-state) · [Best practices for security — Use remote state](https://docs.cloud.google.com/docs/terraform/best-practices/security)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company uses HTTPS requests to trigger a public Cloud Run-hosted service that is available at `https://booking-engine-abcdef.a.run.app`. You need to allow developers to test the service’s latest revisions before the service is made available to customers. What should you do?

options.text: Run the gcloud run deploy booking-engine --no-traffic --tag dev command. Use the https://dev--booking-engine-abcdef.a.run.app URL for testing.
Run the gcloud run services update-traffic booking-engine --to-revisions LATEST=1 command. Use the https://booking-engine-abcdef.a.run.app URL for testing.
Pass the curl –H “Authorization:Bearer $(gcloud auth print-identity-token)” auth token. Use the https://booking-engine-abcdef.a.run.app URL to test privately.
Grant the roles/run.invoker role to the developers testing the booking-engine service. Use the https://booking-engine-abcdef.private.run.app URL for testing.

questions.explanation:
Deploying a Cloud Run revision with `--no-traffic` prevents it from receiving customer traffic, and assigning a revision tag creates a dedicated tagged URL for testing that revision directly. This supports validation before any traffic is routed to the new revision.

**Learn more:** [Rollbacks, gradual rollouts, and traffic migration](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/rollouts-rollbacks-traffic-migration)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You manage a complex microservices application that runs on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). You recently instrumented the services with OpenTelemetry to generate traces. During a performance investigation in Cloud Trace, you observe a high-latency transaction. The trace waterfall does not provide enough detail to determine the root cause, but you suspect the problem lies in the service's business logic. This service sends structured logs to Cloud Logging. You need to rapidly analyze the logs corresponding to the high-latency request. What should you do?

options.text: In the Cloud Trace waterfall view, identify the trace ID of a slow request. Then, in the Logs Explorer, write a query to filter for log entries that contain that specific trace ID.

Configure a log-based metric in Cloud Logging to count the occurrences of error messages. Then, create an alerting policy on this metric to be notified of future issues, and analyze the logs associated with those alerts.

Export all logs from Cloud Logging to BigQuery. Write a SQL query to join the trace data with the log data on the trace ID field, and then filter for the specific transaction to find the related log entries.

Ensure your application’s logging configuration includes the trace ID from the OpenTelemetry context in each structured log entry. Then, in the Cloud Trace details view for a slow request, click the “Show logs” option to view correlated logs directly alongside the trace’s span waterfall.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Logging entries that include the trace context can be correlated with their Cloud Trace trace and spans. With structured logging from an active OpenTelemetry span, the trace fields can be populated from the OpenTelemetry Context. Cloud Trace can then display the correlated entries directly alongside the waterfall through **Show logs**, providing immediate request-specific business-logic evidence.

**Learn more:** [Link log entries with traces | Cloud Trace](https://cloud.google.com/trace/docs/trace-log-integration)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are responsible for creating development environments for your company's development team. You want to provide environments with identical IDEs for every developer while ensuring these environments are not exposed to public networks. You need to select the most cost-effective solution without affecting developer productivity. What should you do?

options.text: Create multiple Compute Engine VM instances with a public IP address and use a Public NAT gateway. Configure an instance schedule to shut down the VMs.
Create multiple Compute Engine VM instances without a public IP address. Configure an instance schedule to shut down the VMs.
Create a Cloud Workstations private cluster. Create a workstation configuration with an idieTimeour parameter.
Create a Cloud Workstations private cluster. Create a workstation configuration with a runningTimeout parameter.

questions.explanation:
A private Cloud Workstations cluster provides standardized managed development environments without exposing them to public networks. An `idleTimeout` automatically stops a workstation only after it no longer receives user traffic, reducing costs while allowing developers to continue active work uninterrupted. In contrast, `runningTimeout` shuts down a workstation after a fixed duration regardless of activity.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Workstations overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/workstations/docs/overview) · [Cloud Workstations configuration reference](https://docs.cloud.google.com/workstations/docs/reference/rest/v1/projects.locations.workstationClusters.workstationConfigs)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company uses Site Reliability Engineering practices. You are responsible for Communications during a large, ongoing incident that affects customer-facing applications. There is still no estimated time to resolve the outage. You are receiving emails from internal stakeholders seeking outage updates, as well as emails from customers asking what is happening. You want to efficiently deliver updates to everyone affected by the outage.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Focus on responding to internal stakeholders at least every 30 minutes. Commit to ג€next updateג€ times.
Provide periodic updates to all stakeholders in a timely manner. Commit to a ג€next updateג€ time in all communications.
Delegate the responding to internal stakeholder emails to another member of the Incident Response Team. Focus on providing responses directly to customers.
Provide all internal stakeholder emails to the Incident Commander, and allow them to manage internal communications. Focus on providing responses directly to customers.

questions.explanation:
The Communications Lead is the public face of incident response and is responsible for managing incident inquiries and providing regular updates to the incident team and all stakeholders. When a resolution time is unknown, committing to a specific time for the next update maintains clear expectations and ensures both internal and external audiences receive consistent communication.

**Learn more:** [Google SRE Workbook: Incident Response](https://sre.google/workbook/incident-response/) · [Google SRE: Managing Incidents](https://sre.google/sre-book/managing-incidents/)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your team recently deployed an NGINX-based application to Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) and made it publicly available through an HTTP Google Cloud Load Balancer (GCLB) ingress. You want to scale the application frontend deployment using an appropriate Service Level Indicator (SLI). What should you do?

options.text: Configure the horizontal pod autoscaler to use the average response time from the Liveness and Readiness probes.
Configure the vertical pod autoscaler in GKE and enable the cluster autoscaler to scale the cluster as pods expand.
Install the Stackdriver custom metrics adapter and configure a horizontal pod autoscaler to use the number of requests provided by the GCLB.
Expose the NGINX stats endpoint and configure the horizontal pod autoscaler to use the request metrics exposed by the NGINX deployment.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Monitoring provides the HTTP(S) Load Balancer request-count metric, which represents incoming request traffic and is a suitable leading indicator for scaling frontend replicas. The Stackdriver custom metrics adapter exposes that metric to Kubernetes so a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler can scale the deployment from it.

**Learn more:** [GKE scalable applications—autoscaling](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/learn/scalable-apps-autoscale) · [GKE Horizontal Pod Autoscaler](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/horizontalpodautoscaler)

questions.domain: Applying site reliability engineering practices
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company is migrating its production systems to Google Cloud. You must implement site reliability engineering (SRE) practices during the migration to reduce customer impact from possible future incidents. Which two SRE practices should you implement? (Choose two.)

options.text: Create up-to-date playbooks with instructions for debugging and mitigating issues.
Ensure that all teams can modify the production environment to resolve issues.
Create an alerting mechanism for your SRE team based on your system's internal behavior.
Automate common tasks to analyze key impact information and intelligently suggest mitigating actions for the on-call team.
Ensure that full autonomy and permissions are only granted to the on-call team.

questions.explanation:
Current playbooks give on-call responders documented procedures to debug and mitigate incidents quickly. Automating common operational tasks reduces repetitive toil and can provide timely impact analysis and mitigation guidance, improving the speed and consistency of incident response. SRE alerting should generally be based on customer-facing symptoms and service objectives rather than a system’s internal behavior.

**Learn more:** [Google SRE incident management and response guide](https://sre.google/resources/practices-and-processes/incident-management-guide/) · [Google Cloud Site Reliability Engineering](https://cloud.google.com/sre)

questions.domain: Optimizing performance and cost

options.text: Deploy the service by using Cloud Run.
Deploy the service by using standard VMs with a 3-year committed use discount.
Deploy the service by using GKE.
Deploy the service by using Spot VMs.

questions.explanation:
Spot VMs are appropriate for fault-tolerant batch workloads that can withstand preemption. Because processing can resume after failure and no processing-time SLO requires uninterrupted execution, preemption only delays work. The service requires VM-based execution rather than a container platform, and Spot VMs offer substantially lower cost than standard VMs.

**Learn more:** [Spot VMs | Compute Engine | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/spot?hl=en) · [Spot VMs pricing | Google Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/spot-vms/pricing)

As part of the company initiative to shift security left, the InfoSec team asks every team to implement guardrails on all Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) clusters so that only trusted and approved images can be deployed.  
  
You need to determine how to meet the InfoSec team's shift-left security objective. What should you do?

options.text: Enable Container Analysis in Artifact Registry, and check for common vulnerabilities and exposures (CVEs) in your container images
Use Binary Authorization to attest images during your CI/CD pipeline
Configure Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies to create a least privilege model on your GKE clusters.
Deploy Falco or Twistlock on GKE to monitor for vulnerabilities on your running Pods

questions.explanation:
Binary Authorization enforces an image-deployment policy for GKE by verifying trusted attestations at deploy time. Attesting images in the CI/CD pipeline records that they have completed the organization’s required approval or validation steps, allowing GKE to block images that lack the required verified attestation.

**Learn more:** [Attestations overview | Binary Authorization](https://docs.cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/attestations) · [Create a Binary Authorization attestation in a Cloud Build pipeline](https://docs.cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/cloud-build)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are designing a secure Cloud Build pipeline for a web application that needs access to a package manager. The package manager credentials are highly sensitive and must be safeguarded from unauthorized access. You need to design a solution that securely retrieves credentials at build time in accordance with Google-recommended practices. You also want to minimize maintenance overhead. What should you do?

options.text: Grant the roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyDecrypter role to the Cloud Build service account. Store Cloud Key Management Service (Cloud KMS) encrypted data in a build config file. Specify the secret under the secrets field.

Grant the roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyDecrypter role to the Cloud Build service account. Store Cloud Key Management Service (Cloud KMS) encrypted data in a build config file. Specify the secret under the availableSecrets.inline field.
Grant the roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor role to the Cloud Build service account used for the build. Specify the secret under the availableSecrets.secretManager field.
Use base64-encrypted data in a web application’s source control repository. Decrypt and use the secret during the build.

questions.explanation:
Secret Manager is the Google-recommended method for managing sensitive data in Cloud Build. Granting the build service account `roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor` and declaring the secret in `availableSecrets.secretManager` lets Cloud Build retrieve it securely at build time while avoiding storage of credentials in source control and reducing Cloud KMS key-management overhead.

**Learn more:** [Use secrets from Secret Manager | Cloud Build](https://docs.cloud.google.com/build/docs/securing-builds/use-secrets) · [Use encrypted credentials from Cloud KMS | Cloud Build](https://docs.cloud.google.com/build/docs/securing-builds/use-encrypted-credentials)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are developing and operating client applications on Cloud Run and Cloud Functions. Your client requires that all logs be available for one year so the client can import them into its logging service. You must minimize the required code changes. What should you do?

options.text: Deploy Falco or Twistlock on GKE to monitor for vulnerabilities on your running Pods.
Configure Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies to create a least privilege model on your GKE clusters.
Use Binary Authorization to attest images during your CI/CD pipeline.
Enable Container Analysis in Artifact Registry, and check for common vulnerabilities and exposures (CVEs) in your container images.

questions.explanation: Enabling Container Analysis in Artifact Registry is a configuration-level control that automatically scans container images for known CVEs without requiring any changes to application source code, satisfying a requirement to minimize code changes while still improving the operational posture of workloads running on Cloud Run and Cloud Functions. Because it operates at the image/registry level rather than the application runtime, teams can adopt it purely through platform configuration.

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are responsible for several production systems that all run on Compute Engine within the same Google Cloud Platform (GCP) project. Each system has its own dedicated set of Compute Engine instances. You need to determine how much it costs to run each individual system. What should you do?

options.text: In the Google Cloud Platform Console, use the Cost Breakdown section to visualize the costs per system.
Assign all instances a label specific to the system they run. Configure BigQuery billing export and query costs per label.
Enrich all instances with metadata specific to the system they run. Configure Stackdriver Logging to export to BigQuery, and query costs based on the metadata.
Name each virtual machine (VM) after the system it runs. Set up a usage report export to a Cloud Storage bucket. Configure the bucket as a source in BigQuery to query costs based on VM name.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud recommends applying labels to resources such as Compute Engine instances to categorize them (for example, by system or application). When you enable BigQuery export of Cloud Billing data, the exported billing records include the labels attached to each resource, allowing you to write BigQuery queries that aggregate and break down costs by label — in this case, per system. This is the standard, supported approach for granular cost analysis when multiple systems share a single project and billing account, as documented in Google's guidance on visualizing and analyzing billing data with labels and BigQuery export.

**Learn more:** [Export Cloud Billing data to BigQuery](https://cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/export-data-bigquery) · [Using labels](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/labeling-resources)

You are the Operations Lead for an active incident affecting one of your services. The service normally operates at roughly 70% capacity. You observe that one node returns 5xx errors for every request, and customer support cases have noticeably increased. You must remove the problematic node from the load-balancer pool so that you can isolate and investigate it. You want to follow Google-recommended practices for managing the incident and minimizing user impact. What should you do?

options.text: 1. Communicate your intent to the incident team.2. Perform a load analysis to determine if the remaining nodes can handle the increase in traffic offloaded from the removed node, and scale appropriately.3. When any new nodes report healthy, drain traffic from the unhealthy node, and remove the unhealthy node from service.

1. Communicate your intent to the incident team.2. Add a new node to the pool, and wait for the new node to report as healthy.3. When traffic is being served on the new node, drain traffic from the unhealthy node, and remove the old node from service.

1. Drain traffic from the unhealthy node and remove the node from service.2. Monitor traffic to ensure that the error is resolved and that the other nodes in the pool are handling the traffic appropriately.3. Scale the pool as necessary to handle the new load.4. Communicate your actions to the incident team.

1. Drain traffic from the unhealthy node and remove the old node from service.2. Add a new node to the pool, wait for the new node to report as healthy, and then serve traffic to the new node.3. Monitor traffic to ensure that the pool is healthy and is handling traffic appropriately.4. Communicate your actions to the incident team.

questions.explanation:
Capacity must be validated and, if needed, increased before taking a backend out of a load-balanced service that is already substantially utilized. This avoids shifting its traffic onto insufficient remaining capacity and creating a wider outage. Clear incident-team communication supports coordinated incident response; once healthy replacement capacity is available, traffic can be drained from the failing node and it can be removed for investigation.

**Learn more:** [Manage incidents and problems](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/framework/operational-excellence/manage-incidents-and-problems?hl=en) · [Manage traffic and load for your workloads in Google Cloud](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/infra-reliability-guide/traffic-load?hl=en)

You support an application that runs on GCP and want to set up SMS notifications for your team for the most critical alerts in Stackdriver Monitoring. You have already identified the alerting policies for which you want to configure this. What should you do?

options.text: Download and configure a third-party integration between Stackdriver Monitoring and an SMS gateway. Ensure that your team members add their SMS/phone numbers to the external tool.

Select the Webhook notifications option for each alerting policy, and configure it to use a third-party integration tool. Ensure that your team members add their SMS/phone numbers to the external tool.

Ensure that your team members set their SMS/phone numbers in their Stackdriver Profile. Select the SMS notification option for each alerting policy and then select the appropriate SMS/phone numbers from the list.

Configure a Slack notification for each alerting policy. Set up a Slack-to-SMS integration to send SMS messages when Slack messages are received. Ensure that your team members add their SMS/phone numbers to the external integration.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Monitoring supports SMS notification channels directly. Configure and verify the team members’ phone numbers, then attach the appropriate SMS notification channels to the selected alerting policies. Google Cloud documentation describes selecting the SMS notification type and choosing a verified phone number from the available list.

**Learn more:** [Create and manage notification channels | Cloud Monitoring | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/monitoring/support/notification-options)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You manage a critical API on Cloud Run that handles an average of 10,000 requests per minute. You must define service level objectives (SLOs) for availability and latency so the API satisfies user expectations, including 99.9% availability and a maximum latency of 200 milliseconds for 95% of requests. You must also ensure that these SLOs are actively measured and monitored. What should you do?

options.text: Configure Cloud Monitoring to send alerts when average API latency exceeds 150 ms or the error rate surpasses 0.1%.
Prioritize latency as the only SLO, targeting 100 ms for 99% of requests.
Set SLOs for 99% availability at 99% and 500 ms latency for 90% of requests. Use Cloud Monitoring to track SLOs and alert on violations.
Set SLOs for the API by using availability and latency service level indicators. Use Cloud Monitoring to track SLOs and alert on violations.

questions.explanation:
Availability and latency service level indicators measure the required user-facing outcomes. Set SLOs from those SLIs to require 99.9% availability and at least 95% of requests completing within 200 ms, then use Cloud Monitoring to track compliance and alert when an SLO is violated. Cloud Monitoring service monitoring defines SLOs from SLIs and supports SLO-based alerting.

**Learn more:** [Concepts in service monitoring](https://docs.cloud.google.com/stackdriver/docs/solutions/slo-monitoring) · [Creating an SLO](https://docs.cloud.google.com/stackdriver/docs/solutions/slo-monitoring/ui/create-slo?hl=en)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are managing an application running on Compute Engine. The application uses a custom HTTP server to expose an API that other applications access through an internal TCP/UDP load balancer. A firewall rule permits access to the API port from `0.0.0.0/0`.  
  
You need to configure Cloud Logging to record every IP address that accesses the API using the fewest steps. What should you do first?

options.text: Enable Packet Mirroring on the VPC.
Install the Ops Agent on the Compute Engine instances.
Enable logging on the firewall rule.
Enable VPC Flow Logs on the subnet.

questions.explanation:
VPC firewall-rule logging writes a connection record to Cloud Logging for traffic allowed or denied by the rule. Each record includes the source and destination IP addresses, protocol, and ports, so enabling logging on the API’s existing allow rule directly records the IP addresses of allowed API connections. VPC Flow Logs are sampled and aggregated, while Packet Mirroring and application-level agent configuration require additional setup.

**Learn more:** [VPC firewall rules logging overview](https://cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/vpc-firewall-rules-logging-overview) · [VPC firewall rules logging format](https://cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/vpc-log-format)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company has bugs, outages, and performance slowness in its production systems. Developers use the production environment to develop new features and fix bugs. Configuration changes and experiments take place in production, causing user outages. Testers also use production for load testing, which frequently slows the production systems.  
  
You need to redesign the environment to reduce production bugs and outages and to allow testers to load test new features. What should you do?

options.text: Create an automated testing script in production to detect failures as soon as they occur.
Create a development environment with smaller server capacity and give access only to developers and testers.
Secure the production environment to ensure that developers can't change it and set up one controlled update per year.
Create a development environment for writing code and a test environment for configurations, experiments, and load testing.

questions.explanation: Development, configuration experiments, and load testing should occur in separate non-production environments before changes are released to production. A development environment isolates code creation and bug fixing, while a test environment supports validation, experiments, and load testing without risking user-facing outages or consuming production capacity.

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You support a high-traffic web application running on Google Cloud Platform (GCP). You must measure application reliability from the user’s perspective without making engineering changes to the application. What should you do? (Choose two.)

options.text: Review current application metrics and add new ones as needed.
Modify the code to capture additional information for user interaction.
Analyze the web proxy logs only and capture response time of each request.
Create new synthetic clients to simulate a user journey using the application.
Use current and historic Request Logs to trace customer interaction with the application.

questions.explanation:
Synthetic monitoring simulates user requests and user journeys, recording success or failure and latency from an external perspective. Existing and historical request logs provide evidence of real customer interactions and request outcomes. Together, these approaches measure both simulated and actual user experience without modifying the application.

**Learn more:** [Synthetic monitoring overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/monitoring/uptime-checks/introduction)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You run a web application that connects to an AlloyDB cluster through a private IP address in your default VPC. Before deploying a new version of the application, you must run a database schema migration from your CI/CD pipeline using Cloud Build. You want to follow Google-recommended security practices. What should you do?

options.text: Set up a Cloud Build private pool to access the database through a static external IP address. Configure the database to only allow connections from this IP address. Execute the schema migration script in the private pool.
Create a service account that has permission to access the database. Configure Cloud Build to use this service account and execute the schema migration script in a private pool.
Add the database username and password to Secret Manager. When running the schema migration script, retrieve the username and password from Secret Manager.
Add the database username and encrypted password to the application configuration file. Use these credentials in Cloud Build to execute the schema migration script.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Build private pools can connect to private resources by using private VPC peering between the pool’s service-producer network and the VPC. Running the build with a dedicated service account that has only the required database-access permissions provides an identity-based, least-privilege access model for the migration.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Build private pools overview](https://cloud.google.com/build/docs/private-pools/private-pools-overview) · [AlloyDB connection overview](https://cloud.google.com/alloydb/docs/connection-overview)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company is implementing supply chain security controls for containerized applications running on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). You need to trace container images used in production back to their source and build processes. The solution must follow Google-recommended practices for software supply chain security. What should you do?

options.text: Store all build artifacts in Artifact Registry, and enable automatic vulnerability scanning.
Enable the Container Analysis API. Configure Cloud Build to use only official base images, and enable automatic vulnerability scanning.
Use Container-Optimized OS for all GKE node pools, enable Binary Authorization in the GKE cluster, and enable automatic security updates.
Enable the Container Analysis API. Configure Cloud Build to generate and sign provenance attestations for each build. Configure Binary Authorization to verify the attestations before deployment.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Build can generate and sign provenance attestations that associate a container image with its trusted build process. Binary Authorization verifies required attestations at deployment time and blocks images that do not meet the policy, providing traceability and enforceable supply-chain integrity for production GKE workloads.

**Learn more:** [Binary Authorization overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/overview) · [Create a Binary Authorization attestation in a Cloud Build pipeline](https://docs.cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/cloud-build)

You recently found that one of your services has exceeded its error budget for the current rolling-window period. Your company’s product team is about to release a new feature. You want to follow Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) practices. What should you do?

options.text: Notify the team about the lack of error budget and ensure that all their tests are successful so the launch will not further risk the error budget
Notify the team that their error budget is used up. Negotiate with the team for a launch freeze or tolerate a slightly worse user experience.
Escalate the situation and request additional error budget.
Look through other metrics related to the product and find SLOs with remaining error budget. Reallocate the error budgets and allow the feature launch.

questions.explanation:
An exhausted error budget indicates that the service has already used the unreliability allowed by its SLO for the measurement window. Error-budget policy is the mechanism for balancing reliability and feature velocity; it calls for prioritizing reliability and negotiating a release freeze or an explicitly accepted reliability tradeoff, rather than reallocating budget or requesting more of it.

**Learn more:** [Google SRE: Example Error Budget Policy](https://sre.google/workbook/error-budget-policy/)
